0.title: The Letter to the Ephesians
0.overview:
Paul wrote this letter from a Roman prison, around AD 60–62, awaiting trial before Caesar. He was chained to a guard. And from that cell he wrote what has often been called the most majestic letter Paul ever penned, a letter that sees so far into the purposes of God, and is so full of praise, that it feels less like a letter and more like a window thrown open onto eternity.

The letter may have been circular: several early manuscripts omit the words “in Ephesus” from 1:1, suggesting it was passed between the churches of Asia Minor. Tychicus carried it personally (6:21). Whether it reached one church or many, it was written for the whole church in every age, including yours.

Did Paul really write it? Many modern scholars think a follower wrote it in his name, pointing to its long sentences and unusual vocabulary, its close overlap with Colossians, and phrases such as his holy apostles and prophets (3:5) that they take to look back on an earlier generation. But the letter names Paul twice (1:1; 3:1), the early church received it as his without dissent, and the differences are well explained by its subject and setting: a letter of praise and teaching rather than controversy, written at the same time as Colossians and carried by the same man (6:21; Col 4:7). A letter claiming to be Paul’s that was not would be a forgery, and the church of that day rejected such letters. The more likely conclusion is that Paul wrote it.

The heartbeat phrase is in Christ, appearing over thirty times. Everything God has done, is doing, and will do for his people is located in the person of his Son. Chosen in him. Redeemed in him. Raised with him. Seated with him. Built together in him. The letter is not primarily about what Christians must do; it is about who Christians already are, and the doing flows from the being.

The grand theme is God’s eternal purpose to unite all things in Christ, things in heaven and things on earth (1:10). The church is not a human institution that God blesses; it stands at the centre of his plan for the whole universe. Through the church God shows his many-sided wisdom to the unseen spiritual powers that are watching (3:10). To be part of this church is to be enrolled in the most significant project in the universe.

The structure is clean and powerful. Chapters 1–3 are facts: what God has done in Christ, from before the world was made until now. Chapters 4–6 are commands: how God’s people now live, in every relationship and every spiritual battle. The hinge is the word “therefore” in 4:1, one of the weightiest words in the letter. The commands always rest on the facts. An adopted child does not help at home to earn a place in the family; he helps because he already has one. We do not obey in order to be accepted; we obey because we already are.

Preach this letter and you will give your congregation the full panorama of God’s saving purpose, from what Father, Son and Spirit planned before creation to the armour for the battle they face this week. There is nothing higher in Paul. There may be nothing higher in Scripture.

1.title: Grace, Election, and Prayer
1.text: <sup>1</sup>Paul, an apostle of Christ Jesus by the will of God, To the saints who are in Ephesus, and are faithful in Christ Jesus: <sup>2</sup>Grace to you and peace from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ. <sup>3</sup>Blessed be the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, who has blessed us in Christ with every spiritual blessing in the heavenly places, <sup>4</sup>even as he chose us in him before the foundation of the world, that we should be holy and blameless before him. In love <sup>5</sup>he predestined us for adoption to himself as sons through Jesus Christ, according to the purpose of his will, <sup>6</sup>to the praise of his glorious grace, with which he has blessed us in the Beloved. <sup>7</sup>In him we have redemption through his blood, the forgiveness of our trespasses, according to the riches of his grace, <sup>8</sup>which he lavished upon us, in all wisdom and insight <sup>9</sup>making known to us the mystery of his will, according to his purpose, which he set forth in Christ <sup>10</sup>as a plan for the fullness of time, to unite all things in Christ, things in heaven and things on earth in him. <sup>11</sup>In him we have obtained an inheritance, having been predestined according to the purpose of him who works all things according to the counsel of his will, <sup>12</sup>so that we who were the first to hope in Christ might be to the praise of his glory. <sup>13</sup>In him you also, when you heard the word of truth, the gospel of your salvation, and believed in him, were sealed with the promised Holy Spirit, <sup>14</sup>who is the guarantee of our inheritance until we acquire possession of it, to the praise of his glory. <sup>15</sup>For this reason, because I have heard of your faith in the Lord Jesus and your love toward all the saints, <sup>16</sup>I do not cease to give thanks for you, remembering you in my prayers, <sup>17</sup>that the God of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Father of glory, may give you the Spirit of wisdom and of revelation in the knowledge of him, <sup>18</sup>having the eyes of your hearts enlightened, that you may know what is the hope to which he has called you, what are the riches of his glorious inheritance in the saints, <sup>19</sup>and what is the immeasurable greatness of his power toward us who believe, according to the working of his great might <sup>20</sup>that he worked in Christ when he raised him from the dead and seated him at his right hand in the heavenly places, <sup>21</sup>far above all rule and authority and power and dominion, and above every name that is named, not only in this age but also in the one to come. <sup>22</sup>And he put all things under his feet and gave him as head over all things to the church, <sup>23</sup>which is his body, the fullness of him who fills all in all.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–14 — Every Spiritual Blessing in Christ
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: After the greeting (vv. 1–2), Paul blesses God for every spiritual blessing in Christ (vv. 3–14). The sentence moves through the Father’s choosing (vv. 4–6), the Son’s redeeming (vv. 7–12) and the Spirit’s sealing (vv. 13–14), each ending in the praise of his glory.
verseByVerse.theology:
Election, Grace, and the Glory of God

God chose his people in Christ before the foundation of the world (v. 4), before they had done anything good or bad (Romans 9:11). God did not choose us because he saw ahead that we would believe. It is the other way round: we believe because he chose us (v. 5).

Its purpose reaches beyond the saved: it is to the praise of his glorious grace (v. 6). In the coming ages God will show in his people the riches of his kindness in Christ (2:7), so that the church is the living evidence that the undeserving can be made heirs.

John Calvin wrote that the knowledge of election is given not to breed pride or speculation but to ground assurance. A believer chosen before the world began, out of God’s free love, has a standing that does not rise and fall with today’s performance.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The Ephesians lived in the shadow of the temple of Artemis, among religions that promised to take people higher through secret ceremonies and secret knowledge. Paul tells them they already have every spiritual blessing, not through ritual or achievement but by being joined to Christ.

Now: Many people today assemble their own spirituality from books, practices and experiences. Ephesians 1 says every spiritual blessing is in Christ. In Christ what the heart most needs is freely and fully given.

verseByVerse.quote: Paul, an apostle of Christ Jesus by the will of God, to the saints who are in Ephesus, and are faithful in Christ Jesus:
verseByVerse.commentary:
Meaning first. Ephesians 1 has two parts. Verses 3–14 are one long outburst of praise, a single sentence in Greek, for what Father, Son and Spirit have given God’s people in Christ. Verses 15–23 turn praise into prayer, that believers would know the hope of their calling and the power that set Christ above every power, as head over all things for the church. The chapter tells believers who they are before the rest of the letter tells them how to live.

Setting and background. Paul writes from prison, probably in Rome about AD 60–62, chained to a soldier (3:1; 4:1; 6:20). Ephesus was the great port of the province of Asia (western Turkey), home of the vast temple of Artemis and famous for magic (Acts 19:19); Paul had spent nearly three years there (Acts 20:31). Most of the believers were Gentiles who had come out of that world of idols, magic and fear of spiritual powers. Much of the letter answers that fear: Christ is above every power (1:21), and his people are safe in him.

Paul, an apostle of Christ Jesus. An apostle (one sent) was an envoy carrying the full authority of the one who sent him. Paul was one of those personally commissioned by the risen Christ to lay the church’s foundation (2:20; Galatians 1:1). His words carry Christ’s authority.

By the will of God. Not a modest disclaimer, but the only explanation for his being an apostle at all. Paul’s apostleship began on a road, with letters in his pocket authorising the arrest of Christians (Acts 9:1–2). He was not recruited from among the interested; he was intercepted mid-crime. A man who talked himself into a ministry can be talked out of it. A man stopped in the road by the risen Christ cannot. In this letter, everything begins with the will of God.

To the saints. Say saint today and people picture an exceptionally good person in a stained-glass window. Paul uses it (hagioi, holy ones) as the ordinary name for every Christian in the city.

Before he finishes he will tell some of these same people to stop stealing (4:28) and lying (4:25). These are the saints. The word is not his verdict on how they are getting on; it is his statement of who owns them. “Holy” means set apart, like a temple bowl, holy not because it was unusually clean but because of whose it was. So it is with you. If you are in Christ, “saint” is not a title you have to earn; it is the name on your post. He did not wait for Saul of Tarsus to become suitable; he took a persecutor and made him a herald, and took idol-worshippers in a city of spells and called them his holy ones.

Faithful in Christ Jesus. “Faithful” here means believing. And in Christ is the key phrase of Ephesians, used about thirty-five times in different forms. It means union with Christ: believers are joined to him, so that what is true of him becomes true of them. Every blessing in this chapter comes in him. A marriage shows how: when a penniless woman married a rich man, his name, his home and his wealth became hers, not because she earned them but because she was joined to him, and Paul uses that very picture of Christ and the church (5:31–32). There are two addresses on this one line: a settled identity in Christ, and a difficult postcode on earth, a city built around the temple of Artemis. Put your own town in place of Ephesus. The letter is written to you at both addresses.

Textual note. Some of the earliest manuscripts (the papyrus known as P46 and the great fourth-century copies Sinaiticus and Vaticanus) omit “in Ephesus”. The letter has no personal greetings, though Paul spent three years there. This commentary’s view: probably a circular letter to the churches of Asia, carried by Tychicus (6:21), with Ephesus as its chief destination. This does not lessen its authority; it widens its reach.

Where Christians differ: did Paul write it? Many modern scholars think a follower wrote it, citing its style and its overlap with Colossians. This commentary’s view: Paul is the author. The style really is different, with long, piled-up sentences and some unusual words, and honest readers feel the question. But the letter claims Paul twice (1:1; 3:1) and speaks of his chains and his messenger (6:20–21), the early church received it without dispute, and its differences fit a letter of praise written at the same time as Colossians.

What it does not mean. Calling every believer a saint does not mean that how we live does not matter. Paul will spend half the letter calling saints to live like saints (4:1). But the order is everything: first who you are, then how to live.
verseByVerse.note: Paul wrote from prison, probably in Rome around AD 60–62. The ESV notes that some early manuscripts omit “in Ephesus”; the letter may have been meant to circulate among several churches of the region.

verseByVerse.quote: Grace to you and peace from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Grace to you. Paul bends the ordinary Greek greeting, chairein, into a word that sounds like it and means far more: charis, God’s free favour to people who have earned only its reverse (2:8–9).

And peace. Eirēnē translates the Hebrew shalom, the Jewish greeting. So a Greek word and a Jewish word stand together in one breath, as Jew and Gentile will in chapter 2 (2:14–16).

Shalom is not a mood but wholeness, everything in its right relation and working as it was made to work. That is why a Christian can have it in a hospital bed, and a man can be entirely without it on a beach. The question is whether the central relationship of your life is in order: first peace with God, since we were once under his wrath (2:3), and then peace between people once divided (2:14–17).

Peace with a name. Paul does not leave peace as an idea. In the next chapter he gives it a name: “he himself is our peace” (2:14). Aaron’s blessing ended with the LORD giving Israel peace (Numbers 6:26), and that peace came in a person, the Prince of Peace (Isaiah 9:6). It was not a kind wish. It was bought: he made peace by the blood of his cross (Colossians 1:20). The grace is his favour, freely given; the peace is his finished work, made at Calvary and never to be unmade.

The order. In every greeting Paul wrote, grace comes first and peace last (the letters to Timothy put mercy between them), never reversed, because one produces the other. Many people want peace without grace, and would rather reach it by managing their lives well enough to deserve it. It cannot be done in that direction. Peace is the state of a person against whom nothing is any longer held, and only grace can produce that. Having been justified by faith, that is, declared right with God, we have peace with God (Romans 5:1). First the gift, then the quiet.

From God our Father. One source, two persons. Paul puts Jesus beside the Father as the giver of the gifts only God can give, something no Jew would ever say of a mere man: a quiet witness to Christ’s deity, two verses into the letter. And our: an apostle and a congregation of former idolaters and thieves address the same Father in the same sentence.

What it does not mean. Not a polite formula. There is no verb in the Greek: it is closer to a blessing pronounced over them.

verseByVerse.quote: Blessed be the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, who has blessed us in Christ with every spiritual blessing in the heavenly places.
verseByVerse.commentary:
One great sentence. Verses 3–14 are one sentence in Greek, by a man so caught up in praise that he cannot find a place to stop. It is shaped by the Trinity: the Father chooses and adopts (vv. 4–6), the Son redeems (vv. 7–12), the Spirit seals (vv. 13–14). Three times it ends with the same refrain, to the praise of his glory (vv. 6, 12, 14).

Blessed be God … who has blessed us. To bless (eulogeō, to speak well of) means two things. When we bless God, we add nothing to him; our blessing is praise. When God speaks good over someone, he does good to them, giving the very thing it names (Genesis 1:28). So the sentence swings on a hinge: we bless God with our lips because he has first blessed us with his hand.

The God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ. God is named here by his Son: we know him truly only as the Father of Jesus. And the blessing comes in Christ because it was his before it was ours. The blessings that follow, chosen, beloved, heir, anointed with the Spirit, belong first to the Son, and reach us only because we are joined to him. But for sinners a curse stood in the way: God’s law pronounces a curse, his just sentence, on everyone who breaks it. Paul says how it was moved: Christ redeemed us from the curse by becoming a curse for us, so that in Christ Jesus the blessing of Abraham might come to the Gentiles (Galatians 3:13–14). The hand that blesses us is the hand that laid our curse on his Son.

Every spiritual blessing. Every: the whole treasury; a believer is not waiting for some further blessing to make him complete in Christ. And spiritual does not mean wispy or unreal; it means given and applied by the Holy Spirit (v. 13). Your salary is temporary and your health is on loan; your adoption is not.

In common speech a blessing is a circumstance that has gone well: the promotion, the clean scan. But the man writing is in chains; his readers include slaves, and Christians in their province would soon die for the name (Revelation 2:13). If blessing meant circumstances going well, Paul would be an unblessed man writing to unblessed people about how blessed they are. In the list that follows, not one item is a circumstance. Not one can be lost in a redundancy, a diagnosis or a bad year.

In the heavenly places. The phrase appears five times in Ephesians and nowhere else in Paul. It cannot simply mean heaven as the home of the redeemed, because in 6:12 Paul places the spiritual forces of evil there. It means the unseen realm of spiritual reality, immediately behind everything we can see. Read the five in order: the treasury of blessing (1:3), Christ’s throne (1:20), your seat with him (2:6), the watching powers (3:10) and the battlefield (6:12): five things that shape your life, all in a realm you have never seen.

For the Ephesians, who had spent their lives and money managing unseen powers with amulets and spells, this was no abstraction. Paul tells them who is enthroned there, and that they are seated with him above everything they used to fear. Yet a letter that begins this high ends at home, with husbands and wives, children and daily work (5:22–6:9). Knowing where the throne is does not lift you out of your Tuesday; it tells you who is over it.

Has blessed. Past tense: already given, though much is still to be enjoyed in full (vv. 14, 18). Asking God for good things is right (Matthew 7:11); but the prayer “Lord, bless me”, offered as though the cupboard were bare, misunderstands where we are standing. The Christian is not a beggar hoping the door will open; he is an heir who has not yet read the inventory. Paul opens the inventory in the next eleven verses.

What it does not mean. Not a promise of earthly comfort, health or wealth. The prisoner who wrote it had none of those. And not that the blessings are vague: the Spirit is not only the one who delivers them, he is himself the down payment of them (v. 14). The Giver has moved in with the gift.

In everyday life. When someone asks how you are on a bad day, you may say honestly that the day is hard, and that you are blessed. Both are true, and the second is the deeper one.
verseByVerse.note: Verses 3–14 are a single long sentence of praise in the Greek. “The heavenly places” is the unseen realm where Christ reigns.

verseByVerse.quote: Even as he chose us in him before the foundation of the world, that we should be holy and blameless before him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Even as he chose us. “Even as” ties this to the last verse: here is the first blessing, which explains all the others. The Greek verb means chose for himself: God picked out a people to be his own. This is election, God’s free decision to save particular people, and it is personal: us.

In him. Election is never apart from Christ. Christ is himself the Chosen One: “Behold my servant, whom I uphold, my chosen, in whom my soul delights” (Isaiah 42:1). God chose a people in his Son, as their head and Saviour, so that his standing becomes theirs. That changes where you must look for assurance. The question “am I chosen?” is not answered by peering back into eternity, where you were never invited and cannot see. It is answered by looking at Christ: all whom the Father gives him will come to him, and whoever comes to him he will never cast out (John 6:37).

Before the foundation of the world. Before the light was made, there was nothing about you for God’s love to be based on: no faith, no obedience, not even existence (Romans 9:11; 2 Timothy 1:9). That is the most secure thing that could be said about it. A love that began before you were anything cannot be ended by your turning out to be something disappointing. Your worst week did not alter the basis of it, because the basis was never you.

Holy and blameless before him. “Blameless” is the word for a sacrifice without blemish. This is the purpose of election: God chose us for holiness, not because of it. And before him: not before our neighbours, who grade on a curve, but before the God at whose holiness the seraphim cover their faces (Isaiah 6:2–5). Does Paul mean sinless perfection? He means two things at once. Now, in Christ, you are already counted holy and blameless in God’s sight, not on your record but clothed in Christ’s (Colossians 1:22). God does not pretend you have never sinned; he credits you with his Son’s perfect record (2 Corinthians 5:21). And one day God will finish what he began, presenting you without fault before his glory (5:27; Jude 24). The standing gives you your footing; the goal gives you your direction. So the believer who sinned badly this week does not come back to God with a smaller holiness, because it was never measured by this week. That is not permission to sin (Romans 6:1–2); it is the mercy that makes repentance possible.

Where Christians differ: why did God choose? Arminian Christians, a large Protestant tradition that includes most Methodists and many evangelicals, hold that God chose those he foresaw would believe (citing Romans 8:29; 1 Peter 1:2); they hold it out of a real concern for God’s fairness and for human responsibility, and they love Christ as truly as anyone. This commentary’s view: unconditional election (Westminster Confession 3.5; 1689 London Baptist Confession 3.5): God’s choice rested on no condition he saw in us. Paul roots the choice in God’s love, will and purpose (vv. 5, 9, 11), never in anything foreseen in us; and he says we were chosen to be holy, which would make no sense if God chose us because he foresaw our holiness. Faith is the result of election (Acts 13:48), not its cause. Is it unfair? The question assumes we were owed a choosing, and we were not. Left to justice, every one of us would be passed by (Romans 3:23). The wonder of this verse is not that some are not chosen, but that any are: that grace should reach into a mass of the justly condemned and lift out a people who deserved what the rest received. No one perishes who wanted Christ and was refused.

Where Christians differ: chosen as individuals, or as a group? Some (following Karl Barth, and some Arminian scholars) hold that God chose Christ, and that the church is elect only as a group, in him; individuals become elect when they join themselves to Christ by faith. This commentary’s view: God did choose a people, the church, and he chose them in Christ; but the people are made up of persons. Paul says he chose us, and v. 5 says he predestined us for adoption, which is personal. Elsewhere election is clearly of individuals: Jacob, not Esau (Romans 9:11–13); names written in the book of life (Revelation 13:8). The group and the individual belong together.

Common questions. If God has chosen, why preach the gospel? Because God chose the means as well as the end: the chosen come to faith through hearing the gospel (v. 13; Romans 10:14). Election is the reason mission cannot fail: “I have many in this city who are my people” (Acts 18:9–10). What about my own choice? Scripture holds both: the letter that says you were chosen pleads with you to walk worthy of your calling (4:1). You heard and believed, and your believing was truly your own (v. 13); God’s rule over all things runs underneath your choice, not instead of it. How the two fit together is deeper than we are able to see, and God has not told us (Deuteronomy 29:29; Romans 9:20). How can I know I am chosen? Not by looking for a secret sign, but by trusting Christ and seeing the fruit of holiness he produces (1 Thessalonians 1:4–5; 2 Peter 1:10).

Is there any point praying for my unbelieving son or daughter, if God has already chosen? Yes, every point. The God who chose the end also chose the means, and prayer is one of them. No one believed in election more firmly than Paul, and he wrote that his heart’s desire and prayer to God was for his unbelieving people to be saved (Romans 10:1). Election does not make your prayers pointless; it makes them hopeful, because you are not asking God to overcome a will he cannot reach. You are asking the God who raises the dead (2:5) to do the very thing he delights to do. You do not know who is chosen, and you are not meant to. So pray by name, keep loving, keep speaking of Christ, and leave the timing with him. Augustine’s mother prayed for him for years before he was converted.

Textual note. “In love” may end verse 4 (holy and blameless in love) or begin verse 5 (in love he predestined us). The ESV links it with verse 5, which fits Paul’s stress on God’s motive.

What it does not mean. Not fatalism, as if it does not matter what we do. Nor a reason for pride: election leaves no room for boasting (2:9). And it is not given to make anyone anxious. Scripture teaches it to comfort believers that their salvation rests on God, not on themselves.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that “in love” may go with verse 4: “holy and blameless before him in love.”

verseByVerse.quote: In love he predestined us for adoption to himself as sons through Jesus Christ, according to the purpose of his will.
verseByVerse.commentary:
In love. The motive behind election is not cold decree but love. Predestination is the Father’s affectionate purpose to have children.

He predestined us. “Predestined” is marked out beforehand (our word horizon shares the root). Election (v. 4) is God choosing whom; predestination is God deciding what he would make of them, and here Paul names it: his children. In Scripture, predestination is almost always spoken of to comfort believers about their destiny, not to make them speculate about others.

Did God also predestine some people to hell? Scripture speaks of the two very differently, and so must we. Those God saves, he actively chose, predestined and brought to life; their salvation is entirely his work. Those who are lost, God passed by, leaving them in the sin they love, and they are condemned for their sin, never for want of being chosen (Westminster Confession 3.7). No one in hell will be able to say that he wanted Christ and was kept from him. Paul marks the difference even in his wording: God himself prepared the vessels of mercy beforehand for glory, while the vessels of wrath are simply said to be prepared for destruction (Romans 9:22–23). God takes no pleasure in the death of the wicked (Ezekiel 33:11), and the gospel is offered freely to all. The question for you is not what God decreed about others, but whether you will come to Christ today.

Adoption as sons. “Adoption” (placing as a son) was a Roman legal act: a new father and name, old debts cancelled, full rights of inheritance, and it could not be undone. We were by nature children of wrath (2:3), outsiders; God brings us into his family as heirs (Galatians 4:4–7; Romans 8:15–17). In that world sons inherited, and every believer, man or woman, receives the full inheritance of a son (Galatians 3:26–28), and belongs to himself.

Why adoption, and not only forgiveness? God could have pardoned us and left us as forgiven servants, standing at the kitchen door. Instead he makes us his children, seated at his table. Forgiveness deals with our guilt; adoption gives us a Father, a family, a home and an inheritance. The Westminster Shorter Catechism (Q. 34) calls it an act of God’s free grace, whereby we are received into the number, and have a right to all the privileges, of the sons of God. The Judge who acquits us steps down from the bench and takes us home.

Through Jesus Christ. God has one eternal Son by nature; we become children by grace, by being joined to him. Paul says how it was carried out: “when the fullness of time had come, God sent forth his Son, born of woman, born under the law, to redeem those who were under the law, so that we might receive adoption as sons” (Galatians 4:4–5). He took our place outside, under the law and its curse, so that we could take his place inside, at the Father’s table. Even the word Abba, which Jesus prayed in Gethsemane (Mark 14:36), is now ours to pray.

According to the purpose of his will. Literally the good pleasure of his will: nothing outside God moved him to it, and that is why it is permanent. A choice that rested on something in us could be undone by something in us. This rests on his good pleasure alone.

What it does not mean. Not that all people are God’s children in this sense. All are his creatures and his offspring as their Creator (Acts 17:28), but adoption comes through Christ, received by faith (John 1:12).
verseByVerse.note: In Roman law an adopted son received the full rights and inheritance of a natural son.

verseByVerse.quote: To the praise of his glorious grace, with which he has blessed us in the Beloved.
verseByVerse.commentary:
To the praise of his glorious grace. The first of three refrains (vv. 6, 12, 14), each closing the work of one person of the Trinity. Salvation has a goal beyond the saved: that God’s grace be seen and celebrated.

Is that not vanity? A modern reader feels the question even if he never asks it aloud. We do not admire a man who arranges every conversation to end in applause for himself. Why is it admirable in God? C. S. Lewis was troubled by exactly this, and what opened it for him was noticing what praise actually is. We spontaneously praise whatever we enjoy, a piece of music, a landscape, a friend’s cooking, not because we have been asked to, but because delight overflows into speech. The enjoyment is not complete until it is spoken: the finest view is only half enjoyed until you say to someone, “Look at that.” Praise is not payment extracted from us; it is enjoyment reaching its full form. Now put that together with who God is. If there is a being of infinite goodness, then calling creatures to praise him is not vanity but honesty, telling them the truth about the most valuable thing there is. And it is kindness, because it points them to their own deepest joy. A father who tells his son to come and look at the sunrise is not fishing for compliments on his taste. He wants the boy to see it.

He has blessed us. Literally which he graced us with, a verb used only once elsewhere in the New Testament, by Gabriel to a girl in Nazareth: greetings, O favoured one (Luke 1:28). She had done nothing to deserve it; she was simply the object of God’s free favour, and the whole course of her life ran from that word. Paul uses it of dockworkers and slaves in Ephesus. In this one respect, being singled out by sheer favour, what was true of Mary is true of you.

In the Beloved. Paul could have said “in Christ” again. He chooses instead the title the Father spoke from heaven over his Son: “This is my beloved Son” (Matthew 3:17). That means the love that falls on you is not a second-class affection God worked up for sinners as a separate exercise. You are inside the Beloved, and so the love that has always passed between the Father and the Son runs over you too. It is exactly what Jesus prayed on the last night: “that the world may know that you sent me and loved them even as you loved me” (John 17:23). Not somewhat as you loved me. Even as.
verseByVerse.note: “The Beloved” is Christ, echoing the Father’s voice at his baptism.

verseByVerse.quote: In him we have redemption through his blood, the forgiveness of our trespasses, according to the riches of his grace.
verseByVerse.commentary:
In him we have redemption. The verb is present tense: a possession now, held on the worst day of your life as securely as on the best. “Redemption” (release by payment of a ransom) is the language of the slave market and of the exodus. A slave cannot buy himself; someone else pays the price, and he walks out having contributed nothing but his chains. In Egypt on the last night, what stands between a household and the destroyer is not their record or their remorse but blood on a doorpost (Exodus 12). In both scenes the freedom is real, total, and entirely someone else’s doing.

Through his blood. “Blood” means his life given in a violent, sacrificial death (Leviticus 17:11). The price was not silver or gold, but the precious blood of Christ, like that of a lamb without blemish (1 Peter 1:18–19).

Why blood? Why can God not simply forgive? To a modern ear blood sounds primitive, and the question underneath is fair: he tells us to forgive freely; why does he require a death before he does it himself? The answer is that nobody ever forgives a real wrong without cost. Suppose someone smashes something of yours. There are only two possibilities. He pays, and then nothing has been forgiven; it has been settled. Or you forgive him, which means you absorb the loss: the thing stays broken and you carry it. There is no third option in which the damage simply evaporates. That is why forgiving a real injury hurts, and why we find it so hard: to forgive is to agree to bear the cost yourself instead of taking it from the one who caused it. So when God forgives, he is not shrugging off a small debt. Real wrong has been done to a holy God by every one of us, and it has to go somewhere. A God who ignored it would not be gracious but indifferent, and a judge who dismissed every case would not be loving but corrupt. What this verse says is that God did what every true forgiver does, at a scale beyond measuring: he absorbed it himself. The blood is the measure of what it cost him.

The forgiveness of our trespasses. “Forgiveness” is sending away; “trespasses” are false steps, plural and particular. The account that was cancelled had your name at the top and your own specific items listed beneath it, including the one you have never told anyone, and the one you did again last week. Those. Paid for, by blood, and gone.

If I am forgiven, why do I still feel guilty? Because feelings are slow to catch up with facts, and because you have an accuser who works on them (Revelation 12:10). First, ask whether the guilt is pointing at something specific you have not yet brought to God or put right with someone. If so, confess it plainly, and where you have wronged a person, go to them; God is faithful and just to forgive those who confess (1 John 1:9). If the sin is already confessed, the guilt is not God’s voice but an echo, and the answer is not more penance but the cross. For those who are in Christ Jesus, Paul says, there is now no condemnation at all (Romans 8:1). Tell yourself what is true: Christ died for that sin, God has sent it away, and he does not bring it up again. If the feeling will not lift, talk to your pastor. Sometimes the gospel needs a friend to say it aloud.

Where Christians differ: how does the cross save? Some modern writers deny that Christ’s death was a substitute bearing our penalty, seeing it only as an example of love or a victory over evil. This commentary’s view: penal substitution is central to the atonement: Christ bore the punishment our sins deserved, in our place. Scripture joins blood, redemption and forgiveness: a price paid, a penalty borne (Romans 3:24–25; Galatians 3:13; Hebrews 9:22). His victory over evil (Colossians 2:15) and his example of love (5:2) belong with it, not instead of it.

The riches of his grace. Not measured by our need but by his wealth, proportioned to the riches of God himself. No sin is too great for riches like these.

In everyday life. The letter will ask you to forgive as God in Christ forgave you (4:32), which means bearing the cost of a wrong instead of passing it on. Is there a debt someone owes you that you could carry today?
verseByVerse.note: Redemption was the word for buying a slave’s freedom.

verseByVerse.quote: Which he lavished upon us, in all wisdom and insight.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Lavished. Made to overflow: God did not measure out grace carefully. He poured. How like God to pour where we would have measured.

In all wisdom and insight. “Wisdom” is the deep grasp of how things truly are; “insight” is its practical cousin. One sees; the other knows what to do on Monday morning.

Whose wisdom? It may describe God’s wisdom in planning salvation, or the wisdom he gives us to understand it. Probably the second. The nearest parallel prays that believers may be “filled with the knowledge of his will in all spiritual wisdom and understanding” (Colossians 1:9); Paul prays for this very wisdom a few verses later (v. 17); and the sentence runs straight on, “making known to us the mystery of his will” (v. 9). A mystery cannot be made known to someone who has not been given the eyes to receive it. Nothing is lost if a reader takes it the other way, for God’s plan is supremely wise (3:10). But the point is this: the grace that saves you does not rescue you and then leave you baffled about what has happened. He gives the gift, and then he gives the eyes to see the gift. That is why this letter can spend three chapters on the eternal purposes of God and still expect ordinary believers in Ephesus to follow every word.

Wisdom with a face. Christ Jesus became to us wisdom from God (1 Corinthians 1:30). So the wisdom poured out on us is not a technique for success but the knowledge of a crucified Messiah, which looked like folly to Greeks and weakness to Jews, and turned out to be the very wisdom by which God saves (1 Corinthians 1:23–24). To be given wisdom is to be given eyes to see Christ, and in him to see everything else rightly, from your sins to your sufferings.

verseByVerse.quote: making known to us the mystery of his will, according to his purpose, which he set forth in Christ as a plan for the fullness of time, to unite all things in Christ, things in heaven and things on earth in him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The mystery of his will. In Paul a mystery is not a puzzle or something unknowable, but a truth once hidden in God and now revealed (3:3–6; Romans 16:25–26).

Set forth in Christ. Christ is the centre of God’s plan from the beginning. History was planned around him.

A plan for the fullness of time. “Plan” is oikonomia, household management (hence economy). A good steward of a great house knows what is to happen in every room and when; nothing is left to chance. God runs history like that. “The fullness of time” is the moment history reaches its goal. It began with Christ’s coming (Galatians 4:4) and will be completed at his return.

To unite all things in him. One long Greek verb, meaning to sum up, as a column of figures is added into one total, or to gather under one head (in v. 22 Christ is called the head). Sin broke the universe apart. It separated people from God and from each other (Jews and Gentiles in chapter 2). It left creation spoiled and groaning (Romans 8:20–22), and spiritual powers in rebellion. God’s plan is to bring it all back into order under its true head. And all things, not only all people: salvation is not only the rescue of souls out of a ruined world but the restoration of everything to its right relation with Christ. The material creation is not discarded but renewed (Revelation 21:1–5).

What would it look like? Let it come down to the ground. A world under one head is a world where the ground no longer throws up thorns and the body no longer grows tumours; where there are no funerals, because there is nothing left to bury. A world with no armies, because there is nothing left to defend against; where families are not quietly divided by something said twenty years ago. A world in which you are no longer divided against yourself, where the person you want to be and the person you are have at last become the same (Romans 7:19). And a world where heaven and earth are no longer two addresses. Now we pray, “your will be done, on earth as it is in heaven” (Matthew 6:10), a prayer that admits a gap. Then the gap closes: “Behold, the dwelling place of God is with man” (Revelation 21:3). And nothing good is lost on the way: the glory and honour of the nations are brought into it (Revelation 21:24–26). Everything you have ever loved is kept; everything that spoiled it is gone. That homesickness you feel under the best music and the worst news, for a world that holds together, is not a defect in you. It is the memory of what the world was made for, and Paul gives it a name: not a system or a golden age, but a Person, under whom everything finally fits.

The thesis of the letter. Verse 10 is the summit of verses 3–14, and the letter unfolds it: one new people of Jew and Gentile (2:14–16), the body growing under its head (4:13–16), marriage and work (5:22–6:9), and rebel powers fighting a war already lost (6:10–12).

Already, and not yet. God’s plan has truly begun, but it is not yet finished. Already, Christ has been raised and seated above every power (1:20–22), and the powers were disarmed at the cross (Colossians 2:15). When a Jew and a Gentile sat down at one table in Ephesus, that was the future arriving early (2:14–16; 3:10). Not yet: “At present, we do not yet see everything in subjection to him.” But we see him, Jesus (Hebrews 2:8–9). That is the honest Christian position, and it is enough to go on with.

Things in heaven and things on earth. Ever since the first sin, rivals have set up their thrones in God’s world. When all things are brought under Christ, every one of them ends, until every knee bows and every tongue confesses that Jesus Christ is Lord, to the glory of God the Father (Philippians 2:10–11). What a Saviour, that the universe should find its meaning in the one who was crucified outside a city wall. And what a God, that he should tell us his secret, letting sinners in on the purpose of the ages before it is complete, so that we may begin the praise now that creation will one day sing together. That is why the refrain keeps returning: “to the praise of his glory”.

Where Christians differ: will everyone and everything finally be saved? Some, from Origen in the third century to modern universalists, read uniting all things as a promise that every person, and in some versions even the devil and fallen angels, will finally be reconciled to God. This commentary’s view: no. To unite under one head means to bring everything under Christ’s rule, not that everything will be saved. In the same letter Paul warns that the immoral have no inheritance in the kingdom and that God’s wrath comes on the disobedient (5:5–6). Some will bow in joyful worship, and others in defeat (1 Corinthians 15:24–28; Philippians 2:10–11). Everything will be put in order; not everything will be saved.

In everyday life. Your fractured world, family, nation or church, has a future in Christ. Every genuine reconciliation you work for now is a small patch of that future showing through.
verseByVerse.note: A “mystery” is something once hidden and now revealed by God.

verseByVerse.quote: In him we have obtained an inheritance, having been predestined according to the purpose of him who works all things according to the counsel of his will, so that we who were the first to hope in Christ might be to the praise of his glory.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Obtained an inheritance. Everything in this sentence hangs on two words: “in him”. “Obtained an inheritance” (were allotted a share) recalls the land being divided by lot among Israel’s tribes (Joshua 14:1–2). The Greek can mean we were given an inheritance, or we were made God’s inheritance. Both are true (v. 18; Deuteronomy 32:9).

God himself is the portion. When the land was divided, the other tribes walked away holding a map. Levi was handed nothing, and God explained: “I am your portion and your inheritance among the people of Israel” (Numbers 18:20; Deuteronomy 10:9). The other tribes were given things God had made. Levi was given God. Test it on yourself. Suppose you were given everything you have ever wanted, your health back, every broken relationship mended, the people you have buried returned, and God himself were not there. Would that be heaven? “Whom have I in heaven but you? And there is nothing on earth that I desire besides you” (Psalm 73:25). Everything else you own can be taken by a diagnosis, a market, a war, or simply time. A portion that is God cannot be repossessed.

And the glory to come. The inheritance has real content. A body, raised imperishable and made like his glorious body (1 Corinthians 15:42–44; Philippians 3:21). A world: new heavens and a new earth, which the meek will inherit (Matthew 5:5; Revelation 21:1–5). A face: “They will see his face” (Revelation 22:4), the one thing Moses asked for and was not given. A likeness: “we shall be like him, because we shall see him as he is” (1 John 3:2). And the measure of it all: we are “heirs of God and fellow heirs with Christ” (Romans 8:17). Whatever belongs to the Son is being settled on you.

The Heir who was killed. The inheritance is ours only because it was first Christ’s: God appointed his Son the heir of all things (Hebrews 1:2). Jesus told of tenants who saw the owner’s son coming and said, “This is the heir. Come, let us kill him, and the inheritance will be ours” (Mark 12:7). Men tried to take the inheritance by killing the Heir; God gives it by the same death. A will takes effect only when the one who made it has died, and Christ died so that “those who are called may receive the promised eternal inheritance” (Hebrews 9:15–17). What the tenants tried to steal, the Son leaves to his people in his will.

Having been predestined. The main verb is past: we have obtained. Your share has already been assigned to you; it only waits to be handed over.

Who works all things. God is not reacting to history; he is carrying it out, every event, according to his own wise decision (Romans 8:28; Proverbs 16:33). And the God who works all things is the one who carries out the will that promised you the inheritance. Nothing can stop him handing it over. That is also rest for the heart that must control everything. The person who has to hold every outcome in his own hands lies awake, because he is trying to do God’s job; the believer may plan carefully and then sleep, because the outcome was never his to hold (Psalm 127:2).

Where Christians differ: does God govern all things, or only some? Many Christians hold that God sets the overall direction of history but leaves most events to human free choices, which he foresees and responds to. Open theists go further and say God does not know free choices in advance. This commentary’s view: Paul says God works all things according to his will: not most things, not the big things only. Scripture shows God governing the fall of a sparrow (Matthew 10:29), the casting of lots (Proverbs 16:33), the decisions of kings (Proverbs 21:1) and even the wicked acts that crucified Christ (Acts 2:23; 4:27–28). This does not make human choices unreal. Joseph’s brothers chose freely and sinned, and God meant it for good (Genesis 50:20). God works through our choices, not around them; how both are true is beyond us, but Scripture teaches both, and the cross proves them both at once. It is the deepest comfort a believer has: nothing in your life is outside his purpose.

The first to hope. Probably Jewish believers, Paul included, who had hoped for the Messiah and believed in Jesus first; verse 13 then turns to “you also”, the Gentiles, and the two are brought together in one people (2:11–22). Their hope too is “to the praise of his glory”, the second refrain.

What it does not mean. Not that God is the author of sin. He governs evil without doing evil or approving it, and turns it to good, as at the cross (Genesis 50:20; Acts 2:23). Every person remains responsible for what he chooses (James 1:13).

verseByVerse.quote: In him you also, when you heard the word of truth, the gospel of your salvation, and believed in him, were sealed with the promised Holy Spirit, who is the guarantee of our inheritance until we acquire possession of it, to the praise of his glory.
verseByVerse.commentary:
In him you also. Now the Gentiles share fully in everything just described (2:11–22).

When you heard … and believed. This is how God’s eternal choice becomes real in history: through ordinary preaching and real faith (Romans 10:14–17). Election never bypasses the gospel; it works through it. You heard, you believed, you were sealed: one moment, not three stages.

Were sealed. On the dock at Ephesus a merchant pressed his signet ring into hot wax across the bindings of his cargo, and every man on the quay could read the mark. This is mine: hands off. This is genuine: not a substitute swapped in on the way. And this is protected: to break that seal is to answer to the man whose ring made the mark. God’s seal is not wax but a Person, the Holy Spirit. In plain words: God marks you as his own, genuine and protected, by coming to live in you himself. That is his answer to the question of whether you will arrive safely (4:30).

With the promised Holy Spirit. Promised by the prophets (Ezekiel 36:26–27) and poured out by the exalted Christ (Acts 2:33). And it is the seal he first bore himself. “On him God the Father has set his seal,” Jesus said (John 6:27), and at the Jordan the Spirit came down on him as the Father named him his beloved Son (Matthew 3:16–17). You are sealed because you are in the Sealed One, and the mark says of you what it said of him: this one is mine.

Who is the guarantee of our inheritance. “Guarantee” (arrabōn) was a down payment, the first instalment of the very same thing, committing the giver to the rest. So what you have of the Spirit now is not a lesser thing than heaven; it is heaven’s first payment, in heaven’s own currency. The peace that came when nothing in your circumstances explained it, the joy that caught you in a hymn, the love you find you have for people you would never have chosen: that is the inheritance, in instalments. It also explains why the Christian life aches. You hold the deposit, not the estate, and the deposit was designed to make you homesick. A man with an engagement ring is not less eager for the wedding than a man without one; he is far more eager, and far more certain.

Until we acquire possession of it. Until God fully takes possession of his people at the resurrection. And note who would lose if that day never came: the one who paid the deposit. God has put down a pledge he does not intend to forfeit.

To the praise of his glory. The third refrain. Father, Son and Spirit have each done their part in the one salvation, and each part ends in the same song.

Where Christians differ: when are believers sealed? Some Pentecostal teaching, and some Reformed writers such as Martyn Lloyd-Jones, treat the sealing as a further experience after conversion, an overwhelming assurance to be sought. They read it out of a real hunger for more of God, which is nothing to despise. This commentary’s view: the text ties it to believing: having heard and believed, you were sealed. The Greek participle describes what happened together with believing, not a later stage. Every believer is sealed with the Spirit at conversion (Romans 8:9). Believers may still seek to be filled afresh (5:18), and God may give special seasons of assurance; but no Christian is unsealed. You can check it, not by hunting for a feeling, but by looking for the marks the Spirit leaves: that you call God Father and mean it (Romans 8:15–16), that sin now grieves you, that Christ has become precious to you and not merely true.

Where Christians differ: can a sealed believer be lost? Those who hold that true believers can finally fall away read the seal as a mark that can be broken, and point to the warnings of Hebrews (Hebrews 6:4–6). Those warnings are real and must be heard. This commentary’s view: the seal is God’s, set until the day of redemption (4:30), and the guarantee pledges the full inheritance. A pledge God gives is not withdrawn. Jesus says of his sheep, they will never perish, and no one will snatch them out of my hand (John 10:28). Those who abandon Christ show they were never truly his (1 John 2:19); the warnings are among the means God uses to keep the people he has sealed. So if you are afraid you are drifting, take that fear as the seal at work, not as its breaking: those who have truly let go of Christ do not lie awake over it.
verseByVerse.note: A seal marked ownership and security. The “guarantee” was a first instalment, pledging full payment later.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul thanks God for their faith and love and prays that the Father of glory will give them the Spirit of wisdom and revelation to know him (vv. 15–17). He asks that the eyes of their hearts be opened to the hope of his calling, the riches of his inheritance in his people, and the power that raised Christ and made him head over all things for the church (vv. 18–23).
verseByVerse.theology:
The Spirit of Wisdom and Revelation

Paul prays for the Spirit of wisdom and of revelation in the knowledge of God (v. 17). The Spirit who inspired Scripture is also needed to give light to its reader. Calvin devoted a famous section of the Institutes to this: Scripture needs no outside proof of its authority, because the Spirit who produced it also produces certainty of it in the believer’s heart.

So Bible reading and prayer belong together. The Puritans habitually prayed for light before they opened the book, because the eyes of the heart do not open themselves. Paul’s prayer for the Ephesians is a prayer every reader of Scripture can pray.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Paul writes this prayer from prison. He cannot visit the Ephesians, but he can pray, and he prays not for his own release but for their understanding.

Now: We have more sermons, commentaries and Bible apps than any generation before us, and we still need what the Ephesians needed: not more content but opened eyes, the Spirit who makes the word alive.

verseByVerse.quote: For this reason, because I have heard of your faith in the Lord Jesus and your love toward all the saints, I do not cease to give thanks for you, remembering you in my prayers,
verseByVerse.commentary:
For this reason. Because of everything in vv. 3–14, Paul falls to his knees. Knowing God’s purposes does not make prayer unnecessary; it gives prayer its confidence. This is the first of the letter’s two prayers (the second is 3:14–21), and both come before a single command (4:1), because Christians obey best when they know what they have.

Because I have heard. Paul is under guard in Rome (Acts 28:16, 20) and may never see these people again. He cannot get to them, so he carries them to God. Prison did not reduce his ministry to prayer; it showed that prayer had always been the larger half of it. Your quiet faith may be reported somewhere too, to people you will never meet.

Faith and love. The two marks of genuine Christianity, always together: trust towards Christ and love towards his people. Faith looks up to Christ; love looks sideways at the people he died for and calls them family (Galatians 5:6; 1 John 3:14). And all: Jews and Gentiles raised to regard each other as unclean now passed the same cup. Not warmth towards the agreeable, but love towards the whole awkward set of them, the only kind that proves anything. The Lord Jesus, who once prayed for all who would believe through his apostles’ word (John 17:20), was answering that prayer in a port city of idols.

Textual note. Some early manuscripts omit “your love”, reading “faith … toward all the saints”. The longer text is probably original (compare Colossians 1:4).

I do not cease to give thanks. Paul thanks God, not the believers, for their faith and love, because these are God’s gifts. He has plenty to correct, but the first thing he says about this church is gratitude for what God has already done in them.

A prisoner who prays, and a Priest who never stops. Behind Paul’s prayer stands a greater one. Israel’s high priest went into the Holy Place with the names of the twelve tribes engraved on his breastpiece, bearing them on his heart before the LORD (Exodus 28:29). Christ is the high priest that picture promised, and he always lives to make intercession for those who draw near to God through him (Hebrews 7:25). Paul prayed when news reached him; Christ never waits for news, and carries every one of his people on his heart, without a break, for ever.

In everyday life. Think of a Christian, or a church, with a long way still to go. Thank God for what he has already done in them, and then tell them.

verseByVerse.quote: That the God of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Father of glory, may give you the Spirit of wisdom and of revelation in the knowledge of him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The God of our Lord Jesus Christ. As a man, Jesus worshipped and prayed to the Father, and called him “my God” (John 20:17). Paul prays to the God Jesus prayed to, and he asks for what Jesus had in full. Isaiah foretold a king from the family of Jesse, David’s father, on whom the Spirit of wisdom would rest (Isaiah 11:1–2). That king is Jesus, and Paul asks that the same Spirit be given to his people. And the knowledge it brings comes through the Son, for “no one knows the Father except the Son and anyone to whom the Son chooses to reveal him” (Matthew 11:27). To know God better is to look longer at Jesus.

The Father of glory. The Hebrew kābôd comes from a root meaning heavy. Glory is weight: what is solid enough to matter. Money in the bank and lines on a CV feel solid, but Scripture calls such things chaff, the husks the wind blows away (Psalm 1:4). God is the one who has real weight, and everything else has weight only as it reflects him. Paul worships before he asks a thing.

The Spirit of wisdom and of revelation. Paul does not assume twelve magnificent verses will be enough: he can put the truth before their minds and not get it into their hearts, so he turns from teaching them to praying for them. Wisdom sees things as God sees them, your own suffering included; revelation is the curtain drawn back on what is already given.

Where Christians differ: the Holy Spirit, or a spirit of wisdom? Some translations read “a spirit of wisdom”, meaning a wise attitude or disposition. This commentary’s view: the Holy Spirit. Wisdom and revelation are his work (Isaiah 11:2; 1 Corinthians 2:10–12), and only God can give revelation. But they already have the Spirit (v. 13), so Paul is not praying for them to receive him again; he is praying for the Spirit’s ongoing work in their understanding.

Revelation without new revelation. “Revelation” here means God opening their eyes to what he has already revealed in Christ, not new truths beyond Scripture. Scripture is complete; but every believer still needs the Spirit to make what is written clear and real to the heart (1 Corinthians 2:14).

In the knowledge of him. Not knowledge about God, but of him (John 17:3; Philippians 3:10). You can know a man’s birthday, his job and the name of his dog, and never have met him. The God who is worth knowing above all things wants to be known. So run the test honestly: is God someone you know a great deal about, or someone you know? The two feel similar from the inside for a long time, and they are not the same.

How do I come to know God, and not only know about him? In the same way you come to know anyone: by spending time in his company, listening when he speaks, and answering him. He speaks in Scripture, so read it as a letter from someone, asking each time, “What does this show me about him?” Then answer him: pray back what you have read in your own words, with thanks for what he has done, confession where the passage finds you out, and requests where it makes promises. Do it with other believers, because you know a person better through the eyes of friends who also know him. And obey, because Jesus promised to show himself to the one who keeps his commandments (John 14:21). Knowing God is not a technique, and it grows slowly, like any friendship. But no one who seeks him with all his heart is left a stranger (Jeremiah 29:13).

Why this prayer? They have every blessing (v. 3), but they need to see what they have. A man who does not know he has inherited a fortune lives like a pauper. Paul could have prayed that their circumstances would ease or their numbers grow; he asked instead that they would know God, because the one who truly knows him is equipped for anything that is coming, and the one who does not is unequipped for everything, however well life is currently going.

parallels.desc: the Spirit of wisdom and understanding

verseByVerse.quote: Having the eyes of your hearts enlightened, that you may know what is the hope to which he has called you, what are the riches of his glorious inheritance in the saints.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The eyes of your hearts. In Scripture the heart is the centre of the whole person, and it has its own eyes. Many Christians know the moment when a verse read a hundred times suddenly opens. Nothing changed in the text; the lights came on in the room. Paul cannot reach in and turn on the light; only God can: the God who said, “Let light shine out of darkness,” “has shone in our hearts to give the light of the knowledge of the glory of God in the face of Jesus Christ” (2 Corinthians 4:6). When the lights come on, they always fall on him.

What if I read the Bible and the lights never seem to come on? Keep reading, and keep asking. Seasons of dryness are normal, even for mature believers, and they are not proof that God has stopped speaking. Much of what Scripture does in us is quiet: like meals you cannot remember, it has fed you even on days when nothing felt memorable. A few practical things help. Read smaller portions, slowly, instead of racing through chapters. Read with two questions: what does this show me about God, and what does it ask of me? Pray before you start, with the psalmist: “Open my eyes, that I may behold wondrous things out of your law” (Psalm 119:18). And read with others, because a friend will often see what you missed. The light comes in God’s time, and often when you have stopped straining for it.

The hope to which he has called you. Christian hope is not wishful thinking but certain expectation of what God has promised: the resurrection of the body, Christ’s return, the renewal of all things, life with God face to face, all guaranteed because Jesus rose. Scripture’s picture is an anchor, gripping ground the crew cannot see: “behind the curtain, where Jesus has gone as a forerunner on our behalf” (Hebrews 6:19–20). Whether you have truly seen this hope tends to show up in three very ordinary places: what happens inside you when money goes, what happens inside you at a graveside, and whether the thought of your own death is a horror or a door. If those places still frighten you, that is not proof that you have no hope; it is the very reason Paul prays this prayer for you.

Where Christians differ: our inheritance, or God’s? Some read this as the inheritance believers receive, kept among the saints. This commentary’s view: most likely God’s own inheritance, which is his people. Paul says his inheritance, and the Old Testament calls Israel the LORD’s portion and inheritance (Deuteronomy 32:9; Exodus 19:5; Malachi 3:17). Both truths are biblical (v. 14 speaks of our inheritance), but here the wonder is that they are God’s treasure.

God’s treasure is his people. What does the God who owns the galaxies count as treasure, bought at cost? Not the stars. His people. Any treasure is priced by what the buyer paid, and Peter gives the figure: “not with perishable things such as silver or gold, but with the precious blood of Christ” (1 Peter 1:18–19). For Gentiles who had been without hope and without God (2:12), this was astonishing. So when you are tempted to think of yourself as someone God barely tolerates for Jesus’ sake, this verse stands in the way. You are not what he puts up with. You are what he is inheriting.

verseByVerse.quote: and what is the immeasurable greatness of his power toward us who believe, according to the working of his great might that he worked in Christ when he raised him from the dead and seated him at his right hand in the heavenly places,
verseByVerse.commentary:
The immeasurable greatness of his power. Beyond measuring. This is the third thing Paul prays they will see, and it meets the objection every honest reader has been forming since verse 18: that people like us are far too weak to make it to the end.

Four words for power. Power, working, might, strength (the last two lie behind the ESV’s great might): Paul piles them up, and ties them all to one event.

When he raised him from the dead. Paul does not say God’s power for us is like resurrection power, but that it is the same exertion, now aimed at you. Jesus had been executed in public by soldiers who knew death when they saw it (John 19:33–34), sealed in and guarded. Death had won completely, with witnesses. Then God exerted himself, and the strongest power in this world, the one that has never lost an argument with anybody, gave way.

Now set your own situation beside that. The habit you have failed to break for twenty years. The person you cannot forgive. The fear you have reasoned with a hundred times and never beaten. The prayer you have carried so long that you no longer expect an answer. Is any of it harder than a corpse? That is not a promise that the struggle will be over by Friday. This power often works as quietly as seed in the ground, and the fact that you are still fighting at all is itself its work in you (Galatians 5:17).

Toward us who believe. Toward is a word of direction. This power is not locked away in a vault for some future day; it is already moving, and it is aimed at you. And it is “toward us who believe”, not us who believe flawlessly. “I believe; help my unbelief!” cried a desperate father, and Jesus acted (Mark 9:24). It has already been used on you: even when we were dead in our trespasses, God made us alive together with Christ (2:5). You were not merely helped. You were raised.

Power for what? Not mostly for spectacle. Power to believe and keep believing (Philippians 2:13). Power over sin, since the strength that broke death can break the grip of an old habit (Romans 6:4–6). Power to endure: the long marriage, the chronic illness, the prayer carried for years, “strengthened with all power … for all endurance and patience with joy” (Colossians 1:11). Power to love the difficult (3:16–17). And power in weakness, made perfect exactly when human strength runs out (2 Corinthians 12:9).

At his right hand. The right hand is the place of supreme honour and authority beside a king: “The LORD says to my Lord: ‘Sit at my right hand, until I make your enemies your footstool’” (Psalm 110:1). It means Christ shares God’s throne and rule. He sits because his saving work is finished (Hebrews 10:12). And believers are seated there with him (2:6).

What it does not mean. Not that believers will always feel powerful or see miracles, or that hardship will be removed. The man writing this prayer is in chains; his power was given for endurance, not escape. Its aim is not to make your outer life spectacular, but to make your inner life like the Son’s.

parallels.desc: sit at my right hand

verseByVerse.quote: Far above all rule and authority and power and dominion, and above every name that is named, not only in this age but also in the one to come.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Far above. Paul’s word is a strong one. It means not only higher in rank, but in a different class altogether. Christ is not the top name on the chart; he drew the chart: all these powers were created through him and for him (Colossians 1:16). Every name that ever made a city tremble, Artemis, Caesar, the spirits of the air, has been outranked by the name of a carpenter’s son who died on a Roman cross.

All rule and authority and power and dominion. The ranks and titles Jews and Greeks used for orders of spiritual beings, including hostile ones (6:12), and also for human rulers. To Ephesians who had lived in dread of named powers, this was liberation: every power you feared is under the feet of the one who saved you. At the cross, which looked like defeat, “He disarmed the rulers and authorities and put them to open shame” (Colossians 2:15). They still operate and still oppose (6:12), but as defeated enemies, not sovereign lords. There is a vast difference between a roaring lion (1 Peter 5:8) and a reigning one.

Every name that is named. In Ephesus this was an attack on an industry: in magic, to know a spirit’s name was to gain leverage over it. So in the same city the seven sons of Sceva tried to use “the Jesus whom Paul proclaims” as one more name in the toolkit, and were beaten out of the house (Acts 19:13–16). The name of Jesus is not a lever to be operated. He is a Lord to be belonged to, and when you have the Person, you no longer need the formulas. We have our own names, whatever we appease: the market, the scan result, the opinion of people whose approval we have never enjoyed. We do not burn incense to them; we lie awake for them. Every one of them is under his feet.

Can curses, horoscopes or evil spirits harm a Christian? They cannot own you, and they cannot undo what God has done. A believer belongs to Christ and is sealed with his Spirit (1:13), and “he who is in you is greater than he who is in the world” (1 John 4:4). No curse can reverse God’s blessing (Numbers 23:8). The devil can still tempt, accuse and oppose you (6:11–12), and he is to be resisted, not ignored (James 4:7). But a Christian should have nothing to do with horoscopes, tarot cards, Ouija boards, charms or spells (Deuteronomy 18:10–12), not because they are stronger than Christ, but because consulting them is looking to another lord for what only he gives. If you have dabbled, confess it and get rid of the things, as the Ephesians burned their scrolls (Acts 19:19). Then stop being afraid. You are seated with the one who is far above them all.

Is it not narrow to say Jesus is above every other name? The charge would stick only if the claim were that Christians are above everyone else. It is the opposite. The name above every name belongs to the one who took the lowest place, obedient to the point of death on a cross (Philippians 2:8–9). He did not climb to his throne over his rivals; he reached it by dying for his enemies, and he promises them a seat beside him on it (Revelation 3:21). And a claim is not arrogant merely because it excludes something: every claim does, including the claim that all religions are equally true. The real question is whether it is true, and Paul rests it on a public event: God raised him from the dead (1:20; Acts 17:31).

In the one to come. Jews divided history into two ages: this present age, marked by sin and death, and the age to come, when God would put everything right. Christ’s resurrection has brought the age to come into the present; the two overlap until his return. Every power that ever terrified anyone had an expiry date. His authority is not up for renewal at the end of history. The end of history is simply when everybody finds out.

verseByVerse.quote: And he put all things under his feet and gave him as head over all things to the church,
verseByVerse.commentary:
He put all things under his feet. Paul quotes Psalm 8:6, which looks back to the task God gave Adam: to rule over all that God had made. Adam lost it by his sin. Hebrews adds the ache: “At present, we do not yet see everything in subjection to him.” Then the turn: “But we see him who for a little while was made lower than the angels, namely Jesus”, crowned with glory and honour (Hebrews 2:8–9). What Adam failed to hold, Christ has won; Paul calls him the last Adam, the head of a new humanity (1 Corinthians 15:45). The feet once nailed to a cross are the feet under which every power is now placed. Their subjection is not yet fully visible, but it is already fully real: “he must reign until he has put all his enemies under his feet. The last enemy to be destroyed is death” (1 Corinthians 15:25–26).

Head over all things to the church. God gave the church a gift: Christ, who is head over all things. And the strangest words are the last three: not to the angels, nor to the nations, but to the church: ordinary people, many of them slaves and tradesmen, meeting in borrowed rooms in a city that would not have noticed if they vanished. We picture two separate stories, the big one out there of empires, markets and wars, and the small one in here of our own life and church. This verse says there is one story, and the big one is being run for the sake of the small one: Christ governs empires, markets and wars for the good of his church.

If Christ rules all things for the church, why does the church suffer so much? Because he rules for her good, and her good is not the same as her comfort. The head over all things is the Lamb who was slain, and his body follows the way he went: through the cross to the crown. So persecution, decline and hardship are not signs that he has lost control; he rules even them. When persecution scattered the church in Jerusalem, the scattered went everywhere preaching the word (Acts 8:1–4). Nothing can separate his people from his love, and in all these things they are more than conquerors (Romans 8:35–37). The church will not always look as if she is winning, but the gates of hell will never overcome her (Matthew 16:18). Pray for the suffering church, and do not measure Christ’s reign by this week’s headlines.

Head. “Head” here plainly includes authority; in 4:15–16 it is also the source from which the body is nourished and held together (Colossians 2:19). So Christ’s rule over everything is not only the guarantee that nothing can crush you; it is the arrangement by which you are fed. And a body goes where its head goes. If the head has been raised and seated above every power, the body cannot be left behind (2:6).

Where Christians differ: the head of the church. Roman Catholic teaching sees the pope as Christ’s visible vicar (stand-in) and head on earth. This commentary’s view: Christ alone is head of the church (Westminster Confession 25.6; 1689 London Baptist Confession 26.4), ruling by his word and Spirit through the elders and pastors he gives his church (Christians differ, charitably, over how those offices are arranged). No human being shares that headship.

parallels.desc: you have put all things under his feet

verseByVerse.quote: which is his body, the fullness of him who fills all in all.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Which is his body. The church is not a club that admires Christ from a distance, but the body of Christ: united to him, living from him, the means by which he acts in the world. A body is how a person is present to things. Christ’s body is not a building but the people who were in the room with you last Sunday, the difficult ones included. When they carry a meal to a widow, that is not only kindness organised by volunteers. It is Christ, present on a particular street.

The fullness of him who fills all in all. Why fills, and not only rules? A king can rule a land he has never visited; to fill is to be present within it. “Do I not fill heaven and earth? declares the LORD” (Jeremiah 23:24). When Solomon dedicated the temple, the cloud of God’s glory filled the house so that the priests could not stand to minister (1 Kings 8:10–11): not overseeing it from above, but filling it from within. The one whose glory filled the temple now fills all things, and his church is the new temple, made of living stones (2:21–22). Yet he has chosen to have a body, and to make poor, quarrelsome, forgiven people the place where his fullness dwells.

Where Christians differ: does the church fill Christ, or does Christ fill the church? There are two main readings. First, the church completes Christ, as a body completes a head. Calvin took this view and found it moving: Christ, who lacks nothing in himself, counts himself in some sense incomplete without his people. Second, the church is filled by Christ: the place he fills with his presence, life and gifts. This commentary’s view: the second is more likely. Paul consistently speaks of Christ filling (4:10, he ascended that he might fill all things) and of believers being filled (3:19; 5:18), never of Christ being filled up by us; and Colossians 2:9–10 says the fullness of deity dwells in Christ and you have been filled in him. Christ lacks nothing. Yet Calvin’s point stands in its own way. Paul could have said king and kingdom, or master and servants, and kept himself entirely separate. He chose the one picture in which the greater looks unfinished without the lesser. A head without a body is not a lesser head; it is a horror. Christ does not need us as we need him, but he has bound himself to us so closely that he is not ashamed to be called our head. That is not a lack in Christ. It is a measure of how far love has committed itself.

Who fills all in all. He fills the universe by his power and the church by his saving presence (4:10). So there is nowhere you can go this week that lies outside him: the ward, the school run, the office where nobody prays, the flat you come home to when it is empty. You do not carry him into those places like a parcel. He is already filling them, and you go in as part of his body.

Can I follow Christ without the church? Not for long, and not as he intends. Paul does not say the church is a helpful extra for keen believers; he says it is Christ’s body, and a hand that has left the body does not become a freer hand, only a dying one. Many who say they love Jesus but not the church have been hurt by Christians, and that hurt is real and should be heard. But the remedy is a faithful church, not none. “Christ loved the church and gave himself up for her” (5:25). You cannot hold the Bridegroom at arm’s length from his bride.

In the flow. Chapter 2 opens with a jolt: “And you were dead” (2:1). The power that raised and seated Christ (1:20) has raised and seated believers with him (2:5–6).

1.overview:
Ephesians opens with one long sentence of praise (vv. 3–14) for every spiritual blessing God has given his people in Christ. The Father chose them before creation and adopted them in love; in the Son they have redemption through his blood and have been told God’s plan to unite all things under Christ; and the Spirit marks them as God’s own, Jewish and Gentile believers alike, and is himself the first instalment of all they will inherit, all to the praise of God’s glory.

Then Paul prays (vv. 15–23), not for new blessings but that they may see the ones they have: the hope of God’s calling, the riches of his inheritance in his people, and the power that raised Christ and seated him far above every power, as head over all things for the church, his body.
