2.title: Dead in Sin, Alive in Christ
2.text: <sup>1</sup>And you were dead in the trespasses and sins <sup>2</sup>in which you once walked, following the course of this world, following the prince of the power of the air, the spirit that is now at work in the sons of disobedience — <sup>3</sup>among whom we all once lived in the passions of our flesh, carrying out the desires of the flesh and the mind, and were by nature children of wrath, like the rest of mankind. <sup>4</sup>But God, being rich in mercy, because of the great love with which he loved us, <sup>5</sup>even when we were dead in our trespasses, made us alive together with Christ — by grace you have been saved — <sup>6</sup>and raised us up with him and seated us with him in the heavenly places in Christ Jesus, <sup>7</sup>so that in the coming ages he might show the immeasurable riches of his grace in kindness toward us in Christ Jesus. <sup>8</sup>For by grace you have been saved through faith. And this is not your own doing; it is the gift of God, <sup>9</sup>not a result of works, so that no one may boast. <sup>10</sup>For we are his workmanship, created in Christ Jesus for good works, which God prepared beforehand, that we should walk in them. <sup>11</sup>Therefore remember that at one time you Gentiles in the flesh, called “the uncircumcision” by what is called the circumcision, which is made in the flesh by hands — <sup>12</sup>remember that you were at that time separated from Christ, alienated from the commonwealth of Israel and strangers to the covenants of promise, having no hope and without God in the world. <sup>13</sup>But now in Christ Jesus you who once were far off have been brought near by the blood of Christ. <sup>14</sup>For he himself is our peace, who has made us both one and has broken down in his flesh the dividing wall of hostility <sup>15</sup>by abolishing the law of commandments expressed in ordinances, that he might create in himself one new man in place of the two, so making peace, <sup>16</sup>and might reconcile us both to God in one body through the cross, thereby killing the hostility. <sup>17</sup>And he came and preached peace to you who were far off and peace to those who were near. <sup>18</sup>For through him we both have access in one Spirit to the Father. <sup>19</sup>So then you are no longer strangers and aliens, but you are fellow citizens with the saints and members of the household of God, <sup>20</sup>built on the foundation of the apostles and prophets, Christ Jesus himself being the cornerstone, <sup>21</sup>in whom the whole structure, being joined together, grows into a holy temple in the Lord. <sup>22</sup>In him you also are being built together into a dwelling place for God by the Spirit.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Verses 1–3 show where we were: dead in sin, following the world, the devil and the flesh, and by nature under wrath. Verses 4–7 show what God did: he made us alive with Christ and seated us with him, to show for ever the riches of his kindness. Verses 8–10 sum it up: saved by grace through faith, not by works, and created in Christ for good works.
verseByVerse.theology:
Total Depravity, Sovereign Grace, and the New Creation

Dead in trespasses and sins is the plainest biblical statement of what Reformed theology calls total depravity. It does not mean fallen people are as evil as they could be, but that every part of us, mind, will, affections and conscience, is corrupted, so that no part naturally seeks God or can save itself.

Against that, God does not respond to a seeking sinner; he acts on a dead one. This grace does not force the will but renews it, making the unwilling willing, and the faith through which we receive salvation is his gift (v. 8).

Verse 10 answers the charge that grace makes people passive. The law could tell us to do good, but it could not make us want to. Grace does. The person saved by grace alone no longer has to do good in order to be accepted by God. He is accepted already, and so he is free to do the good works God prepared beforehand, gladly, in the Spirit’s strength.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: For Paul’s readers, dead in trespasses and sins was autobiography. Many had worshipped Artemis or practised magic; converts in Ephesus burned their books of spells (Acts 19:19). The “But God” of v. 4 was the turning point of their own lives.

Now: The same diagnosis covers everyone outside Christ, however educated, moral or sincere. A person who thinks he is merely ill will not seek the remedy for death, so the church states both clearly: dead, but God.

verseByVerse.quote: You were dead in the trespasses and sins in which you once walked, following the course of this world, following the prince of the power of the air.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Meaning first. Ephesians 2 shows what the power of chapter 1 has done for us, in two movements. Verses 1–10 describe salvation as resurrection: we were dead and under wrath, but God, rich in mercy, made us alive with Christ and seated us with him, by grace through faith, for good works. Verses 11–22 describe salvation as reconciliation: Gentiles far off have been brought near by Christ’s blood, made one new people with Jewish believers, and built into a temple where God lives by his Spirit. The gospel in miniature: dead, but God; far off, but now.

The connection. Chapter 1 ended with God’s power raising Christ from the dead and seating him above every power (1:19–23). Chapter 2 shows the same power at work in us. The sentence that begins in verse 1 does not reach its main verb until verse 5: “God … made us alive”. Verses 1–3 are the grave; verses 4–7 are the resurrection.

You were dead. Not sick or weakened, but cut off from the life of God (4:18). A corpse can be dressed beautifully; it is still a corpse. Spiritual death means no power to perceive God (1 Corinthians 2:14), no desire for him (the mind set on the flesh does not submit to God’s law; indeed, it cannot, Romans 8:7), and no ability to change it. Lazarus did not help Jesus raise him. He heard a voice speak life into death, and came out (John 11:43–44). This is what God warned of in Eden (Genesis 2:17): Adam did not drop dead that day, but he hid from God, and death began.

In the trespasses and sins. A trespass crosses a line God has drawn; a sin misses the mark he set. And it says dead in them, not only because of them. Sin is not only what caused the death; it is the element the dead man lives in, as water is a fish’s. That is why the cure cannot be moral improvement: you do not improve a corpse, you raise it.

In which you once walked. “Walk” is the Bible’s word for a way of life, and the paradox is that the dead were busy. Careers, families, religion, pleasure, all lived as if God were not there.

The course of this world. “The world” here is not the planet but human society organised without God, telling us what to want and whom to admire. It is a current, and the dead do not feel it, because nothing feels less like being swept along than swimming with the tide. You discover the current only when you turn and try to swim against it (1 John 2:15–17).

The prince of the power of the air. Satan, called elsewhere “the ruler of this world” (John 12:31) and “the god of this world”, who blinds the minds of unbelievers (2 Corinthians 4:4): a real person, not a figure of speech for society’s bad habits. The air was thought the home of spirits, and Paul uses that language: the powers his readers feared are real, and ruled by one evil prince. But he is not equal to God; he is a creature already defeated (1:21; Colossians 2:15).

Now at work. The same verb as God’s power raising Christ (1:20): two powers are at work in the world. “Sons of disobedience” means people marked by disobedience.

Three enemies. Verses 1–3 name the world around us, the devil above us and the flesh within us. Culture makes sin normal, the devil makes it attractive, and our own nature wants it. And the dead man is not fighting them but following them: not a prisoner straining at the bars, but a body carried by the tide.

But I know kind unbelievers. Many feel this and few say it aloud: “‘Dead’? I know unbelievers kinder, steadier and more generous than half the congregation.” Think of cut flowers. A florist’s arrangement can be lovelier than anything still growing in the garden, brighter and more fragrant in the room. Nobody looking at it would say it is dead. Yet it has been cut from its root, and everything you admire about it is running on borrowed time. Paul is not claiming that unbelievers behave worse than believers. He is speaking of connection, not comparison. The kindness is real. The beauty is real. The root is what is missing.

What it does not mean. Not that unbelievers are as bad as they could possibly be, or that they cannot do kind or good things in a human sense. Total depravity means sin has reached every part of us, mind, will and desires, and nothing in us can turn us back to God. Nor is everyone outside Christ consciously serving Satan; most simply follow the crowd. And it does not remove responsibility: the dead walked in sins; they did what they wanted.

Where Christians differ: how dead? Semi-Pelagian traditions (which hold that the first move towards God can be ours) and Arminian ones, held by many faithful believers, teach that the fall left people weakened but still able, with God’s general help (called prevenient grace), to accept or refuse the gospel; they read dead as separated from God rather than unable, and point to Jesus’ promise to draw all people to himself (John 12:32). Reformed theology holds total inability: the fallen will is free to choose what it wants, but it does not want God, and no one can come to Christ unless the Father draws him (John 6:44; Romans 8:7–8). This commentary’s view: total depravity and inability (Westminster Confession 9.3; 1689 London Baptist Confession 9.3). Paul’s image decides it: a corpse does not cooperate with its resurrection. And Paul does not say “dead” to crush us. He says it to prepare us for verse 5, as a dark night makes the sunrise plain. The depth of the death is the measure of the miracle (Ezekiel 37:1–14).

Signs of life. Corpses do not develop appetites. So if you find in yourself any hunger for God at all, if you would rather be near him than not, if his word sometimes lands with weight, if sin now grieves you where once it barely registered, then something has happened to you that you did not do. You are not looking at evidence of your strength. You are looking at evidence that a voice has spoken into a grave, and that you heard it.

In everyday life. When you share the gospel, argue clearly, but pray first: you are speaking to people who need resurrection, not merely persuasion. And no one is too far gone, because God raises the dead.
verseByVerse.note: “The prince of the power of the air” is Satan. The air was thought to be the realm of spiritual powers.

verseByVerse.quote: among whom we all once lived in the passions of our flesh, carrying out the desires of the flesh and the mind, and were by nature children of wrath, like the rest of mankind.
verseByVerse.commentary:
We all once lived. Verses 1–2 said “you”, the Gentile readers. Now Paul says “we”. Paul, the strictest of Pharisees (Philippians 3:4–6), says Jew and Gentile alike were dead. If both were equally lost, both are saved the same way, and neither can look down on the other (Romans 3:9, 22–23).

The passions of our flesh. “Flesh” here does not mean the body, which God made good. It means fallen human nature, the whole person turned in on itself, what Luther, following Augustine, called the heart curved in on itself. It is a self that has made itself the centre, so that even its good gifts (love, work, religion) are bent back towards its own comfort and glory (2 Timothy 3:2–4). So its passions are not only sexual (Galatians 5:19–21): the flesh produces boardroom sin as readily as bedroom sin.

The desires of the body and the mind. Literally the wills of the flesh and of the thoughts. Paul deliberately adds the mind, so the person who thinks self-control has made him good has nowhere left to hide. Master your bodily appetites and you may only have moved the problem upstairs, into the mind: pride in your own cleverness, the hunger for power, the craving to be admired. A man can be sober, chaste and hard-working and still live entirely in the desires of the mind. The respectable sins of clever and moral people are as much flesh as any other.

By nature children of wrath. Not only did we do wrong; we were wrong. “By nature” is original sin in a phrase: by birth, by what we are as children of Adam, before and beneath any choice (Psalm 51:5). We are not sinners because we sin; we sin because we are sinners. “Children of wrath” means people on whom wrath rests (John 3:36). Nobody has ever had to teach a child to grab, or to say “mine”. Every parent is an unwilling witness to this verse.

Wrath. Not a fit of temper, and not something unworthy of a loving God. God’s wrath is his settled, holy, just opposition to evil (Romans 1:18). A God who was not angry at child abuse, cruelty and betrayal would not be good. It is always fair. And this truth is not cruelty; it is ground on which deep gratitude is built: the one who is forgiven little, loves little (Luke 7:47). The shallowness of our worship usually matches the smallness of our sense of what we were saved from. Read this verse as a sinner looking at the wrath he deserved, and then look at who stood in its path.

Like the rest of mankind. No exceptions, but one. God sent his own Son in the likeness of sinful flesh (Romans 8:3), “one who in every respect has been tempted as we are, yet without sin” (Hebrews 4:15). He took our flesh but not its curve inward: he is the only man in whom the passions of the flesh and the desires of the mind never once ruled, the only child of Adam on whom wrath did not rest by nature. Paul calls Christ the last Adam (1 Corinthians 15:45). He was born into the first Adam’s family, so that a new family might begin with him.

The tense is the comfort. We were by nature children of wrath. Not are. Every dreadful word in these three verses stands in the past tense, dead, walked, followed, lived, were, and they are all held there, waiting, until two words in verse 4 break over them: “But God”. So if you are in Christ, this passage is not your diagnosis. It is your medical history. Read it the way a healthy man reads an old chart from the worst year of his life, and marvels that he is sitting up reading anything at all.

What it does not mean. Not that the body or physical desire is evil in itself. Hunger and sexual desire are God’s gifts (Genesis 1:31). Nor does “children of wrath” mean God hates his creatures or takes pleasure in their ruin (Ezekiel 33:11). The very next words are “But God, being rich in mercy”.

Where Christians differ: original sin. Pelagius (fifth century) taught that each person is born innocent and sins only by following bad examples. Eastern Orthodoxy teaches that we inherit mortality and a tendency to sin from Adam, but not his guilt. Augustine and the Reformers taught that we inherit both a corrupt nature and the guilt of Adam’s first sin, counted (imputed) to us, because the whole race sinned in Adam, its head (Romans 5:12–19). “By nature children of wrath” fits only the last: wrath rests on us by nature, not only after we choose. This commentary’s view: original sin as both inherited corruption and imputed guilt (Westminster Confession 6.3; 1689 London Baptist Confession 6.3). And the very thing that sounds unfair here is what saves us. Adam acted for all of us, as a king who declares war puts his whole people at war. In the same way Christ acted for all who are in him: as Adam’s sin was counted to us, so Christ’s righteousness is counted to them. Nor are you an innocent bystander punished for somebody else’s crime. You were born into Adam’s family, and every day since you have agreed with his choice by sinning yourself.

A common question: what about infants who die? If all are by nature children of wrath, what of babies and young children who die before they can believe? Scripture does not answer this directly, and believers should speak humbly. The 1689 London Baptist Confession (10.3), with the Westminster (10.3), says that elect infants dying in infancy are regenerated and saved by Christ through the Spirit, who works when, where and how he pleases. Many in the Reformed tradition, among them Charles Spurgeon and B. B. Warfield, went further and held that all who die in infancy are among the elect, pointing to God’s judgment according to deeds done (Romans 2:6; 2 Corinthians 5:10), which infants have not done, and to David’s confidence that he would go to his dead child (2 Samuel 12:23). Jesus took the little children in his arms and blessed them (Mark 10:16). What is certain is that if any infant is saved, it is by grace in Christ, not by innocence; and that grieving parents may entrust their child to the Judge of all the earth, who will do what is just (Genesis 18:25). If you have buried a child, this is not a cold debate about your little one: it is the Saviour who took children in his arms who holds yours now.

verseByVerse.quote: But God, being rich in mercy, because of the great love with which he loved us, even when we were dead in our trespasses, made us alive together with Christ—by grace you have been saved—
verseByVerse.commentary:
But God. After three verses of death, the subject of the sentence finally appears. Martyn Lloyd-Jones said these two words in a sense contain the whole gospel. If the story were “But we”, there would be no hope, because dead people cannot act.

Being rich in mercy. Mercy is God’s pity moving towards misery: it sees the corpse, is not repelled, and moves first. And God is rich in it: mercy that does not run low or grow harder to obtain the more you have needed it.

The great love. The reason lies in God, not in us. Paul piles up the words: love, great love, love with which he loved. He looked at the spiritually dead, the children of wrath, and loved them, not what they would become, but what they actually were (Romans 5:8). We were not lovable; he loved us anyway, and his love made us lovely.

Even when we were dead. Not once we had begun to stir: when there was least to work with and nothing whatever to reward, he acted. And that settles the question every anxious believer returns to: might God yet think better of it and change his mind about me? You contributed nothing to your first resurrection. Your standing has never rested on your contribution, and it is not about to start now.

Made us alive together with Christ. The main verb of the whole sentence: not helped or improved, but raised. This is regeneration, the new birth (John 3:3–8; Titus 3:5): God giving spiritual life to the spiritually dead. And it is made alive with: our new life is not a separate miracle that happens to resemble Christ’s; it is a share in his. When Jesus came out of the tomb, you came out with him. In him your resurrection already happened, outside Jerusalem, long before you were born.

By grace you have been saved. Paul breaks into his own sentence. The Greek perfect means a completed act with lasting results. Saved, and still saved.

Life before faith. Reformed theology reads this verse as showing that new birth comes before faith in order, though not in time, as a lamp lights a room the instant it is switched on, yet the light comes because of the switch. We believe because we have been born again (John 1:12–13; 1 John 5:1).

I cannot remember a moment when I was made alive. Does that mean it never happened? No. You do not remember being born either, and you are plainly alive. Many believers, especially those raised in Christian homes, cannot name a day; others can name the day but could not tell you what was happening. Scripture never asks for a date. It asks whether there is life now. The question is not “When did I first believe?” but “Am I trusting Christ today?” The signs are the ones a newborn shows: a hunger for God’s word (1 Peter 2:2), a cry of Father to God (Romans 8:15), a new grief over sin, and love for his people (1 John 3:14). If those are there, however weak, the one who raised you knows the day. Like the man born blind, you may not be able to explain how, but you can say that once you were blind and now you see (John 9:25).

Where Christians differ: does God’s life-giving work depend on our consent? Arminian Christians, who love the gospel of grace too, hold that God’s grace enables every person to believe, but that grace can be resisted, so the decisive factor in who is saved is the human response. Reformed theology holds that God’s regenerating grace is effectual: when God makes alive, the dead live (John 6:37; Acts 16:14, where the Lord opened Lydia’s heart). This commentary’s view: effectual calling, God’s call that does not fail to bring the dead to life (Westminster Confession 10.1–2; 1689 London Baptist Confession 10.1–2). God does not drag the unwilling; he makes them willing by giving them new hearts (Ezekiel 36:26).

verseByVerse.quote: And raised us up with him and seated us with him in the heavenly places in Christ Jesus.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Three “with” words. Made alive with, raised with, seated with: each matches a step in Christ’s story in 1:20. This is what theologians call union with Christ. In plain words: we are joined to him, he acted for us, and so what happened to him counts as having happened to us (Romans 6:4–5; Colossians 3:1–3). When the captain lifts the cup, the whole team has won it, even the player who never left the bench.

Raised us up with him. Spiritually, now: we have passed from death to life (John 5:24). Physically, later: our bodies will be raised at his return (1 Corinthians 15:20–23). The first guarantees the second.

Seated us with him. Stated as a fact, in the past tense. To be seated is to be at rest, in a place of authority. The priests of the old covenant stood daily at their service, because their work was never done (Hebrews 10:11). Christ “sat down at the right hand of the Majesty on high” because his one sacrifice was final (Hebrews 1:3; 10:12), and you are seated with him, sharing his rest, because you are in him. He keeps his people where he is, because he will not be in glory without them (John 17:24). Once the evil powers of verse 2 ruled over the Ephesians. Now those powers are beneath Christ, and the Ephesians sit with him. They used to be under those powers; in Christ they are above them.

In Christ Jesus. We are not seated there by our own spiritual height, and so nothing here is graded. Paul does not say the mature are seated while the struggling stand at the back. The believer converted last Thursday, who still cannot find Habakkuk and is fighting something he has not told anybody about, is seated exactly where the apostle is seated, because neither is there on his own account. They are both there in Christ, and Christ has only one seat: the highest.

Seated already, still fighting. This is our position, though our experience does not yet match it. We are seated (2:6), yet we must stand and fight (6:10–13), and the realm we are seated in is the very realm where the battle is (6:12). So this is not escapism but your position in the conflict: the difference between a soldier pinned down in a trench, who cannot see whether his side is winning, and a man standing beside the commander with the whole battle laid out before him. Both are in the war. Only one knows how it ends. The fight is real, but it is fought from victory, not for it.

In everyday life. When the accuser says you are disqualified, do not produce your record; point to your seat. The boss, the diagnosis and the fear are real, but they are beneath your Lord’s feet, and you are seated with him.

verseByVerse.quote: So that in the coming ages he might show the immeasurable riches of his grace in kindness toward us in Christ Jesus.
verseByVerse.commentary:
So that. God saved his people for their good, but above all to display his glory, as in the refrain of chapter 1 (1:6, 12, 14). And God’s glory and our good are not rivals: he is glorified precisely by being kind to us.

In the coming ages. Not one coming age but ages, one after another without end. What we have tasted here is the down payment; the coming ages are the feast. The moment when grace was most real to you came through a fallen mind, a weak faith and a tired body; what will it be when every barrier is gone? C. S. Lewis caught it at the end of The Last Battle: the further up and further in you go, the larger everything becomes, each circle bigger than the last, and the cry is, “This is the land I have been looking for all my life.”

He might show. To exhibit publicly (Romans 9:22–23), with angels and powers in the audience (3:10). What will be on display through the ages is not galaxies, which never cost God anything, but what he did with people. You are the exhibit.

The immeasurable riches of his grace. The word used of his power in 1:19: grace overflows, and eternity will not exhaust it. And this turns something painful inside out. Many of us carry a chapter we would rather were left out: the wasted years, the thing we still cannot say aloud. We assume heaven will keep a discreet silence about it. But what is displayed is not your record but the riches of his grace, and grace can only be measured against what it had to overcome. A restorer’s skill is never shown by a painting that was never damaged. The chapter you would erase will testify most loudly, for ever, to what he is like.

In kindness toward us. Grace is not a judge reluctantly signing a pardon. It comes in kindness (Titus 3:4), someone leaning towards you. Eternity is not a reward you were owed; it is God, for ever, delighting to be kind to people who had nothing coming.

In Christ Jesus. All this kindness reaches us through one channel. And the exhibit of the coming ages has a centre. When John was shown heaven, he saw in the midst of the throne “a Lamb standing, as though it had been slain” (Revelation 5:6), and every creature singing to him. The risen Jesus kept his wounds; he showed them to Thomas (John 20:27). So the riches of grace will be shown in a Person, and the marks in his hands and side will explain every saved sinner standing round the throne. You will be part of the display; he will be the reason for it.

verseByVerse.quote: For by grace you have been saved through faith. And this is not your own doing; it is the gift of God, not a result of works, so that no one may boast.
verseByVerse.commentary:
By grace. The source: God’s free favour towards those who deserve wrath (v. 3). If it is deserved in any way, it is no longer grace (Romans 11:6).

You have been saved. Perfect and passive: done to you, finished, its effect continuing. That is why assurance is not arrogance. The one who says he is saved is no more boasting about his performance than a rescued swimmer boasts about the lifeboat. He is reporting what somebody else did.

Through faith. The means: the empty hand that receives the gift. Faith is not a contribution but trust, relying on Christ instead of ourselves, and its whole value lies in its object. Weak faith in a sound bridge will carry you over the river; robust faith in a rotten one will drop you into it. The father who cried, “I believe; help my unbelief!” saw his son healed (Mark 9:24–27). So the question is never whether your faith is big enough, but what you are trusting. Put a trembling hand on Christ and you have all that he is; and the empty hand, which is all faith ever was, does not become any emptier for shaking. We are saved through faith, never because of faith.

Not your own doing. In Greek a word like “this” (touto) changes its form to match the word it points to, and here it matches neither “grace” nor “faith”. So “this” does not point to faith alone, nor to grace alone, but to the whole thing just described: salvation by grace through faith. That only strengthens the point. Grace, salvation and the faith that receives it are all gathered into one word: gift.

Not a result of works. “Works” is anything we do to put God in our debt; Paul had the law in view, but the principle covers every human attempt to earn salvation (Romans 4:4–5; Titus 3:5).

So that no one may boast. The ancient world ran on honour, and the only question was what you boasted in. Paul counted his own record as rubbish beside knowing Christ (Philippians 3:4–8). If we contributed even one per cent, we could boast of it: “I chose wisely when others did not.” God removes every ground of pride, so that the only boast left is in the Lord (1 Corinthians 1:29–31). And boasting takes quiet forms: the sense that I believed because I was wiser or more open than others; the Calvinist grateful for election who privately feels more perceptive; the long-standing member eyeing the new convert with a touch of seniority. Both came to the cross with nothing; both left with the same righteousness of Christ. A properly told testimony does not make the speaker the hero. This gives a simple test of any version of the gospel: does it leave room for anyone to boast?

What it does not mean. Not that faith is unnecessary because God does everything: no one is saved without believing. Not that good works do not matter: verse 10 follows at once. And “not a result of works” does not mean that God saves people while they remain unchanged. He saves us from sin, not in it. Works are never the reason God accepts us. They are what grows in the life of someone he has accepted.

Where Christians differ: is faith itself a gift? Arminians hold that God offers salvation and gives everyone the ability to believe, but that faith itself is the human response. Reformed theology holds that faith, too, is God’s gift, granted to those he has made alive (Philippians 1:29; Acts 13:48; 2 Peter 1:1). Even if “this” in verse 8 refers to the whole package, faith is part of the package. This commentary’s view: faith is God’s gift; we believe, but we believe because God has given us life (v. 5).

If faith is God’s gift, what should I do if I do not have it? Do what the gospel tells you to do: come to Christ, and ask. God does not give faith in some sealed room; he gives it through his word, because “faith comes from hearing, and hearing through the word of Christ” (Romans 10:17). So put yourself where that word is: read the Gospels, sit under faithful preaching, talk with a Christian you trust. And pray honestly, even if your prayer is only, “Lord, I want to believe; help me.” Jesus promised that the Father gives the Holy Spirit to those who ask him (Luke 11:13), and he has never turned away anyone who came to him (John 6:37). The very fact that you want faith may be the first stirring of the life this chapter describes. Do not wait until you feel ready. Turn to him now.

Where Christians differ: justification. Roman Catholic teaching (Council of Trent, 1547) holds that justification includes the inner renewal of the person, begins at baptism, can be increased by good works, and can be lost by mortal sin. The Reformers taught that justification is a legal declaration: God pronounces the sinner righteous, not because of any righteousness in him, but because Christ’s righteousness is counted to him, received by faith alone (Romans 3:24–28; 4:5). Renewal always follows, but it is not the ground of our standing with God. This commentary’s view: by grace alone, through faith alone, in Christ alone (Westminster Confession 11.1; 1689 London Baptist Confession 11.1). Verses 8–10 together say it exactly: saved not by works, but for works.

In everyday life. When you feel you have been a good Christian this week and God must be pleased with you, or a bad one and he must be finished with you, come back to this verse. Your standing rests on his gift, not on your week.
verseByVerse.note: “This” most naturally refers to the whole of salvation by grace through faith.

verseByVerse.quote: For we are his workmanship, created in Christ Jesus for good works, which God prepared beforehand, that we should walk in them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
His workmanship. Salvation cannot come from our works, because we ourselves are God’s work. Poiēma (hence poem) appears only twice in the New Testament: here, and in Romans 1:20, where it means the created universe, “the things that have been made”, through which God’s power and divine nature are clearly seen. The word Paul reaches for to describe the galaxies is the word he reaches for to describe you. Of those two works, the second cost God far more. The first he spoke into being; the second required a death.

Created in Christ Jesus. Salvation is a new creation (2 Corinthians 5:17), not a touching-up of the old self, though the new creature still has growing to do. You are still you, with your name, your memories and your personality, but the deepest thing about you has changed: you now love what you once ignored, God, his word and his people, because he has given you a new heart (Ezekiel 36:26).

For good works. The purpose of the new creation. Good works are actions that please God: done in faith, according to his commands, from love, for his glory. They include the large and visible, mission, justice, generosity, and the small and hidden (4:25–32). The plumber who works well and charges fairly, the employee who works as to the Lord (6:7), the parent who disciplines with warmth (6:4), the one who goes back to apologise: these are good works in Paul’s sense. We are God’s masterpiece, and masterpieces are made not to be stored, but displayed (Matthew 5:16).

Which God prepared beforehand. As God planned our salvation before the foundation of the world (1:4), he planned the good works that would follow. Not that you are a robot running a script: God prepares good works for us, and his Spirit works in us (1:19–20). So the question is not “What good works should I invent?” but “What has God put in front of me today?” The neighbour in need, the unexpected chance to serve, the gift waiting to be used.

What if I miss the good works God prepared for me? You will sometimes fail to do the good in front of you, and that is sin to confess, not a plan you have ruined. God prepared these works knowing exactly who you are, failures included, and his purpose for your life does not hang on your never putting a foot wrong (Romans 8:28). Nor are they hidden in a maze for you to find. Most of them are plain: the commands of Scripture, and the needs God puts in front of you, met as you have opportunity (Galatians 6:10). For the bigger decisions, a job, a move, whom to marry, choose wisely within what Scripture allows, take counsel, pray, and go forward without fear that you have picked the wrong door. The God who prepared the road also guides the walker.

That we should walk in them. The verb of verse 2, the opposite road. Not admire good works, nor intend them: walk, one step at a time, usually with nobody watching. Conversion did not stop you walking; it changed the road (4:1, 17; 5:2).

Not by works, but for works. Verses 8–10 together are the whole Reformation in miniature. Works are the fruit of salvation, never the root: a child obeys not to earn a place in the family but because he belongs. The faith that justifies is never alone (James 2:17–18). And since even our best works are never perfect, they are accepted not on their own merit but for Christ’s sake, whose perfect obedience is counted as ours (Romans 5:19).

Not a masterpiece? Some readers meet the word masterpiece and think: “Not me.” But you are not the one asked to assess the work. You are standing inside it while it is still being made, the one place from which no work of art ever looked finished. A house halfway through renovation looks worse than before anyone touched it, walls opened, floors lifted, dust everywhere, and that is not evidence that the builder has failed. It is evidence that he has begun. The worth of a work is set by the artist, never by the material’s opinion of itself. “He who began a good work in you will bring it to completion” (Philippians 1:6), and he does not abandon his canvases.

For worship. God works to a pattern: those he foreknew he predestined to be conformed to the image of his Son (Romans 8:29). In plain words, he is making each of us like Jesus: every stroke is copied from that one face. When the finished work is at last unveiled, no one will admire the clay. They will praise the hands that shaped it.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul asks the Gentile believers to remember what they were: without Christ, outside Israel, strangers to the covenants, without hope and without God (vv. 11–12). Now, in Christ, they have been brought near by his blood (v. 13). Christ is our peace: he made Jew and Gentile one, reconciled both to God through the cross, and gives both access to the Father by one Spirit (vv. 14–18). So they are citizens, family and a temple where God lives by his Spirit (vv. 19–22).
verseByVerse.theology:
The Atonement and the New Community

We often think of Christ’s death only in individual terms, and that is true as far as it goes. But the cross also made a new community. Christ reconciled sinners to God and, in the same act, to one another: he reconciled “us both to God in one body through the cross” (v. 16).

So the unity of the church is not only a practical goal; it is something Christ bought with his blood. To keep up the walls he has torn down is to live against what the cross did. A reconciled congregation of very different people says, simply by existing, that the wall is down.

The temple picture (vv. 19–22) adds that the church’s holiness matters. The old temple was guarded because God dwelt there, and the church is now his dwelling by the Spirit. That gives every local church both dignity and responsibility.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The temple barrier, the soreg, was not a metaphor, and Paul’s Jewish and Gentile readers knew which wall he meant; now they sat side by side at the Lord’s table as members of one household.

Now: Churches still struggle with the walls Christ has torn down: race, class and political tribe can shape a congregation more than we notice. Ephesians 2 says the wall is down and the new humanity is more basic than any of those divisions. A church gladly one across them is showing what the cross accomplished.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore remember that at one time you Gentiles in the flesh, called “the uncircumcision” by what is called the circumcision, which is made in the flesh by hands —
verseByVerse.commentary:
Therefore. Because of verses 1–10. If God saved both Jew and Gentile by grace alone, with no works to boast of, then the wall between them has no ground left to stand on.

Remember. Forgetting is natural: the believer of thirty years drifts towards feeling like the sort of person God would naturally have wanted. God trained Israel in deliberate recollection, nearly always attached to a command about somebody else: remember you were a slave, therefore release your servant generously (Deuteronomy 15:15); you know the heart of a stranger, therefore do not oppress him (Exodus 23:9). Paul is about to tell a mixed church to live as one body, so he reminds the Gentile half how far outside they once stood.

You Gentiles in the flesh. “In the flesh” means by birth: not born into God’s covenant people.

The uncircumcision. Circumcision was God’s covenant sign to Abraham (Genesis 17:9–14) and had become the badge of Jewish identity, and many Jews called Gentiles “the uncircumcision” with contempt, as David spoke of “this uncircumcised Philistine” (1 Samuel 17:26). The name labels a whole people by what they lack, and Paul quotes it so that his readers will never be comfortable using its like about anybody else. A man who genuinely remembers being on the outside cannot easily keep another person there. And Paul says “so-called” of both labels: both are names given by people, not God’s final verdict.

Made by hands. In the Greek Old Testament the phrase “made with hands” is used of idols (as in Isaiah 46:6): circumcision valued for itself is merely human. God always wanted circumcision of the heart (Deuteronomy 10:16; 30:6; Jeremiah 4:4), and in Christ believers receive “a circumcision made without hands” (Colossians 2:11). The true Jew is one inwardly (Romans 2:28–29).

The offspring the mark pointed to. Circumcision was the sign of a promise, and the promise had a person at its heart. God told Abraham that in his offspring all the nations of the earth would be blessed (Genesis 22:18), and Paul says plainly who that offspring is: not many, but one, and that one is Christ (Galatians 3:16). So when the Gentiles of Ephesus came to Christ, they did not slip in by a side door; they arrived at the very place the mark had been pointing all along, and in him they too became “Abraham’s offspring, heirs according to promise” (Galatians 3:29). Christ was born under the law and circumcised on the eighth day (Luke 2:21), bearing in his own body the very mark the nations lacked, and he kept the covenant that every son of Abraham had broken. Then, on the cross, he bore the curse of the covenant breakers, Jew and Gentile alike (Galatians 3:13).

What it does not mean. Not that circumcision was a mistake or that God’s covenant with Israel was worthless: it was his gift and pointed to Christ (Romans 3:1–2; 9:4–5). Paul objects to the outward sign being treated as the ground of standing with God, and used to despise others.

verseByVerse.quote: remember that you were at that time separated from Christ, alienated from the commonwealth of Israel and strangers to the covenants of promise, having no hope and without God in the world.
verseByVerse.commentary:
At that time. Paul lines up five descriptions of life outside, each deeper than the last, so that the rescue in verse 13 lands with full weight.

1. Separated from Christ. The hope of the Messiah belonged to Israel (Romans 9:5); Gentiles had never been promised a Saviour, so they were not even waiting for one.

2. Alienated from the commonwealth of Israel. Citizenship: Israel was the people God had formed, ruled and lived among; Gentiles could only watch from outside.

3. Strangers to the covenants of promise. A covenant is a solemn, binding promise that creates a relationship, as wedding vows do. God made covenants with Abraham (Genesis 12; 15; 17), with Israel at Sinai, and with David (2 Samuel 7), and promised a new covenant (Jeremiah 31:31–34). All carried one promise: “I will be your God, and you shall be my people.” A stranger had no claim on what God had bound himself to give.

4. Having no hope. Not that they had no wishes or plans, but no sure hope beyond death. The ancient world was full of temples but had no certain promise that death was not the end. A common epitaph on ancient tombs ran: “I was not; I was; I am not; I do not care.” Paul says the same elsewhere of those who “grieve as others do who have no hope” (1 Thessalonians 4:13).

5. Without God in the world. Greek atheoi, in a city crowded with gods: they did not know the one true God who had revealed himself by name and kept his promises. Gods everywhere, and God nowhere.

What about people who have never heard of Christ? Paul does not soften it: outside Christ there is no hope, because there is no other name by which we must be saved (Acts 4:12). But God’s judgment is perfectly fair. No one will be condemned for rejecting a Christ he never heard of. People are judged for their sins against the light they had, the witness of creation and conscience, which all of us have resisted (Romans 1:20; 2:12–16). No one is innocent, and no one will be able to say that God was unjust. That is exactly why the church sends missionaries: Paul asks how anyone can believe in one of whom he has never heard (Romans 10:14). God has people in every tribe and language, and he will gather them (Revelation 5:9). So leave the judgment to the Judge of all the earth, who will do right (Genesis 18:25), and give, pray and go.

The vocabulary of exclusion. If you have ever stood at the edge of a group and known you did not belong, you know the taste of every word here, and it was once your standing before God. The outsiders were not given advice, a procedure or a probation. They were brought near, in a single movement, by somebody else’s blood, and the five losses are reversed one by one: no longer separated from Christ but in him; no longer alienated but citizens; no longer strangers to the covenants but heirs; no longer without hope but holding an inheritance; no longer without God but his dwelling. Every privilege this list names was his by right as Israel’s Messiah, and every one of them he shares with those who had none. The answer to the whole catalogue of exclusion is not a policy but a Person.

verseByVerse.quote: But now in Christ Jesus you who once were far off have been brought near by the blood of Christ.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But now. Matching “But God” in verse 4: there from death to life, here from distance to nearness. And in Christ Jesus is the exact reversal of “separated from Christ” (v. 12): the first loss is undone, and with it all the others.

Far off … brought near. These were almost technical terms. Jewish writers seem to have used “far off” for the Gentile world, and “brought near” for a proselyte, a Gentile admitted into the covenant people. Isaiah had promised “Peace, peace, to the far and to the near” (Isaiah 57:19), and Peter preached that the promise is “for all who are far off” (Acts 2:39). Paul takes these words and blows the standard meaning apart. Not admitted to an outer court and told to be grateful: within nine verses these people are fellow citizens, then members of the household, and finally stones built into the temple where God lives. And the verb is passive: we did not travel the distance; we were carried. What does “near” actually mean? It means welcome: your sins no longer stand between you and God, he hears you as his child, and you may come to him at any hour (Romans 5:1–2).

By the blood of Christ. “Blood” in Scripture means life given up in death, especially in sacrifice: “the life of the flesh is in the blood, and I have given it for you on the altar to make atonement” (Leviticus 17:11). The distance was not a matter of miles or of race. It was sin, which is why goodwill could never close it, and it was never only a Gentile problem. The Jew inside the barrier could not walk into God’s presence either. He watched the high priest go in for him, once a year, and never without blood (Hebrews 9:7). The wall kept Gentiles out of the court; sin kept everybody out of the holiest place. So blood is not the outsider’s entry fee; it was always the only door, and at the cross the final sacrifice was offered once, and both walked through it together (1:7; Colossians 1:20).

What it does not mean. Not that Gentiles now join Israel by becoming Jewish, nor that Jews remain near without Christ. Both come near to God in exactly the same way: through Christ, by the Spirit (v. 18). And the nearness is not undone by your feeling far from God; it rests on an event outside you. A believer may feel a very long way off on a Tuesday afternoon and still be, in the only sense this verse means, near.

parallels.desc: peace, peace, to the far and to the near

verseByVerse.quote: For he himself is our peace, who has made us both one and has broken down in his flesh the dividing wall of hostility
verseByVerse.commentary:
For he himself. “He” comes first, with emphasis. Peace is not a treaty or a feeling but a Person. “Not as the world gives do I give to you” (John 14:27): the world manages conflict; Christ gives himself. Micah promised a ruler from Bethlehem of whom it would be said, “he shall be their peace” (Micah 5:5), and Isaiah named the Messiah the Prince of Peace (Isaiah 9:6).

Our peace. Peace here has two dimensions, which the passage takes in turn: peace between peoples (vv. 14–15), and peace with God (v. 16). The second is the foundation of the first.

Has made us both one. Jew and Gentile, the deepest religious division of the ancient world. Not brought closer: made one, through union with Christ. Two people each joined to him are thereby joined to each other, whatever their cultures say, because the ground at the foot of the cross is perfectly level (Galatians 3:28).

The dividing wall of hostility. In the temple a stone balustrade separated the Court of the Gentiles from the inner courts, with notices (one found in 1871) warning any foreigner who went beyond it that he would be responsible for his own death. That wall said, in stone and law: “The presence of God is not for you; stay outside.” Paul himself was nearly lynched when he was accused of bringing a Gentile past it: Trophimus, an Ephesian (Acts 21:28–29). Christ broke it down, not lowered it. When Paul wrote, it was still standing; it fell with the temple in AD 70. But in God’s eyes it had already fallen at the cross, the day “the curtain of the temple was torn in two, from top to bottom” (Matthew 27:51).

Of hostility. The wall of stone expressed a wall in hearts: mutual hatred, contempt and suspicion.

In his flesh. On a Roman cross, on a particular Friday, not by education or goodwill. The one who hung there took both hostilities, between God and man and between Jew and Gentile, into himself, and did not pass them on (Colossians 1:20–22).

Was the Son undoing the Father’s work? If the separation between Jew and Gentile was in a real sense God’s own doing, the law, circumcision, all the rules that kept Israel apart from the nations, how can Christ be praised for demolishing it? Because he is finishing it, not undoing it. The separation was like a cast on a broken limb. Its purpose was to preserve the people through whom the Messiah would come, and to teach the world, in terms nobody could mistake, that God is holy and access to him is no casual matter. The law was a guardian until Christ came (Galatians 3:23–25). When the bone has knitted, the cast comes off, not because it was a mistake, but because it has done its work.

It was expensive. For a Jewish believer it meant eating at a Gentile’s table, setting aside food laws his forebears had died rather than break; for a Gentile, accepting salvation through a nation he thought peculiar. Acts shows how hard it proved (Acts 10; 15), with Peter himself later withdrawing from Gentile tables until Paul opposed him to his face (Galatians 2:11–14). Paul announces an accomplished fact, and spends the rest of the letter urging the church to live inside it.

Is it wrong to have separate churches for different languages or cultures? Not in itself. Where people cannot understand one another, a congregation in their own language may be the loving thing, and the apostles took practical care that Greek-speaking widows were not overlooked by appointing men from among them (Acts 6:1–6). It becomes wrong when the arrangement becomes a wall: when a church is closed in practice to people unlike its members, or when Christians pick a church to avoid people of another colour, class or background. Test your own church with honest questions. Would a stranger from another culture be welcomed, befriended and given a full share, including in leadership? Do we treat Christians in other congregations as family? Do we ever pray or work with them? Christ has made us one. Our churches should look, as far as we can make them, like people who believe it.
verseByVerse.note: The temple courts had a stone barrier with inscriptions forbidding Gentiles, on pain of death, to go further.

parallels.desc: he shall be their peace

verseByVerse.quote: by abolishing the law of commandments expressed in ordinances, that he might create in himself one new man in place of the two, so making peace,
verseByVerse.commentary:
By abolishing. To put out of action: the cross brought the old arrangement to its end.

Commandments expressed in ordinances. Paul means the law given through Moses, the arrangement under which Israel lived with God, especially the parts that marked Israel off from the nations: circumcision, food laws, sacrifices, the calendar of feasts and Sabbaths, purity rules (Colossians 2:14–17). These were God-given and good, a fence until the Messiah came (Galatians 3:23–25), but they also made Jew and Gentile two peoples who could not eat together. When the reality arrived, the scaffolding came down so the building could be seen.

What it does not mean. Not that God’s moral will has been abolished. Paul quotes the fifth commandment in this very letter (6:2–3), and chapters 4–5 are full of moral commands. The moral law, which reflects God’s character, still binds (see the next paragraph). Jesus came not to abolish the law but to fulfil it (Matthew 5:17). What is abolished is the law as a covenant that divided and condemned, not God’s holy will. Nor do Christians become lawless: they keep God’s law from a new heart, by the Spirit (Romans 8:4).

How do I know which Old Testament commands I should still keep? Read each one through Christ, and ask what the New Testament does with it. The sacrifices, priesthood, food laws, feasts and purity rules pointed to him and are fulfilled in him: you keep them by trusting the sacrifice they foreshadowed, not by repeating them (Hebrews 10:1–14; Mark 7:19; Colossians 2:16–17). The civil laws of Israel as a nation are not a code for modern states, though they still teach principles of justice and mercy (Westminster 19.4; 1689 19.4). The moral law, summed up in the Ten Commandments and in loving God and neighbour, still shows how God’s children live, and the New Testament repeats it again and again (Romans 13:8–10). On the Sabbath command Reformed Christians differ: many godly brothers keep it on the Lord’s Day, the first day of the week, as the Christian Sabbath set apart for worship and rest (Westminster 21.7–8; 1689 22.7–8), a view that deserves respect, while others see the Sabbath fulfilled in Christ’s rest (Colossians 2:16–17) and still gladly give the Lord’s Day to worship. The second is the view this commentary takes: Christ is our Sabbath rest (Hebrews 4:9–10), and the Lord’s Day is a gift rather than the fourth commandment moved to Sunday, so no one should bind another’s conscience over it (Romans 14:5). You obey all this not to be saved, but because you have been.

Create in himself. Not negotiated or organised: creation language, as of you personally in v. 10. Committees found institutions every week, but nobody can make a creature. God made the church’s unity, and the most any of us can do is refuse to damage it.

One new man. A new humanity: not Jews absorbing Gentiles, nor Gentiles absorbing Jews, but a third thing: a new humanity in Christ, in which the old division no longer defines anyone (Galatians 3:28; Colossians 3:11). A Jew does not stop being a Jew, nor a Gentile a Gentile: remain as you were called (1 Corinthians 7:18–20). The last picture Scripture gives of the redeemed is not a uniform crowd but a great multitude “from every nation, from all tribes and peoples and languages” (Revelation 7:9). Neither a melting pot nor a federation keeping a polite distance, it is one new humanity in which the differences remain and simply stop deciding anything. Your background is still yours; it is no longer your standing.

So making peace. Peace was made, with materials, labour and cost: his flesh, a crucifixion, everything he had. So peace in a church is never simply the absence of friction; it is the keeping of something expensive that somebody else paid for. So Paul says to maintain it, not create it (4:3).

Where Christians differ: Israel and the church. Dispensationalists, among them many devoted students of the Bible, hold that Israel and the church are two distinct peoples with distinct promises: the church is a parenthesis, and God will resume his earthly plan for national Israel in a future millennium. Some have taught that the church has simply replaced Israel, and that the Jewish people have no further place in God’s purposes. Covenant theology holds that there is one people of God throughout history, the one olive tree of Romans 11, now including believing Jews and Gentiles together, and that the promises to Israel find their fulfilment in Christ and his church. This commentary’s view: one people of God in Christ, as “one new man” and “one body” say. Gentiles are grafted into Israel’s olive tree, not planted beside it (Romans 11:17). But God has not finished with the Jewish people: Paul expects many Jews to come to faith in Christ (Romans 11:23–26), and they will come into the same one body, not a separate one.

verseByVerse.quote: And might reconcile us both to God in one body through the cross, thereby killing the hostility.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Reconcile. To turn enemies into friends by removing the cause of the hostility. Reconciliation assumes real enmity: “while we were enemies we were reconciled to God by the death of his Son” (Romans 5:10). The trouble was never that God was distant and we were confused. There was hostility, and that is why the remedy had to be a death and not an explanation.

Us both to God. Here is the logic of the whole passage. Jew and Gentile could not be at peace with each other while both were at war with God. Call our quarrel with God the vertical problem, and our quarrels with one another the horizontal one. The vertical lies beneath the horizontal. When both are reconciled to God through the same cross, they find themselves standing side by side. That is why purely social attempts at unity cannot last: they try to mend things between people while leaving things with God unmended.

Whose hostility? Our hostility to God is real (Romans 8:7; Colossians 1:21). But Scripture also speaks of God’s just opposition to us: we were children of wrath (v. 3). Reconciliation deals with both. At the cross, God’s wrath against sin was borne by Christ as our substitute (Romans 5:9–10; 2 Corinthians 5:21), and so the cause of the enmity is removed on God’s side; and through the gospel our hearts are won, so the enmity is removed on ours.

In one body. Probably both Christ’s body on the cross (Colossians 1:22) and the church (1:23; 4:4): one body died, so that one body might live. You are not saved privately and later invited to consider joining a church. The same act that brings you to God sets you down among people you did not choose, and who did not choose you.

Killing the hostility. Not soothed or managed: put to death, because hostility has a life of its own, grows when fed and outlives the people who started it. Human hostility usually kills people. They took Christ out and killed him, and in being killed, he killed the thing that was killing everybody. The cross is the one place where hostility did its absolute worst and was destroyed by the very thing it did. Christ did not kill his enemies; he died for them.

Why could God not simply forgive, without a cross? Because real forgiveness always costs the one who forgives. If someone wrecks your car and you forgive him, the damage does not vanish; you pay for it yourself instead of making him pay. Sin against God is real damage, to his honour, his world and his creatures, and a holy Judge cannot pretend it never happened (Proverbs 17:15). At the cross God did not overlook sin. He paid for it himself, in his Son, so that he is both just and the one who justifies the one who has faith in Jesus (Romans 3:26). The cross is not God being paid off by someone else. It is God bearing the cost of his own forgiveness.

Must I be reconciled with a believer who wronged me and will not admit it? You must forgive, and you must be willing; but full reconciliation takes two. Forgiving means letting go of revenge and handing the account to God (Romans 12:19; Mark 11:25), and that you can do alone, today. Reconciliation means restored trust, and that needs repentance on the other side (Luke 17:3). So do what lies with you: pray for him, refuse to speak against him, and go to him privately; if he will not listen, follow the steps Jesus gave (Matthew 18:15–17). You are to live at peace as far as it depends on you (Romans 12:18), and not further. Where there has been abuse, forgiveness never means returning to danger. Get safe, tell the elders, and report any crime to the police. Trust, once broken, is rebuilt slowly, by evidence of real change.

What it does not mean. Not that the cross changed God from hating to loving: God’s love sent Christ (Romans 5:8). God himself provided the sacrifice that satisfied his own justice. Nor does it mean that everyone is automatically reconciled whether they believe or not: reconciliation is received through faith, which is why the next verse speaks of preaching (v. 17; 2 Corinthians 5:20).

In everyday life. If you are at odds with a fellow believer, the order is not negotiable: vertical first. Go to the cross and look at what was forgiven you there, as the servant forgiven ten thousand talents should have done before collecting a hundred denarii (Matthew 18:23–35).

verseByVerse.quote: And he came and preached peace to you who were far off and peace to those who were near. For through him we both have access in one Spirit to the Father.
verseByVerse.commentary:
He came and preached peace. Paul is echoing Isaiah: “How beautiful upon the mountains are the feet of him who brings good news, who publishes peace” (Isaiah 52:7), and “Peace, peace, to the far and to the near” (Isaiah 57:19). Jesus never preached in Ephesus; Paul means chiefly the risen Christ, preaching through his messengers by his Spirit (Romans 10:14–15). When the gospel is faithfully preached, even by somebody nervous and doing it badly, Christ himself is preaching. When he first stood among his gathered disciples after rising, his words were, “Peace be with you” (John 20:19–21).

Far off and near. Both needed it equally: nearness was not peace. Those raised in the church, fluent in its songs, need it preached on exactly the same terms.

Access. Being ushered into a king’s presence by someone with the standing to bring you. Under the old covenant, Gentiles could go no further than the outer court, only priests entered the holy place, and only the high priest the Most Holy Place, once a year (Hebrews 9:7). Now every believer, Jew or Gentile, can come straight to God, at any time, with confidence (3:12; Hebrews 10:19–22). The torn curtain (Mark 15:38) meant the same thing as the broken wall.

In one Spirit. The Spirit makes the access real now. Coming to God is more than recalling what Christ did long ago: the Spirit who lives in the believer brings him to the Father today. God has sent the Spirit of his Son into our hearts, crying, “Abba! Father!” (Galatians 4:6). The very cry of “Father” in your prayers is the Spirit at work. And it is one Spirit: not a Jewish route and a Gentile route, but the same welcome for both (1 Corinthians 12:13).

The Trinity. Through the Son, in the Spirit, to the Father. The goal of access is family. Whenever a believer prays, however haltingly, the Father is approached, through the Son who opened the way, by the Spirit who carries the prayer from within (Romans 8:26–27). The door into the throne room of heaven stands open, and the Son holds it. The King of heaven has made his throne a place where children are expected.

What it does not mean. Not that every religion or every sincere seeker has access to God. Access is “through him”, through Christ alone (John 14:6). Nor does it mean we need no mediator: we need exactly one, and we have him (1 Timothy 2:5). No priest, saint or ritual stands between the believer and the Father.

verseByVerse.quote: So then you are no longer strangers and aliens, but you are fellow citizens with the saints and members of the household of God, built on the foundation of the apostles and prophets, Christ Jesus himself being the cornerstone,
verseByVerse.commentary:
So then. Paul gathers up everything from verses 11–18, and reverses the losses of verse 12 one by one, in three pictures: a city, a family, a temple. The movement is from the edge to the centre, from outside to home.

No longer strangers and aliens. A stranger passes through; an alien lived in the city as second-class. The Gentiles had been both. Now neither.

Fellow citizens with the saints. Roman citizenship was the most prized status in the empire. The officer who nearly flogged Paul had bought his for a large sum; Paul replied, “But I am a citizen by birth” (Acts 22:25–29). These Gentiles have been made citizens of a commonwealth beside which Rome is a temporary local arrangement, and they did not buy it. They were born into it. “Our citizenship is in heaven” (Philippians 3:20). Gentiles are not guests; they have full and equal citizenship with God’s people. And this exposes a quiet idol. Many of us draw our sense of worth from some lesser citizenship: a nation, a class, a profession, a church tradition, the circle we were admitted to. None is wrong, but none can carry the weight of who you are, and each tempts you to look down on outsiders. The citizen of heaven has nothing left to prove.

Members of the household of God. Warmer than citizenship: not a guest on probation, but family: a Father who provides, brothers and sisters in every nation, a home that cannot be taken away (1 Timothy 3:15).

Built on the foundation. Now the picture changes to a building, temple language on purpose. A foundation is laid once, and everything rests on it.

Of the apostles and prophets. The prophets here are most likely New Testament prophets (3:5; 4:11). They are the foundation in their teaching: the revelation of Christ they received and passed on, now preserved in the New Testament. Calvin said plainly that the foundation is the doctrine they preached; move away from it and the whole building falls. That is why sola Scriptura, Scripture alone as the final authority over all the church believes and does, is not a preference but a structural necessity. A church that leaves apostolic teaching does not build higher; it builds on sand.

The cornerstone. Probably the foundation cornerstone, laid first, from which every other stone took its line and level. So an error there is never small: a wall built off a crooked corner is wrong all the way up, more obviously the higher it rises. Churches drift that way, quietly taking their line from a founder’s personality, the culture’s instincts or whoever gives most, and every stone laid after that is out of true. Isaiah promised a precious cornerstone laid in Zion (Isaiah 28:16); “The stone that the builders rejected has become the cornerstone” (Psalm 118:22), and Jesus claimed it for himself (Matthew 21:42; 1 Peter 2:4–7). The builders said, “This one does not fit.” God said, “This one holds everything together.”

What it does not mean. Not that the apostles and prophets are more important than Christ: the foundation is their witness to him, and he is the stone that fixes it. Nor that new apostles and prophets with the same foundational authority continue today. A foundation is laid once; the building rises on it. This is one reason Scripture is closed: the foundation is complete, and the church is built on it, not added to it.

Where Christians differ: the continuation of prophecy. Continuationists hold that the gift of prophecy continues, often as a lesser, fallible gift distinct from the foundational prophets of this verse. Cessationists hold that apostles and prophets belonged to the foundation-laying period and ceased with it, and that God now speaks through the completed Scriptures. Continuationists point to Paul’s urging to desire the gift (1 Corinthians 14:1) and to Joel’s promise for the last days (Acts 2:17), and many faithful believers and churches hold this view with love for Scripture. This commentary’s view: cessationist, held charitably. If the apostles and prophets are the foundation, they cannot also be the walls. And whatever view one takes, no claimed word today may add to or stand alongside the apostolic foundation.

If prophecy has ceased, does God still speak to me personally? Yes: every time you open the Bible. Scripture is not God’s old voice, now silent; it is his living voice, and the Spirit uses it to comfort, warn and direct you personally (Hebrews 4:12; 2 Timothy 3:16–17). He also guides you by his providence and through the counsel of wise believers, and he may bring a verse or a person to mind at just the right moment. Such promptings can be his kindness, but they are not new revelation. Test every impression by Scripture, weigh it with others, and never say that God told you something as though it bound anyone else (Westminster Confession 1.6; 1689 London Baptist Confession 1.6). In his word you have everything you need for faith and life, so you need not hunt for hidden messages. Open the book: he is speaking.
verseByVerse.note: A cornerstone was the first, carefully placed stone that set the line of the whole building.

parallels.desc: a precious cornerstone

verseByVerse.quote: in whom the whole structure, being joined together, grows into a holy temple in the Lord.
verseByVerse.commentary:
In whom. In Christ the whole structure rises, because he is not only the first stone of the temple. He is the temple. Jesus said, “Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up,” and John explains that he was speaking about the temple of his body (John 2:19–21). The place where God meets sinners is no longer a building in Jerusalem but the risen Son. So the church can be a holy temple only because it is built in him, joined to the one in whom “the whole fullness of deity dwells bodily” (Colossians 2:9).

Being joined together. A builder’s word (again in 4:16): stones fitted so that each bears on the next. Each believer is a living stone (1 Peter 2:5), and God shapes us to fit with others, often through the friction of living with very different people. The verb says this is being done to us, and is still going on: no stone chose its neighbours, which is worth remembering when the people beside you are not the people you would have picked. They did not pick you either. Neither of you is the mason.

Grows. Buildings do not grow; Paul mixes the pictures on purpose. The building gives the church its solidity: God is here. The body gives it life: still becoming what it is meant to be (4:15–16). A church goes wrong by losing either picture. Lose the growing, and you have a congregation beautifully maintained in which nothing happens, kept open like a heritage site. Lose the building, and you get warmth without shape, a movement that glows for five years and then finds it has no foundation.

A holy temple. The inner sanctuary. Beside the vast temple of Artemis, Paul says the true temple is not marble but people, and the temple whose wall kept Gentiles out (v. 14) is replaced: Gentiles are now not only allowed in, they are part of the building (1 Corinthians 3:16–17; 2 Corinthians 6:16). It is holy because it is in the Lord: he is in it, and it belongs to him. That should sober us as well as comfort us (Leviticus 10:1–3). Gossip, division and sin quietly tolerated in a congregation are not bad manners; they defile God’s house, which is why Paul warns that God will destroy anyone who destroys his temple (1 Corinthians 3:17).

Unfinished, and not ashamed of it. The building grows into a holy temple; it has not arrived. So when your church disappoints you, and it will, because a growing thing is always partly unformed, you are not looking at a ruin. You are standing on a building site. The dust and noise and half-built walls are not evidence that the project has failed. They are evidence that it is still going on, and that the Builder has not left.

In everyday life. Ask two questions. Is anyone in your church bearing weight on you, someone for whom your absence would be a real problem, not just an empty seat? And whose weight are you carrying? If the honest answer to both is nobody, you are living like a stone leaning against the wall, when Christ has already set you in it. The difference is invisible from the road and total in a storm. If that is because you are ill, new or lonely rather than unwilling, it is no failure: tell one person, and let the Mason fit you in.

verseByVerse.quote: In him you also are being built together into a dwelling place for God by the Spirit.
verseByVerse.commentary:
In him you also. The emphasis falls on “you also”: you who were far off, without God (v. 12), are now part of his dwelling. The outsiders have become the house.

Built together. The church is not finished: each conversion adds a stone.

A dwelling place for God. The God who fills all things (1:23) has always longed to live among his people. He walked with Adam in the garden (Genesis 3:8). When sin shattered that, he told Israel, “let them make me a sanctuary, that I may dwell in their midst” (Exodus 25:8), and his glory filled the tabernacle (Exodus 40:34–35). Because of Israel’s idolatry, Ezekiel watched the glory leave the temple (Ezekiel 10–11), yet he was promised that the glory would return (Ezekiel 43:1–5), and it returned in a form no one expected. “The Word became flesh and dwelt among us”, literally pitched his tent among us, “and we have seen his glory” (John 1:14). Then at Pentecost the Spirit came down not on a temple but on people (Acts 2:3): God moving in again, now into his people (1 Corinthians 3:16). And one day the whole new creation will be his home: “Behold, the dwelling place of God is with man” (Revelation 21:3). The gathered church is the present chapter of that story.

By the Spirit. God lives in the church not symbolically but really, by the Holy Spirit. So when believers gather, God is not merely remembered or imagined; he is present, hearing their prayers, speaking through his word and binding them together, so that even an outsider may sense that God is really among them (1 Corinthians 14:25; Matthew 18:20).

The address. Many look for God’s presence in a place, a view or a quality of silence, and the hunger is not silly. But Paul’s address is a people. The people near you on Sunday, the awkward ones, the one who talks too long afterwards, the family whose children never sit still, are not the setting in which you might meet God. Together, they are the place where he has chosen to live. The chapter opened with corpses and ends with the same people as the house God lives in. That is the distance grace covers, in twenty-two verses.

In the flow. Chapter 3 begins to pray for this temple, and chapter 4 urges the church to keep the unity of this one building (4:1–6): chapters 1–3 tell the church what God has made it, and chapters 4–6 how to live as what it already is.

For worship. When a handful of forgiven sinners meet in his name, the God of the burning bush and the filled temple is not visiting. He lives there. He makes his home with the unworthy, and he will never move out.

2.overview:
Chapter 2 tells the gospel twice. First as the story of every believer (vv. 1–10): we were dead in sin and by nature under God’s wrath, but God, rich in mercy, made us alive with Christ and seated us with him. Salvation is by grace through faith, God’s gift and not our achievement, and it creates us for the good works he prepared for us.

Then as the story of two peoples (vv. 11–22). Gentiles were once far off, without Christ, hope or God, and by Christ’s blood they have been brought near. Christ broke down the wall between Jew and Gentile, made one new humanity and reconciled both to God through the cross. Now they are fellow citizens and members of God’s household, a temple built on Christ the cornerstone, where God lives by his Spirit.

3.title: The Mystery of Christ and the Fullness of God
3.text: <sup>1</sup>For this reason I, Paul, a prisoner of Christ Jesus on behalf of you Gentiles — <sup>2</sup>assuming that you have heard of the stewardship of God’s grace that was given to me for you, <sup>3</sup>how the mystery was made known to me by revelation, as I have written briefly. <sup>4</sup>When you read this, you can perceive my insight into the mystery of Christ, <sup>5</sup>which was not made known to the sons of men in other generations as it has now been revealed to his holy apostles and prophets by the Spirit. <sup>6</sup>This mystery is that the Gentiles are fellow heirs, members of the same body, and partakers of the promise in Christ Jesus through the gospel. <sup>7</sup>Of this gospel I was made a minister according to the gift of God’s grace, which was given me by the working of his power. <sup>8</sup>To me, though I am the very least of all the saints, this grace was given, to preach to the Gentiles the unsearchable riches of Christ, <sup>9</sup>and to bring to light for everyone what is the plan of the mystery hidden for ages in God, who created all things, <sup>10</sup>so that through the church the manifold wisdom of God might now be made known to the rulers and authorities in the heavenly places. <sup>11</sup>This was according to the eternal purpose that he has realized in Christ Jesus our Lord, <sup>12</sup>in whom we have boldness and access with confidence through our faith in him. <sup>13</sup>So I ask you not to lose heart over what I am suffering for you, which is your glory. <sup>14</sup>For this reason I bow my knees before the Father, <sup>15</sup>from whom every family in heaven and on earth is named, <sup>16</sup>that according to the riches of his glory he may grant you to be strengthened with power through his Spirit in your inner being, <sup>17</sup>so that Christ may dwell in your hearts through faith — that you, being rooted and grounded in love, <sup>18</sup>may have strength to comprehend with all the saints what is the breadth and length and height and depth, <sup>19</sup>and to know the love of Christ that surpasses knowledge, that you may be filled with all the fullness of God. <sup>20</sup>Now to him who is able to do far more abundantly than all that we ask or think, according to the power at work within us, <sup>21</sup>to him be glory in the church and in Christ Jesus throughout all generations, forever and ever. Amen.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul explains why he, a prisoner, writes to Gentiles as he does: the mystery once hidden is now made plain, so that through the church God’s wisdom is displayed to the heavenly powers, and believers come to God with boldness through faith in Christ. His sufferings are no reason to lose heart.
verseByVerse.theology:
The mystery hidden and revealed

In Paul a mystery (mystērion) is not a puzzle but a secret kept in God and now disclosed in the gospel. The inclusion of the Gentiles was not absent from the Old Testament: it was there in the promise to Abraham (Genesis 12:3), in the prophets (Isaiah 49:6; 60:3) and in the Psalms (Psalm 87; 96:3). What waited for Christ was its full disclosure: Gentiles brought in as equals, in one body, without first becoming Jews.

The whole Bible works this way: first the outline, then the real thing, as a sketch comes before the finished painting. The two Testaments are one message unfolding. So reading the Old Testament with Christ in view is not forcing something onto it. It is following where it was already going.

Paul’s description of himself as “the very least of all the saints” (v. 8) shows what grace does to a person. The man who had dragged believers to prison counts himself the least worthy of the grace he preaches.
