The nearer a believer comes to Christ, the more clearly he sees his own shortfall, and the more wonderful it is that grace reached him.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Ephesus knew plenty of riches that could be counted: the wealth of Artemis’ temple, gods who could be appeased, secrets that could be bought by initiation. Paul announces something of another kind, “the unsearchable riches of Christ” (v. 8): riches with no edge that can be traced, which are not used up by being given away.

Now: Paul writes this from a Roman cell and tells the church not to lose heart over his sufferings (v. 13). God still carries his glorious gospel in plain containers: a persecuted church, a small congregation the world ignores. Paul calls this “treasure in jars of clay” (2 Corinthians 4:7): something priceless kept in a cheap pot, so that nobody mistakes the pot for the treasure. Such a church may look weak, yet it is where the powers are watching God’s wisdom on display.

verseByVerse.quote: For this reason I, Paul, a prisoner of Christ Jesus on behalf of you Gentiles—
verseByVerse.commentary:
Meaning first. Ephesians 3 is a prayer interrupted by an explanation. Paul begins to pray (v. 1), then stops to explain why he, a prisoner, may speak to Gentiles this way (vv. 2–13): God made him steward of the mystery that the Gentiles are fellow heirs in Christ, so that through the church God’s wisdom is displayed to the powers. Then he resumes the prayer (vv. 14–19) and closes the teaching half of the letter with a doxology, a burst of praise (vv. 20–21).

For this reason. Because of everything in chapter 2: Gentiles have been brought near and are being built into God’s temple (2:19–22). Paul begins to pray, breaks off, and picks the prayer up again in verse 14 with the same words. Verses 2–13 are a digression: they need to know why he can say this.

I, Paul, a prisoner of Christ Jesus. The emphatic “I, Paul” is used when Paul puts his own authority and story on the line (2 Corinthians 10:1; Galatians 5:2). Humanly, Paul was a prisoner of Rome, chained to a soldier (Acts 28:16, 30). But he does not write “a prisoner of Nero”. He names a different master. Rome believes it is holding him; Paul knows that Christ put him there, and why: so that the gospel would spread (Philippians 1:12–14). Christ Jesus is Lord even over a Roman cell, and he turns his servant’s prison into a pulpit for the nations. Christ himself was once bound and led away to die, so that Gentiles might go free.

On behalf of you Gentiles. This is far more literal than it looks. Paul was seized by a mob in the Jerusalem temple, shouting that he had brought Greeks past the barrier and defiled the holy place. Luke says why they thought so: they had seen him in the city with Trophimus the Ephesian (Acts 21:27–29). Paul had not taken him through. But in a deeper sense the charge was true, because Paul had insisted that the wall was down (2:14). The doctrine of chapter 2 cost him his freedom, and he is explaining it to the very people it was about.

In everyday life. Listen to how you describe your situation: “I am stuck here because of” the employer, the diagnosis, the person. Paul had every right to that sentence and never used it. He does not call the chains good; he simply says whose they are. You are not the prisoner of your situation, but a servant of Christ placed where he wants you.
verseByVerse.note: Paul was imprisoned because of his mission to the Gentiles; he breaks off here and resumes in verse 14.

verseByVerse.quote: assuming that you have heard of the stewardship of God's grace that was given to me for you, how the mystery was made known to me by revelation,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Assuming that you have heard. Or “surely you have heard”: a polite expression, not real doubt. The letter was probably meant for several churches around Ephesus (the words “in Ephesus” are missing from some of the earliest manuscripts of 1:1), so some readers had not met Paul, but would have heard of his calling.

The stewardship of God’s grace. “Stewardship” is oikonomia, the running of a household, the same word as God’s own plan in 1:10. A steward was often a trusted slave who ran the whole estate: the keys, the accounts, the distribution of food to the household (Luke 12:42). Nothing in his hands was his, and everything in his hands was there to be given out. A steward who hoarded his master’s grain was not being careful; he was being unfaithful. God is not a hoarder. The grace Paul stewards is God’s own wealth, meant for distribution, and its supply never runs low. Paul is the steward of grace, not its owner (1 Corinthians 4:1–2).

That was given to me for you. The grace of his commission, his calling as apostle to the Gentiles (v. 8; Romans 15:15–16). It arrived addressed to somebody else: not for his honour, but for their benefit.

The mystery. In everyday English a mystery is a puzzle that cannot be solved. In Paul it means almost the opposite: a secret of God, hidden until God chose to reveal it, and now openly made known (Romans 16:25–26; Colossians 1:26).

Made known to me by revelation. Paul did not work it out. He had trained under Gamaliel (Acts 22:3), and none of it produced this. It was disclosed to him on a road, by the one he was travelling to persecute (Galatians 1:11–12; Acts 26:16–18). The mystery reached Paul first not as a doctrine but as a Person: “I am Jesus whom you are persecuting” (Acts 26:15). If the mystery had to be deduced, only the clever would ever have it. It is revealed, and so it belongs to anyone willing to receive it.

In everyday life. Take an honest inventory: money, skills, a spare room, years of experience, the gospel itself. Do not only ask, “Am I using this wisely?” A careful man can say yes to that and still keep every bit of it for himself. Ask instead: “Who was this given to me for?”
verseByVerse.note: A stewardship is a trust given to a household manager.

verseByVerse.quote: as I have written briefly. When you read this, you can perceive my insight into the mystery of Christ,
verseByVerse.commentary:
As I have written briefly. Paul refers back to this very letter, especially 1:9–10 (God’s plan to unite all things in Christ) and 2:11–22 (Jew and Gentile one in Christ), not to an earlier, lost letter. And “When you read” means read aloud: letters were read in the congregation (Colossians 4:16; 1 Thessalonians 5:27), publicly and repeatedly.

You can perceive my insight. “Insight” (synesis) means understanding, the ability to put things together. Paul is not boasting. The authority of his message can be tested by reading it: it hangs together, and it unlocks the Old Testament promises.

The mystery of Christ. Paul’s word echoes Daniel, where the God in heaven reveals mysteries that no wise man could tell (Daniel 2:27–28). His readers also knew the word from the mystery cults, the secret religious societies of their cities. There a mystērion was a secret ceremony, and members swore never to tell outsiders. Paul’s mystery is the opposite: announced to all nations, written down and read aloud. And the secret is Christ himself: what God has done in him, including the joining of Jew and Gentile in one body (v. 6). What Paul received by revelation, we receive by reading, and the Spirit who gave it is glad to open it to you.

verseByVerse.quote: The mystery of Christ, which was not made known to the sons of men in other generations as it has now been revealed to his holy apostles and prophets by the Spirit.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Not made known as it has now been revealed. “Sons of men” simply means human beings. And the word “as” matters: not completely unknown, but not known as it is now. The Old Testament did promise blessing to the nations (Genesis 12:3; Isaiah 49:6). What was not clear was how: that Gentiles would come in not by becoming Jews, through circumcision and the law, but directly in Christ, as full and equal members of one new body.

Stand with the men who did not get to see it. Peter says the prophets “searched and inquired carefully, inquiring what person or time the Spirit of Christ in them was indicating when he predicted the sufferings of Christ and the subsequent glories” (1 Peter 1:10–11). Isaiah writes of a man pierced for our transgressions and crushed for our iniquities, and then goes back over his own page trying to work out whose face he has just described. And “it was revealed to them that they were serving not themselves but you” (1 Peter 1:12). Many prophets and righteous people longed to see what you see, and did not see it (Matthew 13:16–17). So on an ordinary morning, with an open Bible, you know whose face it was. That is no reason for pride. It is a reason to stop handling your Bible as a duty and start handling it as the answer to somebody else’s lifelong question, put into your hands.

To his holy apostles and prophets. “Holy” means set apart by God for this task, not personally sinless. The apostles and prophets are the foundation of the church (2:20) because they received the revelation of the mystery and passed it on. The prophets here are New Testament prophets, listed after the apostles (2:20; 4:11). They received it by the Spirit, the revealer (1 Corinthians 2:10–13; John 16:13).

When someone says “God told me”, is that the same thing? No, not in the sense of this verse. What the apostles and prophets received was revelation binding on the whole church, and it was written down once for all as Scripture (Hebrews 1:1–2; Jude 3). God still guides his people today: by his word, by the Spirit opening our eyes to it, by the counsel of others and by his providence. A verse may come home to you with great force, and that is the Spirit at work. But an impression in your heart, however strong, is not a new word from God, and it never carries Scripture’s authority (the Westminster Confession 1.6; the 1689 London Baptist Confession 1.6). So test every “God told me”, your own included, by the Bible. If it adds to Scripture or contradicts it, set it aside. If it agrees, the authority lies in Scripture, not in the impression. Many Christians in charismatic and Pentecostal churches believe gifts such as prophecy continue today, and most agree that no such word carries Scripture’s authority. This commentary holds that revelation of this foundational kind ended with the apostles and prophets, while gladly honouring brothers and sisters who differ.

Why did God wait so long to make it known? Because he was not idle while he waited. The centuries of promise, sacrifice and law were a schoolroom, teaching what kind of Saviour was needed (Galatians 3:24). Christ came in the fullness of time (Galatians 4:4), not late. Nor were those generations left out. Abraham believed the promise and it was counted to him as righteousness (Romans 4:3), and the Old Testament saints died in faith, greeting from afar what we now see (Hebrews 11:13). They were saved by the same Christ, looked for in advance.

Where Christians differ: was the church entirely hidden? Classic dispensationalists, who read the Bible as a series of distinct eras with separate plans for Israel and the church, teach that the church was completely unknown in the Old Testament, a parenthesis inserted into God’s programme for Israel, which will resume after the church is removed. Covenant theology, which reads the Bible as one unfolding covenant of grace, holds that the church fulfils God’s promises to Abraham and the prophets, now revealed far more clearly. Paul’s word “as” (not known as it is now) implies that something was known before, and elsewhere he shows that the Gentiles’ inclusion fulfils the promise to Abraham (Galatians 3:8, 29) and the prophets (Romans 15:8–12). This commentary’s view: the church is the fulfilment of God’s one plan, partly foreseen and now fully revealed. Dispensationalist believers love Christ and his word, and this is a disagreement among brothers about how the Bible’s story fits together, not about the gospel.

verseByVerse.quote: This mystery is that the Gentiles are fellow heirs, members of the same body, and partakers of the promise in Christ Jesus through the gospel.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Three “fellow” words. Now Paul says exactly what the mystery is, in three Greek compounds beginning with syn (with, together). The middle one appears nowhere in surviving Greek before this letter: a man reaching for a word that does not exist, because the thing he is describing had never existed either.

First, fellow heirs. Synklēronoma: co-heirs. Gentiles inherit everything God promised Abraham and his descendants (1:11, 14, 18; Galatians 3:29). They are not tenants or guests on Israel’s estate; they inherit it equally.

Second, members of the same body. Syssōma: co-bodied, the coined word. Not two bodies side by side, but one body with one head, Christ (2:16; 4:4). The Gentile believer is not an extra part fastened on from outside. He belongs to the same body as you, as your hand and your foot are both you.

Third, partakers of the promise. Symmetocha: co-sharers. The promise is God’s great promise to Abraham and his offspring, summed up in the gift of the Holy Spirit (1:13; Galatians 3:14) and in God’s pledge to be their God.

Made one where his body was broken. Everything they share is in Christ Jesus: joined to him by faith, so that what is true of him is counted true of us, his standing with the Father, his inheritance, his future (Galatians 3:26–29). He is the true offspring of Abraham (Galatians 3:16), so the whole inheritance is his, and all who are in him inherit it with him. And Christ reconciled Jew and Gentile to God in one body through the cross (2:16). The one body of the church was made where his own body was broken for both. No Gentile earns his way onto Israel’s estate, and no Jew keeps it by ancestry; both stand in the one Son.

Through the gospel. The means of inclusion is the good news believed, not ancestry, circumcision or law-keeping. This is why Paul fought so hard against those who wanted Gentiles circumcised (Galatians 2:3–5; 5:2–6).

Second-class, without anyone saying so. Nobody writes second-class membership into a church constitution. It simply grows, quietly, in who gets treated as family and who as a guest: the convert with a visible past whom people are glad to see and slow to trust, the newcomer who has not learned the vocabulary, the one who arrives with noisy children. None of them is told they are lesser; they are simply never quite folded in. But fellow heir means they will inherit exactly what you inherit: not less, not later, not on conditions. The way you treat them this week is either a rehearsal for the age to come or a contradiction of it.

What it does not mean. Not that Gentiles replace Jews, or that Jewish believers lose anything. It is fellow heirs: sharing, not taking over. Nor that ethnic identity is erased (see 2:14). The point is equal standing before God and equal belonging in his family.

Does God still have a purpose for the Jewish people? Yes. Paul says plainly that God has not rejected the people he foreknew (Romans 11:1–2), and that his gifts and calling are irrevocable (Romans 11:29). But that purpose is not a separate road to salvation running beside the church. Paul pictures God’s people as one olive tree: Israel is the tree, and Gentile believers are wild branches grafted in. There is one tree, one body and one way in: faith in Jesus the Messiah (Romans 11:17–24; John 14:6). Jewish people need Christ exactly as Gentiles do, and many Reformed Christians, reading Romans 11:25–26, expect a great turning of Israel to Christ before the end, natural branches grafted back into their own tree; others read “all Israel” there as the full number of God’s people, Jew and Gentile, gathered through the whole age. On either reading, a Jew is saved exactly as a Gentile is, by faith in the Messiah. So love your Jewish friends and neighbours, pray for them, and share the gospel with them gladly. It came to them first (Romans 1:16), and the promises you now share were spoken first to their fathers.

verseByVerse.quote: Of this gospel I was made a minister according to the gift of God’s grace, which was given me by the working of his power. To me, though I am the very least of all the saints, this grace was given, to preach to the Gentiles the unsearchable riches of Christ.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Of this gospel I was made a minister. “Minister” is diakonos, servant, the word from which deacon comes, used of a waiter at table. And “I was made”: God appointed him; he did not apply.

By the working of his power. The same language as 1:19–20: the power that raised Christ from the dead. It took resurrection power to turn Saul the persecutor into Paul the apostle (Acts 9:1–22), and it takes the same power to sustain his ministry (Colossians 1:29).

Though I am the very least of all the saints. Paul bends the language again: “leaster”, less than the least. It is not false modesty. “Saul was ravaging the church, and entering house after house, he dragged off men and women and committed them to prison” (Acts 8:3). Picture a door opening at the wrong hour, a husband or a wife dragged out past the neighbours. And he speaks in the present: decades on, an apostle with churches across the empire, this is what he still counts himself. The memory never left him. It never disqualified him either. Watch his self-description move: least of the apostles (1 Corinthians 15:9, about AD 55), least of all the saints (here, about AD 61), foremost of sinners (1 Timothy 1:15, about AD 63). The older he grew in grace, the lower he saw himself. And what had made him that man was not unbelief but religion: zeal for God, blameless by the law’s standard (Philippians 3:5–6; Acts 26:9). Religion used to earn God’s favour had made him cruel. Grace rescues the respectable as surely as the rebel.

This grace was given. Paul cannot speak of his ministry without speaking of grace (1 Corinthians 15:10): to me, the very least, this grace was given. He never forgets what he was, and he never doubts what he has been given. He holds both together. And the grace was given for one task: to bring the Gentiles good news (euangelisasthai, the verb behind our word evangelise).

The unsearchable riches of Christ. “Riches” is one of Paul’s favourite words in this letter: of grace (1:7; 2:7), of glory (1:18), and now of Christ himself. “Unsearchable” (anexichniaston) means beyond tracing out, like a path through a forest whose tracks simply stop (Romans 11:33). And these riches are not an asset Christ hands out at arm’s length; they are him: forgiveness, adoption, wisdom, the Spirit, hope, and deepest of all, “the surpassing worth of knowing Christ Jesus my Lord” (Philippians 3:8; Colossians 2:3). No lifetime of preaching empties them. Here is a Saviour whose wealth does not shrink when it is shared, who gives himself away to the unworthy without ever coming to the end of what he is. And they were handed, for preaching, to a man who had dragged women out of their houses for believing in him.

In everyday life. Is there something in your past that you assume has ruled you out of usefulness? When someone says, “God uses ordinary people”, do you add silently, “but not people who have done what I did”? Put it beside what Paul did. He is not the exception; he is the pattern. Your past does not disqualify you from serving him; only pride does.

verseByVerse.quote: and to bring to light for everyone what is the plan of the mystery hidden for ages in God, who created all things,
verseByVerse.commentary:
To bring to light. To illuminate, and for everyone, because God’s plan is public. Light does not make what it shows. Switch a lamp on in a dark room and nothing is created: the furniture was there all along, and you had been barking your shins on it. The plan of God stood complete before the world was made; at Christ’s coming the light went on. A Christian is someone who has been shown the room he was already standing in. Faith does not make these things true; it opens your eyes to them.

The plan of the mystery. “Plan” is oikonomia again (v. 2; 1:10). The church, the one new humanity made of Jew and Gentile, is not an emergency measure or a change of plan. It is exactly what God was working towards from the beginning.

Hidden for ages in God. The plan was kept in God’s own mind from eternity (1:4, 9–11). No searching could have found it, because it was hidden not in the world but in the one who stands behind the world. “None of the rulers of this age understood this, for if they had, they would not have crucified the Lord of glory” (1 Corinthians 2:7–8).

Who created all things. Why mention creation here? Because the God who saves is the God who made everything. Redemption is not a repair job on a project that went wrong, but the Creator carrying through his original purpose: “to unite all things in Christ” (1:10). The new creation, the people God is remaking in Christ (2:10, 15), is what the first creation was always for.

The light has a face. What switched the lamp on was a Person. The God who said, “Let light shine out of darkness,” “has shone in our hearts to give the light of the knowledge of the glory of God in the face of Jesus Christ” (2 Corinthians 4:6). The Creator made all things through the Son and for him (Colossians 1:16). To be shown the plan is to be shown him.

Nothing wasted? That is an easy sentence to write and a hard one to believe on a Thursday afternoon. Many of us can point to stretches that look like waste: the years in a job that led nowhere, the decade lost to illness or a broken marriage, the door that closed and never opened. Paul does not deny the experience. He names who is doing the managing. And here is something you can do on paper tonight. Trace how you came to hear the gospel at all. Who actually told you? How did you come to be in that room, that school, that ward, that friendship? Follow it back four or five links, and you will find a chain of things that looked entirely accidental, most of them arranged by people who had no idea what they were doing. Someone moved house. Someone fell ill. Someone invited the wrong person by mistake. That is God running his household. If he managed all that without once consulting you, the years you have written off are far more likely to be rooms in the same house than evidence against it.

Textual note. Later manuscripts, followed by the King James Version, read “fellowship” (koinōnia) instead of “plan” (oikonomia), and add “by Jesus Christ” after “created all things”. This commentary’s view: “plan” is original, supported by the earliest manuscripts, and “by Jesus Christ” is a later expansion. The truth it adds is biblical (Colossians 1:16), but it is not part of this verse.

verseByVerse.quote: so that through the church the manifold wisdom of God might now be made known to the rulers and authorities in the heavenly places.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Through the church. This is the purpose of Paul’s preaching (vv. 8–9), and of the mystery itself. Not through the stars, or the great events of world history, but through the church: ordinary people gathered in Christ. The church is God’s display to the universe.

The manifold wisdom of God. “Manifold” (polypoikilos), found only here in the New Testament, means many-coloured, the word used of embroidered cloth or a meadow of flowers. God’s wisdom is seen in the variety of people he gathers: Jew and Gentile, slave and free, rich and poor, every culture, joined in one body without losing their variety. No diplomacy ever dissolved the division between Jew and Gentile. The wisdom shows in the method too: a crucified Messiah as cornerstone, a persecutor as chief missionary, forgiven sinners as the display of his glory (1 Corinthians 1:27–28). The cross looked like Christ’s defeat, and God made it the place where he was crowned King. A church of people who are all alike shows less of this wisdom.

The back of the cloth. Embroidery has two sides. From the back it is a mess: knots, loose ends, colours stopping dead in the middle of nowhere. Turn it over, and every thread turns out to have been going somewhere. From where you sit, the church does not look like the display of the wisdom of God. It looks like a rota that keeps failing, two families not speaking, a treasurer worried about the roof, and a man in the third row you privately gave up on. You are looking at the back of the cloth. Paul does not say the knots are imaginary. He says the front is facing somewhere else: God sees the finished picture, and he is showing it to the powers of heaven.

To the rulers and authorities in the heavenly places. The display is happening now, in this age, and its audience is spiritual beings, angelic and demonic (1:21; 6:12), unusually prominent in this letter perhaps because Ephesus was gripped by fear of named powers (Acts 19:19). Good angels watch with wonder. Evil powers watch their defeat. What does it mean that they are defeated, when evil is plainly still at work? At the cross Christ cancelled the record of debt that gave the accuser his case against us, put the powers to open shame, and broke the power of the fear in which they held us (Colossians 2:14–15; Hebrews 2:14–15); their end is fixed (Revelation 20:10), though their final destruction is still to come. The church is the ongoing public announcement of that victory. Every time former strangers call the same God Father, God is saying to every power in the universe: “Look what my wisdom has done.” And the moments on display are not the ones anyone photographs. Two members quietly reconciling after eighteen months of coldness. A widow driven to the hospital by someone who does not much like her. Six people at a prayer meeting on a wet Tuesday. A former enemy passing the bread to a former enemy. That is the embroidery. The powers are studying it, and it tells them that the crucified one has won.

In the flow. Verse 10 explains why this letter cares so much about church life. The unity of 4:1–16 is not good manners, and the same rulers and authorities are named again in 6:12. So the next time you decide some relationship in the church is not worth the effort, remember that it is not a distraction from the display. It is the display.

What it does not mean. Not that the church preaches to angels, or that we should try to address or command spiritual powers. The church makes God’s wisdom known simply by being what it is: a reconciled people. Nor does “wisdom” mean cleverness. God’s wisdom is his skill in achieving his good purposes, above all through the cross, which looks like foolishness to the world (1 Corinthians 1:18–25).

Do angels not already know everything about God? No. Angels are wise and holy, but they are creatures, and they learn as creatures do. Jesus said that even the angels in heaven do not know the day of his return (Matthew 24:36), and Peter says they long to look into the things of the gospel (1 Peter 1:12). They saw God make the world and shouted for joy (Job 38:7), but they had never seen anything like a crucified Lord gathering former enemies into one family. They learn the depths of God’s wisdom by watching what he does, and here they watch it in the church. That should change how you think of an ordinary Sunday. Heaven is not bored by your congregation. It is studying it.

verseByVerse.quote: This was according to the eternal purpose that he has realized in Christ Jesus our Lord, in whom we have boldness and access with confidence through our faith in him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The eternal purpose. Literally the purpose of the ages. The church is not plan B: God planned it before time (1:4, 11). “Realized” means carried out, in Christ’s life, death, resurrection and ascension.

In whom we have boldness. Paul said this in 2:18, and now he says it stronger. His readers had come out of a world of spiritual dread: gods unpredictable and unapproachable, managed by ritual. “Boldness” (parrēsia) was the free citizen’s right to speak openly in the assembly, in his own words, without first getting permission. Listen to the praying of someone who does not believe he has that right. It is hedged. “If it be your will” comes early, not as submission but as insurance, so that nothing has quite been asked and nothing can be refused. The requests stay small. And after a bad week the praying stops, on the grounds that it would be decent to stay away until things improve. Every one of those instincts belongs to a servant on probation, and Paul says that is not what you are. The grief may come out as grief, the anger where there is anger, because a son does not brief his father the way a petitioner briefs an official.

And access. Prosagōgē: the right of entry into the king’s presence, granted by one with the standing to bring you in (2:18). Your introducer is Christ himself, and his welcome does not rise and fall with how your week has gone.

With confidence. Assurance that we will be welcomed, not turned away. Those who were far off and without God (2:12–13) can now come boldly to the throne of grace (Hebrews 4:16; 10:19–22). Feel what that overcomes: when Isaiah saw the holy Lord he cried that he was lost (Isaiah 6:3–5), and a careless approach to the holy place meant death (Leviticus 16:2). And check the tense: we have. Present possession, held at this moment by a man in chains, and shared with everyone reading over his shoulder.

Through our faith in him. You do not come to God saying, “I have had a good week, so hear me”; you come saying, “Jesus died and rose for me, so hear me.” The first confidence rises and falls with you; the second stands as firm as he does (Hebrews 10:19–21).

Textual and translation note. The phrase can be translated “through his faithfulness” (Christ’s own faithfulness), and some scholars argue for that. This commentary’s view: the usual translation, faith in him, best fits Paul’s usage in Ephesians, where faith is the believer’s trust in Christ (1:15; 2:8). Either way, our confidence rests on Christ.

What it does not mean. Not casualness or presumption. We draw near with confidence, and what we draw near to is a throne (Hebrews 4:16; 12:28): with reverence and awe, but without fear of rejection, as children come to a father.

In everyday life. Think of the thing you have not yet said to God because it seemed too small, too angry or too late. In Christ there is no wrong size and no wrong hour. The door you are hesitating at is already open.

verseByVerse.quote: So I ask you not to lose heart over what I am suffering for you, which is your glory.
verseByVerse.commentary:
So I ask you. The digression ends where it began: with Paul’s chains (v. 1). And the man in the cell is worried about the morale of the people who are free.

Not to lose heart. To grow weary, to lose your nerve, to give up (enkakein). The readers might reason: if the apostle of this gospel is in prison, perhaps the gospel is failing. That danger is real, and it still empties pews. What makes people give up is very often not their own suffering but somebody else’s. A respected pastor is diagnosed at fifty-two. A couple who prayed for years for a child end up burying one. A missionary family comes home broken. Nobody announces a change of belief; it happens quietly, in the gap between what was preached and what was watched, and people conclude that the thing does not seem to work. Paul knows the Ephesians are doing that arithmetic about him, and he interrupts it.

Suffering for you. Paul is in prison because he took the gospel to the Gentiles (Acts 21:28–29). But the words “for you” were not first his: “This is my body, which is for you” (1 Corinthians 11:24). His cell is no sign that the gospel is failing. It shows a servant’s life taking the shape of his Lord’s. Christ did not save us by avoiding pain but by entering it, and the Father exalted him because he humbled himself (Philippians 2:8–9). That is the way of our God: he wins by losing, gives life through death, and makes the hardships of his servants serve the joy of his people.

Which is your glory. In plain words: my chains are nothing for you to be ashamed of; they are to your honour. They show how much your salvation is worth: a man will go to prison to bring it to you. And they carry forward the gospel through which you will one day share Christ’s glory (2 Timothy 2:10; Philippians 1:12–14): raised bodies, sin gone for good, and the sight of Christ’s face as we are made like him (Romans 8:18, 30; 1 John 3:2). And Paul is restrained. He does not explain why God allowed the arrest, or when release might come. He gives one sentence about what the suffering is for, and leaves everything else alone. Our attempts to comfort one another often go wrong by trying to supply reasons we do not have.

What it does not mean. Not that Paul’s sufferings add anything to what Christ did on the cross to pay for sin, or earn the Gentiles’ salvation. Christ’s suffering alone saves. Paul suffers to bring that salvation to others (Colossians 1:24).

In everyday life. When someone faithful is suffering, it is easy to look for the flaw, the hidden sin, the weak faith, because a flaw would explain it: he suffers because he did wrong, so the rest of us are safe. Paul offers no flaw to find. He offers a purpose.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul kneels before the Father and asks for one thing in a chain of steps, ending in the fullness of God, and then breaks into praise of the God whose power at work in us does far more than we ask or think.
verseByVerse.theology:
The indwelling Christ and the fullness of God

This prayer names the goal of the Christian life: to be “filled with all the fullness of God” (v. 19). Paul sets no ceiling on what he asks for the Ephesians, because God sets none on what he gives.

The way to that fullness is Christ dwelling in the heart through faith (v. 17). This is called union with Christ: the believer is really joined to the risen Lord, as a branch is joined to its vine and lives by its sap. God does more than clear our record; he gives us Christ himself. The whole Christian life flows from that bond: assurance, holiness, prayer, service and joy.

The closing burst of praise, the doxology (vv. 20–21), also teaches us how to pray. God is not limited by the smallness of our asking, and the power by which he answers is already at work within us, the same power that raised Christ (1:19–20).
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The mystery cults around Ephesus promised union with the divine through costly initiation, one stage after another, always with another level to reach. Paul prays for a fullness no initiation could buy: the fullness of God himself, freely given, received through faith and sustained by the Spirit.

Now: When we cannot find words, the Spirit helps us (Romans 8:26), and when a situation seems past recovery, we pray to the God who raises the dead. Each time the church says this doxology, it reminds itself, and the watching powers, that its God is generous beyond our prayers.

verseByVerse.quote: For this reason I bow my knees before the Father, from whom every family in heaven and on earth is named.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For this reason. The words of verse 1 again: Paul resumes the prayer.

I bow my knees. Jews normally stood to pray (Mark 11:25; Luke 18:11, 13). Kneeling marked unusual earnestness (1 Kings 8:54; Daniel 6:10). And this man is in custody: a prisoner going down on a stone floor, probably watched, to pray for churches he may never see again. There is nobody in that room to impress.

Abba, on a stone floor. Prayer is addressed to the Father, through the Son, by the Spirit (2:18), and Paul can kneel and say “Father” only because another man knelt first. In Gethsemane the Son knelt (Luke 22:41) and said “Abba, Father” (Mark 14:36). The cup he prayed about was God’s just anger against our sin. That anger stood between us and God, and while it stood we could never have called him Father. Jesus took the cup and drank it at the cross. Because he drank it, God has sent the Spirit of his Son into our hearts, crying, “Abba! Father!” (Galatians 4:6).

From whom every family in heaven and on earth is named. A wordplay English loses: Father is patēr, family is patria, a family group descended from one father. To name something, in the Bible, is to give it its identity (Genesis 2:19–20). God is not called Father because human fathers exist, as if we projected the idea upward. He is Father first, eternally, and human fathers are faint copies. And for anyone whose father was absent, harsh or cruel: your experience is not the standard by which God is measured. He is the standard, and what you knew was a distortion of an original that is undistorted and unfailing (Luke 15:20–24; Psalm 68:5). “In heaven and on earth” probably includes the angels, and since Jew and Gentile are now one family (2:19), Paul prays to the Father of them all.

Textual note. Later manuscripts, followed by the King James Version, add “of our Lord Jesus Christ” after “the Father”. This commentary’s view: not original. The shorter reading is found in the earliest manuscripts and makes the wordplay with “family” clearer.

What it does not mean. Not that every human being is a child of God in the saving sense. All are God’s creatures and owe him their being (Acts 17:28), but the fatherhood that saves is adoption through Christ (1:5; John 1:12; Romans 8:15): God takes sinners into his family as his own children, with full rights and a share in the inheritance (Galatians 4:4–7). And kneeling is not required for prayer: posture is a help, not a law.

In everyday life. Next time you pray, notice what face you are imagining: disappointed but too polite to say so, or already looking for the fault. That face usually belonged to somebody, a parent or a teacher perhaps, and you have been putting it on God ever since. Change it by looking at Jesus, the exact imprint of God’s nature (Hebrews 1:3): “Whoever has seen me has seen the Father” (John 14:9). Watch him touch the leper (Mark 1:41), promise paradise to a dying thief (Luke 23:43). That is not Jesus being kinder than the Father. That is the Father, showing you his face.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that “family” renders patria, a word closely related to “father” (pater) in verse 14.

verseByVerse.quote: That according to the riches of his glory he may grant you to be strengthened with power through his Spirit in your inner being.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The shape of the prayer. In Greek, verses 14–19 are a single sentence, a chain of requests like steps on a staircase: strengthened by the Spirit (v. 16), so that Christ dwells in your hearts (v. 17), so that you may grasp and know his love (vv. 18–19), so that you may be filled with all the fullness of God (v. 19).

According to the riches of his glory. Not out of his riches, which could mean a small gift from a large fortune, but in proportion to them: without limit. And inner strength is not achieved by self-effort; it is granted.

To be strengthened with power. Two words for strength, piled up. And not power over circumstances, health or protection from trouble, good as those are to pray for. Power in the inner being.

Through his Spirit. The strengthening is done by a Person, “the Spirit of him who raised Jesus from the dead” (Romans 8:11). He does not strengthen his people from a reserve that might run out, or by lending them a little more of their own resolve. He gives his Spirit, God himself, to dwell in the hidden self and hold it fast. It is Christ’s risen life at work in you, and it works in you as it did in him: “he was crucified in weakness, but lives by the power of God” (2 Corinthians 13:4). So it seldom arrives as a feeling of being strong; it arrives in weak people and carries them through. The right response to finding yourself weak is not a programme of self-improvement. It is to ask.

In your inner being. Literally the inner man: your will, your faith, your capacity to trust God when nothing visible supports it. Two people facing the same grief look alike from outside, but one is quietly falling apart while the other is held somewhere the storm cannot reach. And if you are the one falling apart, this is not a verdict on you but a prayer for you: Paul asks God to give exactly this strength, because no one can produce it. “Though our outer self is wasting away, our inner self is being renewed day by day” (2 Corinthians 4:16). This strength gives endurance (Colossians 1:11) and a peace that does not depend on circumstances (Philippians 4:7). God’s first work is not rearranging your circumstances, but building something in you that they cannot shake.

How do I actually pray this prayer? Use Paul’s words as your outline; that is partly why they were written down. Take verses 16–19 slowly and turn each clause into a request, for yourself and then for others by name: “Father, strengthen her inside by your Spirit; make Christ at home in his heart; root them in your love; help me grasp how wide and long and high and deep it is; fill us with all your fullness.” It is right to pray it for yourself, since Paul prays it for whole churches and you are in yours. Do not wait to feel something first, and do not judge the answer by tomorrow morning’s mood. This is a prayer God delights to answer, because it asks for what he has already promised to give (1 John 5:14–15). Then close as Paul does, with the doxology of verses 20–21, thanking him in advance.

verseByVerse.quote: So that Christ may dwell in your hearts through faith, that you, being rooted and grounded in love.
verseByVerse.commentary:
So that Christ may dwell. The word is katoikeō: not to lodge, but to settle down and make one’s permanent home, to move in and unpack. The eternal Son, by whom all things were made (John 1:3), is willing to make his home in a human heart, and not as a guest who keeps his coat on. He who had nowhere to lay his head on earth (Matthew 8:20) now makes his dwelling among sinners. Christ already lives in every believer (Romans 8:9–10). Paul prays that he would be more fully at home: not visiting in a crisis, but present at work, in the argument with your spouse, in the moment of temptation. The Puritans pictured a house: Christ enters at conversion, but we must open every room to him.

In your hearts. In the Bible the heart is the centre of the person: thought, will, desire and feeling together (see 1:18). Christ’s dwelling there means he rules and shapes everything we are.

Through faith. Not a single decision, but the daily turning of the heart to him (John 15:4–5).

Rooted and grounded in love. Two pictures. “Rooted” is from the garden: a tree is only as strong as its hidden roots, and everything above ground, its height, its fruit, its standing in a storm, depends on what is underground (Colossians 2:7; Psalm 1:3). “Grounded” is from building: a house is only as safe as its unseen foundation (Matthew 7:24–25). Love here is above all Christ’s love for us (vv. 18–19), which then produces our love for him and others. The deeply rooted believer bends in the storm but does not fall, because he knows what the wind cannot change: I am loved, and that is not in question. And English hides something here. In Greek both words describe something already done to you, and still true: you have been rooted; you have been founded. Trees do not plant themselves, and no building ever laid its own foundation. Someone put you in the soil and set you on rock. Sending your roots deeper is real work, but it answers a planting that already happened and was never your idea. You are not asked to manufacture a foundation; you are asked to build on one.

What your worst week shows. You will never discover what you are rooted in on a good day, and the most revealing storm is your own sin. After you have failed badly, what happens to your sense of being loved by God? If it collapses, and stays collapsed until you have made up the ground with a stretch of better behaviour, then whatever you believe about grace, you are leaning on your own performance. If that is you, do not despair of yourself. The way back is not a better week but a fresh look at Christ: go back within the hour and tell him plainly what you did, because you are not earning your way in again; you are standing on what somebody else laid. And if, under the real grief over the sin, there remains a floor you have not fallen through, the stubborn knowledge that you are loved by a God who knew about this before you did it, then you have found the foundation. It is the one thing your worst week cannot get underneath.

What it does not mean. Not that Christ enters and leaves believers depending on their mood or behaviour. His indwelling is permanent (John 14:23). Paul prays for a deeper experience of it, not its beginning. Nor is “love” here a vague feeling: it is the self-giving love shown at the cross (5:2, 25).

What does opening a room to Christ actually look like? Begin by naming the room. It is usually the part of life where you would rather not have his opinion: how you spend money, what you watch when alone, the grudge you are keeping, the plans you have already made. Bring it to him in plain words: “Lord, this is yours too; show me what you want here.” Open your Bible on that subject, not only on comfortable ones, and let it speak. Tell one trusted believer about it, because rooms kept secret tend to stay locked. Then do the first obedient thing you can see, however small: give the gift, cancel the subscription, make the call, say sorry. Christ does not batter the door down. He makes his home with those who love him and keep his word (John 14:23).

verseByVerse.quote: may have strength to comprehend with all the saints what is the breadth and length and height and depth,
verseByVerse.commentary:
May have strength to comprehend. The odd word comes first: strength. Understanding normally calls for intelligence or time, not strength; nobody says he lacked the strength to follow an argument. And here the prayer knits together, because this answers a question left open two verses earlier. Paul asked that they be strengthened with power in the inner being (v. 16). What is the power for? Not for miracles, or surviving persecution, or great achievements. It is so that you can take in how much you are loved. It takes little strength to accept a compliment. It takes a great deal to accept a gift you can never repay, from someone who knows exactly what you are, with no way of ever levelling the account. Everything in us resists being loved on those terms. We would rather be admired for something, or at least be useful. To stand still and be loved, with nothing to contribute, undoes a person, and it takes the power of God in the inner man not to flinch and start earning again.

With all the saints. We grasp the love of Christ together, not alone. The old saint who has suffered, the new believer full of joy, the church in another culture: each sees aspects of Christ’s love the others need. The saints of every age have explored it together, and none has ever come back reporting that it ran out.

Breadth and length and height and depth. Verse 19 makes clear he means the love of Christ. Many preachers map the four onto the cross; it preaches well, but Paul does not make that link. Four directions were a common ancient way of describing the whole of space: go as far as you can in any direction, and the love is still there.

Breadth. Wide enough to embrace Jew and Gentile and every nation (chapter 2): wide enough to include you, your failures, your doubts, and the person beside you whose life looks nothing like yours.

Length. From before the foundation of the world (1:4) to the ages to come (2:7). It did not begin when you became lovable, and it never ends: neither death nor life will be able to separate us (Romans 8:38–39).

Height. High enough to seat you with Christ in the heavenly places (2:6) and bring you before the Father with boldness (3:12).

Depth. Deep enough to reach you where you actually are, not where you pretend to be: the shame, the addiction, the thing you have never told anyone. It went down into death itself at the cross (Romans 5:20). This is the love that held him to the cross when he could have called for angels (Matthew 26:53), and that holds his people now.

Background. Zophar asks whether anyone can find out the deep things of God, higher than heaven, deeper than Sheol (Job 11:7–9). Paul says that in Christ this immeasurable love is now known.

In everyday life. It is possible to describe the love of Christ accurately and not be moved by it at all. If you have ever read a passage like this, felt something begin to rise, and then found yourself changing the subject or remembering a job that needed doing, that is not a lapse in concentration. It is the very thing Paul is praying about. Stay a little longer.

parallels.desc: higher than heaven, deeper than Sheol

verseByVerse.quote: and to know the love of Christ that surpasses knowledge, that you may be filled with all the fullness of God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
To know the love of Christ. “Know” (gnōnai) in the Bible is personal knowledge, as one knows a friend (John 17:3). Paul prays not that they would learn facts about Christ’s love, but that they would experience it more deeply.

That surpasses knowledge. It sounds like a contradiction: how can you know what is beyond knowing? You can know facts about the ocean without ever standing on the shore and feeling its size. Paul wants you on the beach, knowing in your bones that this ocean has no far shore. We can know Christ’s love truly but never fully.

With all the fullness of God. This is the goal of the whole prayer, and the largest thing Paul could ask. Literally filled up to all the fullness of God. “Fullness” (plērōma) is a key word in Ephesians and Colossians: in Christ “the whole fullness of deity dwells bodily” (Colossians 2:9), and the church is his fullness (1:23). Paul prays that believers would be filled with everything God is and gives: his life, love, holiness, joy and peace, as fully as creatures can be filled. Picture a jug held under a waterfall. The waterfall is beyond all comparison larger, yet the jug can be completely full, every inch, with nothing in it but what pours from the fall. In practice it means a life increasingly marked by what God is: loving more deeply because he is love, a patience not native to your temperament, a joy that does not evaporate when things are hard.

Be filled. Passive (plērōthēte), not “fill yourselves”. The fullness of God is a gift, not the reward for a disciplined enough life. The jug does not fill itself; it holds itself under the water: prayer, the word, worship, confession, the company of the saints (5:18).

What if I believe Christ loves me but cannot feel it? Then you are in good company, and you are not outside this prayer. Feelings rise and fall with health, sleep, grief and temperament; Christ’s love does not, and it is measured at the cross, not by what you feel this week (Romans 5:8). Paul prays that we may know it, which means God is willing to make it more real to us, and he usually does so over time. So keep to the ordinary ways he does it. Look long at Christ in the Gospels, especially at how he treats sinners. Pray this very prayer for yourself. Sing truths you cannot yet feel. Take the Lord’s Supper as his pledge to you. Stay close to believers who have known his love in dark times. This knowing often arrives slowly, like dawn, and it is no less real for being quiet.

The hollow. You do not pray for someone to be filled unless there is a space in them. Everyone knows the feeling, though we do not always name it: the restlessness that survives getting what you wanted. The promotion is pleasant for a fortnight. The house is bought, the qualification finished, the relationship secured, and within a season the same low hum returns, the sense that something has still not arrived. We usually assume we picked the wrong thing, and choose another. But Paul is describing a capacity that no created thing was ever the right size for. The hollow is not a design fault. It is the shape of a container built for the fullness of God, and nothing smaller will ever sit in it.

Every “you” is plural. Paul asks that a congregation, this mixed, awkward Jew-and-Gentile assembly, would together be filled (1:23). Some of this filling only ever arrives through the people you have been joined to, including the ones you would never have chosen.

What it does not mean. Not that believers become God or lose their creaturely nature. A cup filled from the ocean is full of the ocean, but it is still a cup. The Eastern Orthodox speak of deification, believers coming to share in God’s own life; Reformed theology speaks rather of union with Christ, being joined to him, and of being made like him (Romans 8:29). And it is a growing filling, complete when we see him face to face (1 John 3:2).

verseByVerse.quote: Now to him who is able to do far more abundantly than all that we ask or think, according to the power at work within us,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now to him who is able. Paul ends the prayer with a burst of praise. He has asked for enormous things; now he steps back: the God I have been praying to can do immeasurably more than all of it.

Far more abundantly. Paul stacks the words (hyperekperissou) because no single word goes far enough. Our requests are limited by our words, our imagination by our minds; God is limited by neither. The God who can do more than all we ask is the God who has already done more than anyone thought to ask: he gave his Son. No one in Israel prayed for a crucified Messiah, and no Gentile imagined adoption into the family of God.

But my prayer was answered no. Handle this honestly, because this promise can wound. Someone reads it with a prayer in mind that met a plain no: the healing that did not come, the marriage that ended anyway, years of asking that returned only silence. To them the verse can sound like mockery. The answer is in two small words easily skipped: or think. God does more than we know to ask. Our prayers are often asking for the lesser thing because we cannot yet see the greater, and when a loving father says no, his love has not failed. The no is his love at work. Paul asked three times for his thorn to be removed. The answer was no, and the “more” turned out to be grace sufficient and power made perfect in weakness (2 Corinthians 12:8–9). And where no better thing is yet visible, the more is not cancelled but kept, for the coming ages (2:7), for the day God wipes away every tear (Revelation 21:4). The account does not close at the grave.

According to the power at work within us. Not distant, not dormant, not waiting to be switched on by enough faith: working now (energoumenēn). And Paul has named it already: the power that raised Christ from the dead (1:19–20) and raised us with him (2:5–6). Why does it so often not feel like it, the same old sin, the same weakness? For three reasons. It works whether you feel it or not, as a seed breaks through concrete without anyone seeing it move. It is aimed first at the inner person, not the outer circumstances: you may be waiting for it to change your situation while God is using your situation to change you. And it shows most clearly in weakness (2 Corinthians 12:9). The one who has run out of his own strength is exactly where God’s power takes over: not his power plus God’s, but God’s power where his used to be.

The hinge of the letter. This doxology is not a decorative flourish. Everything from 1:3 to here has been about what God has done: chosen, redeemed, sealed, raised, seated, reconciled, built, revealed. Apart from one call to remember (2:11) and one plea not to lose heart (3:13), not one command has been given in three chapters. Then, the moment the praise ends, the tone changes: “I therefore, a prisoner for the Lord, urge you to walk in a manner worthy of the calling” (4:1), and the rest of the letter is almost all instruction. And look at what Paul has put between the doctrine and the duty. Not a summary. Praise: a man on his knees running out of words. That order is deliberate and it does not reverse. Anyone who takes up chapters 4–6 without first being undone by chapters 1–3 will find the commands crushing, trying to produce by effort a life that was only ever meant to overflow from astonishment. The obedience of this letter runs downhill from a doxology. If it is running uphill in your life, you may have started in the wrong chapter.

What it does not mean. Not a promise that big prayers guarantee health, wealth or success. Paul is still in prison. God’s “more” is more of what verses 16–19 ask, and more of his good purposes for us than we could ever plan (Romans 8:28–32).

verseByVerse.quote: to him be glory in the church and in Christ Jesus throughout all generations, forever and ever. Amen.
verseByVerse.commentary:
To him be glory. Behind the word stands the Hebrew kābôd, from a root meaning heavy: the weight, worth and splendour of who God is (see 1:17). To give him glory is not to add anything to him, as though he grew more glorious by our saying so; the sun does not brighten because someone looks at it. It is to recognise and declare what is already true, and to live in line with it. That takes three ordinary forms. Honest praise: kneeling by your bed on a Tuesday night, no audience, saying, you are good and I am not; you saved me when I had nothing, and I am grateful (Psalm 50:23). A life that points to him: when you are patient with a difficult colleague and they wonder what you have that they do not, God is glorified without a religious word spoken (1 Corinthians 10:31; Matthew 5:16). And trusting him when it is hard: “Though he slay me, I will hope in him” (Job 13:15). That may be the deepest of all, because it tells every watching soul that this God is worth trusting when it costs. This is the goal of everything in chapters 1–3 (1:6, 12, 14).

In the church and in Christ Jesus. These two stand side by side as the places of God’s eternal glory. One is the risen Son, seated above every power. The other is a congregation, with its awkward silences and its hymns nobody can quite sing. Paul does not apologise for the pairing: the church is his body, and the glory of the head shines in the body he fills (1:22–23), as a mirror displays the sun. You are one of the places where God’s glory is meant to be seen.

Throughout all generations, forever and ever. Literally to all the generations of the age of the ages. Empires rise and fall; the church goes on, and its praise of God will never end.

Amen. A Hebrew word meaning firm, true, so be it, the people’s response in worship (1 Corinthians 14:16; Nehemiah 8:6). Paul has written the sentence; the Amen is where the reader signs it. The first half of the letter, about what God has done, has ended in worship.

Is God vain to want glory in the church? In us it would be vanity, because we are not the greatest good, and demanding praise is a lie about our size. God is the greatest good, so pointing us to himself is not vanity but truth and kindness: anywhere else he pointed us would be something less. And look at how this God seeks glory. Jesus said the hour had come for the Son of Man to be glorified, and he meant his death (John 12:23–24). The God who wants glory gets it by washing feet and carrying a cross.

For worship. Christ is himself “the Amen, the faithful and true witness” (Revelation 3:14). Every promise of God finds its Yes in him, and so it is through him that the church says its Amen to God’s glory (2 Corinthians 1:20), generation after generation, and the song will still be his when time has finished.

3.overview:
Paul begins to pray (v. 1), then breaks off to explain his own part in God’s plan (vv. 2–13). God made him, a prisoner for the Gentiles’ sake, a steward of grace and showed him the mystery of Christ, now revealed by the Spirit: through the gospel the Gentiles are fellow heirs with Israel, members of the same body and sharers in the promise. Paul, the least of all the saints, was sent to preach Christ’s unsearchable riches, so that through the church God’s many-sided wisdom is shown to the powers in the heavenly places.

Then he resumes the prayer (vv. 14–21). Kneeling before the Father, he asks that they be strengthened by the Spirit, that Christ may dwell in their hearts through faith, and that, rooted in love, they may grasp the love of Christ that surpasses knowledge and be filled with all the fullness of God. A doxology, a short burst of praise, to the God who can do far more than we ask or think closes the first half of the letter.

4.title: Unity, Gifts, and the New Self
4.text: <sup>1</sup>I therefore, a prisoner for the Lord, urge you to walk in a manner worthy of the calling to which you have been called, <sup>2</sup>with all humility and gentleness, with patience, bearing with one another in love, <sup>3</sup>eager to maintain the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace. <sup>4</sup>There is one body and one Spirit — just as you were called to the one hope that belongs to your call — <sup>5</sup>one Lord, one faith, one baptism, <sup>6</sup>one God and Father of all, who is over all and through all and in all. <sup>7</sup>But grace was given to each one of us according to the measure of Christ’s gift. <sup>8</sup>Therefore it says, “When he ascended on high he led a host of captives, and he gave gifts to men.” <sup>9</sup>(In saying, “He ascended,” what does it mean but that he had also descended into the lower regions, the earth? <sup>10</sup>He who descended is the one who also ascended far above all the heavens, that he might fill all things.) <sup>11</sup>And he gave the apostles, the prophets, the evangelists, the shepherds and teachers, <sup>12</sup>to equip the saints for the work of ministry, for building up the body of Christ, <sup>13</sup>until we all attain to the unity of the faith and of the knowledge of the Son of God, to mature manhood, to the measure of the stature of the fullness of Christ, <sup>14</sup>so that we may no longer be children, tossed to and fro by the waves and carried about by every wind of doctrine, by human cunning, by craftiness in deceitful schemes. <sup>15</sup>Rather, speaking the truth in love, we are to grow up in every way into him who is the head, into Christ, <sup>16</sup>from whom the whole body, joined and held together by every joint with which it is equipped, when each part is working properly, makes the body grow so that it builds itself up in love. <sup>17</sup>Now this I say and testify in the Lord, that you must no longer walk as the Gentiles do, in the futility of their minds. <sup>18</sup>They are darkened in their understanding, alienated from the life of God because of the ignorance that is in them, due to their hardness of heart. <sup>19</sup>They have become callous and have given themselves up to sensuality, greedy to practice every kind of impurity. <sup>20</sup>But that is not the way you learned Christ! — <sup>21</sup>assuming that you have heard about him and were taught in him, as the truth is in Jesus, <sup>22</sup>to put off your old self, which belongs to your former manner of life and is corrupt through deceitful desires, <sup>23</sup>and to be renewed in the spirit of your minds, <sup>24</sup>and to put on the new self, created after the likeness of God in true righteousness and holiness. <sup>25</sup>Therefore, having put away falsehood, let each one of you speak the truth with his neighbor, for we are members one of another. <sup>26</sup>Be angry and do not sin; do not let the sun go down on your anger, <sup>27</sup>and give no opportunity to the devil. <sup>28</sup>Let the thief no longer steal, but rather let him labor, doing honest work with his own hands, so that he may have something to share with anyone in need. <sup>29</sup>Let no corrupting talk come out of your mouths, but only such as is good for building up, as fits the occasion, that it may give grace to those who hear. <sup>30</sup>And do not grieve the Holy Spirit of God, by whom you were sealed for the day of redemption. <sup>31</sup>Let all bitterness and wrath and anger and clamor and slander be put away from you, along with all malice. <sup>32</sup>Be kind to one another, tenderhearted, forgiving one another, as God in Christ forgave you.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–6 — Walk Worthy: The Unity of the Spirit
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul, a prisoner for the Lord, urges them to live worthy of their calling, with humility, gentleness, patience and love, eager to keep the unity the Spirit has already given. That unity rests on the one God: one body, one Spirit, one hope, one Lord, one faith, one baptism, one God and Father of all.
verseByVerse.theology:
The unity of the church

The unity of the church is not a goal to be reached but a fact to be kept. The Spirit has already made one body. The question is whether our behaviour honours it.

The four graces that keep unity, humility, gentleness, patience and bearing with one another, are a portrait of Christ applied to church life. They are not soft virtues: gentleness is strength in the service of love (Matthew 11:29), and bearing with one another keeps choosing the person in front of you when he disappoints.

Seven times in verses 4–6 Paul says “one”, and that roots this unity in shared truth. We are not called to unity by pretending doctrine does not matter, but because there really is one Lord, one faith and one baptism, and the people who confess them are one.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The Ephesian church gathered former worshippers of Artemis, Jewish believers, slaves and free, merchants and harbour workers. Every natural instinct pulled them apart along old social lines. Paul’s “therefore” ties his call to chapter 2: the wall has already come down, the body is already one, so walk like it.

Now: Churches still split along political, cultural and stylistic lines, and it is easy to shop for a church that suits our preferences and keeps us among people like ourselves. Paul calls for a costly unity rooted in shared confession, not shared taste. A local church that holds together through its differences, with patient and humble love, bears witness to the one God “who is over all and through all and in all”.

verseByVerse.quote: I therefore, a prisoner for the Lord, urge you to walk in a manner worthy of the calling to which you have been called.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Meaning first. With Ephesians 4 the letter turns: having shown what God has done (chapters 1–3), Paul now shows how to live because of it (chapters 4–6). He urges believers to walk worthy of their calling, guarding the unity the Spirit has already created (vv. 1–6). The ascended Christ has given gifts to each believer, and leaders to equip all the saints, so that the church grows to maturity (vv. 7–16). They must no longer live as the unbelieving world does, because that is not how they learned Christ (vv. 17–24), and Paul spells out what the new self looks like in speech, anger, work and forgiveness (vv. 25–32).

Therefore. It is the sharpest turn in the letter. For three chapters Paul has given almost no commands: one call to remember (2:11) and one plea not to lose heart (3:13). He has been describing: chosen, redeemed, sealed, made alive, raised, seated, reconciled, built, indwelt. Then a doxology. Chapters 4–6 hold some forty commands. And the order matters. Paul does not say, “Live like this, and God will accept you.” He says, “God has accepted you; therefore live like this.” Christian ethics flows out of grace, never the other way round. Theologians call this the move from indicative (what is true) to imperative (what to do).

I … a prisoner for the Lord. Literally in the Lord. Paul is in prison because he obeyed Christ, as he said in 3:1. He says it again so that we know he asks nothing of us that has not cost him first. The man who tells us to walk can himself walk only the few steps of a cell.

Urge. Parakaleō: to call alongside, to appeal. Not a cold order, but a pastor’s earnest plea; the same word is used for comfort.

To walk. After the size of chapters 1–3 you might expect something towering. What arrives is: walk. It is the plainest verb available, and it is chosen on purpose. It organises everything that follows: walk worthy (4:1), not as the Gentiles walk (4:17), walk in love (5:2), walk as children of light (5:8), walk wisely (5:15). Walking is what a person does all day without thinking about it. Nobody schedules it, nobody photographs it, and it cannot be done in bursts. That tells you where the Christian life is actually lived: not in the peaks, but in the ordinary going-along of an ordinary week.

In a manner worthy. “Worthy” (axiōs) means fitting, in keeping with. In plain words: live in a way that matches what God has made you. The picture behind the word is a market trader’s scales, with two pans. In one pan lies your calling: all that God has done for you in chapters 1–3. In the other lies your daily life. You cannot add anything to the calling side; God filled it before the world was made. You are asked to bring the other side up to match it. And the weight on the calling side is Christ himself: God called you into the fellowship of his Son (1 Corinthians 1:9), so a worthy walk is a life that looks like his. None of us makes the scales balance. He did: from the manger to the cross he never once fell short of his Father’s will, and God counts that perfect life as belonging to everyone who trusts him. A son who bears the family name worthily is not earning the name; he already has it, and nothing today will win or lose it. He is asked to live like a man who has it.

Of the calling to which you have been called. In Paul, God’s calling is more than an invitation that a person may take or leave. It is the call that actually brings a person to Christ (1:18; Romans 8:30; 2 Timothy 1:9). And he calls us to something: to be holy (1:4), his children (1:5), one body (4:4). When you believed, more was happening than your own decision. God was calling you by name, the way Jesus called Lazarus out of the tomb (John 11:43): the call itself gave the life to answer it.

What it does not mean. Not that God calls those who are worthy. He calls the dead (2:1–5). Nor is it a life of grim effort under a heavy load: the same God who called also equips (4:7, 11–12), and the Holy Spirit now works in us with the power that raised Christ from the dead (1:19–20; 3:16, 20). That is what makes the walk possible.

If God has already accepted me, why should I bother to obey? Because grace does not leave a person where it found him. Paul expects the question and answers it with horror: are we to go on sinning so that grace may increase? By no means (Romans 6:1–2). A man pardoned by a king and adopted into his house does not ask how little he can do now that he is safe. The same grace that saves also trains us to renounce ungodliness (Titus 2:11–12). And the question cuts the other way too. If your obedience is your way of getting God to accept you, you have turned even religion into a way of paying your own way and reversed Paul’s order. Obedience is not the price of acceptance. It is what accepted people do, gladly, because they love the one who accepted them (John 14:15).
verseByVerse.note: Chapters 1–3 set out what God has done; chapters 4–6 show the life that follows.

verseByVerse.quote: With all humility and gentleness, with patience, bearing with one another in love.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Why these come first. What most often destroys unity is not doctrine but pride. Paul’s sentence runs without a break from “walk worthy” to “maintain the unity”, and these four qualities stand in between. They are what hold a church together in peace, as ligaments hold a body together.

With all humility. Tapeinophrosynē: lowliness of mind. In the Greek world it was usually a fault, the cringing posture of a slave. Christ showed what it truly is: he washed his disciples’ feet (John 13:1–17), and humbled himself to the point of death (Philippians 2:3–8). Humility is not thinking badly of yourself; it is thinking of yourself less, and seeing yourself truly before God. False modesty is still focused on self.

And gentleness. Prautēs could be used of a horse broken to the bridle. The animal has lost none of its strength; the strength now answers to a hand other than its own. A naturally timid man is not gentle in this sense; he simply has nothing that needs restraining. Jesus called himself “gentle and lowly in heart” (Matthew 11:29), and he drove the traders out of the temple.

With patience. Makrothymia: long temper, the opposite of short-tempered. It is the patience God shows us (Romans 2:4), especially patience with people, the slow, the difficult, the wrong, more than with circumstances.

Bearing with one another in love. The word means to put up with, to carry the weight of. And Paul does not say bear with the difficulties, or the world outside. He says “one another”: the weight in question is other Christians. Make it concrete. The man who tells you the same story every time you meet. The woman who is late to everything and always has a reason. The one whose theology is slightly off and who would like to discuss it after the service, at length. Nobody in that list is sinning. They are simply heavy, in the way people are, and the instruction is to pick up the weight and keep walking, as Christ has carried ours. He has borne with us, not for an afternoon but through every year of our wandering, and he carried the full weight of our sins on the cross. Bearing with personal faults is not excusing evil: Paul will command speaking the truth in love (v. 15) and exposing wrong (5:11). Love is what makes the others last. Without it, humility becomes self-contempt, gentleness becomes passivity, and patience becomes resentment.

In everyday life. It is natural to cast yourself as the one doing the bearing. Turn it round: who in your church is bearing with you? Someone finds your manner difficult, your opinions tiring, your blind spot wearing, and has decided, quietly, to put up with it and go on loving you. You are the heavy person in somebody else’s week. Once you see that, humility is no longer just an idea. It becomes possible.

verseByVerse.quote: Eager to maintain the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Eager. Spoudazontes: making every effort. Unity is a gift; keeping it is work. A house is maintained by somebody clearing the gutters in November; a marriage by two people apologising more often than they would like.

To maintain. You are not asked to build unity; you could not. You are asked to keep and guard it, because it already exists. Nobody creates his own family. He finds himself in it, and what remains to be settled is how he treats people he did not choose.

The unity of the Spirit. The unity the Spirit creates. Every believer has the same Spirit (2:18, 22; 1 Corinthians 12:13), and Christ has already made Jew and Gentile one (2:14–16). This unity is a fact, not a goal; God’s work, not a human agreement. It was bought, not negotiated. Christ made peace by the blood of his cross (Colossians 1:20), breaking down the dividing wall in his own flesh, and the Spirit then bound us together with a cord no quarrel can finally cut. God did not wait for his people to agree before making them one. What we so easily fray, he wove. We can display it or obscure it, guard it or damage it. Bring it down to one relationship: if you and the believer you find hardest both trust Christ, you are already joined to the same Lord by the same Spirit. You did not arrange it and you cannot cancel it. What is left in your hands is whether the way you treat each other tells the truth about that bond or hides it (John 17:21).

In the bond of peace. A bond is something that ties together, like a cord or a ligament. Christ is our peace (2:14), and the peace he made at the cross must be lived out between people. And be concrete about what damages it, because we imagine the threat is doctrinal and it very seldom is. Churches do not usually divide over the person of Christ. They divide over a message never returned, a decision taken without consulting someone who expected to be consulted, a remark repeated to the wrong person, a slight at the door that was probably not even intended. The breach is almost never theological at the start. Theology gets recruited afterwards, to give the wound a respectable name. The bond never breaks in the abstract; it breaks between two particular people, and no amount of general goodwill towards the church covers that.

What it does not mean. Not unity that ignores truth. Paul grounds it in one faith (v. 5) and a unity of the faith (v. 13), and it cannot include those who deny the gospel itself (Galatians 1:8–9; 2 John 10). But among those who share the gospel, Christians should not divide over church government, the details of the last things or the style of worship. They may worship in different churches, but they should treat one another as brothers.

Is it ever right to leave my church? Yes, but more rarely than we think, and never lightly. It is right to leave when a church abandons the gospel, will not teach the Bible faithfully, refuses to deal with serious sin or abuse, or binds your conscience where Scripture does not. It may also be right when you move house, or are genuinely needed elsewhere. It is not usually right to leave because the music changed, a friendship cooled or someone offended you; those are exactly the places where verse 3 is meant to be obeyed. If you do go, speak to your elders first, leave without running anyone down, and join another faithful church soon. Leaving a church is sometimes necessary. Drifting away from church altogether never is (Hebrews 10:24–25).

verseByVerse.quote: There is one body and one Spirit — just as you were called to the one hope that belongs to your call — one Lord, one faith, one baptism,
verseByVerse.commentary:
The shape. One body, one Spirit, one hope, one Lord, one faith, one baptism, one God and Father: seven times in three verses Paul strikes the same note. And the list is arranged around the Trinity: one Spirit (v. 4), one Lord (v. 5), one God and Father (v. 6). We are one because Father, Son and Spirit are one, and this one God has brought us all to himself: the Father is our Father, the Son is our Lord, and the Spirit lives in each of us.

One body. The church, the body of Christ (1:23; 2:16). There are many congregations, but one church, with one head.

One Spirit. There is no believer without the Spirit (Romans 8:9; 1 Corinthians 12:13).

The one hope that belongs to your call. When God called us, he called us to a single future: the inheritance in Christ, his return, the resurrection, the new creation (1:18). And take it personally, because it has an edge. The same finish line means the same finishing group. The people you find hardest in your church are not a temporary arrangement you will be relieved of at the end. They are the people you will be with, in unshadowed friendship, for ever. Learning to love them now is an early start on what you will be doing for eternity anyway.

One Lord. In the Roman world “Lord” was Caesar’s title; for Christians, there is one Lord (1 Corinthians 8:6; Romans 10:9). To say “Jesus is Lord” was to say Caesar is not, and every age has its own Caesar, whether the state, the market, the crowd or the self, asking for the bow that belongs to Christ alone.
