The other five are easy to recognise; wrath makes a scene you regret, and slander you know is unkind even as you say it. But bitterness feels like justice. It grows in genuinely wronged soil: you really were treated badly, and the resentment feels less like a sin to repent of than a fact to be honoured. That is why it is so dangerous, and perhaps why Paul lists it first. And it does not punish the person who wronged you. It punishes you, daily, on his behalf. He may be asleep, untroubled, having forgotten the whole thing, while you lie awake rehearsing it, giving him free lodging in a mind he does not know he occupies. Hebrews adds what we never see coming: a root of bitterness springs up and causes trouble, and by it many become defiled (Hebrews 12:15). It leaks into your tone, your assumptions, the warnings you pass on, the slight coldness a whole room can feel.

Wrath and anger. Wrath (thymos) is often the sudden hot flare (James 1:19–20); anger (orgē) its cold twin, brooding resentment that builds a case and waits.

Clamour. Kraugē: shouting, brawling, a private grievance turned into a public scene.

Slander. Blasphēmia: speech that damages another person’s name, whether false or maliciously true. The same word is used for blasphemy against God, and in the church it attacks the members of Christ’s body, and so Christ himself (Acts 9:4).

Along with all malice. Kakia: ill will, taking pleasure in others’ misfortune, perhaps last because it is the soil the others grow in.

The progression. Read in order, the list shows resentment growing when it is not dealt with: from a bitter spirit within, to outbursts, to shouting, to slander, to a settled wish for the other’s harm. It begins in the heart, and so must the cure.

What it does not mean. Not that Christians must pretend they have never been hurt. Grief over wrong is not bitterness; bitterness is refusing to let the wrong go. Paul does not say the wrong did not happen. He says set down the thing you are carrying. Nor does this forbid naming wrong or seeking justice through proper channels.

Textual note. Jesus’ prayer, “Father, forgive them” (Luke 23:34), is missing from some early manuscripts of Luke, but it is found in many others and many scholars think it a true record of his words, so most modern Bibles keep it, often with a footnote.

For worship. Christ had more cause for bitterness than anyone who has ever lived. “When he was reviled, he did not revile in return” (1 Peter 2:23), and on the cross he prayed for the men who drove the nails (Luke 23:34). The malice poured out on him became the very means of our healing (Isaiah 53:5).

verseByVerse.quote: Be kind to one another, tenderhearted, forgiving one another, as God in Christ forgave you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Be kind to one another. “Kind” (chrēstos) means useful, good, generous: the word was used of old wine, mellowed and no longer sharp (Luke 5:39), and of Jesus’ easy yoke (Matthew 11:30). God is kind even to the ungrateful and evil (Luke 6:35; 2:7).

Tenderhearted. Eusplanchnos: literally with good bowels, where the ancients located deep emotion. A heart moved by another’s pain, the compassion of Christ for the crowds (Matthew 9:36), the opposite of the hardened heart of verse 18.

Forgiving one another. Charizomenoi shares its root with charis, grace: gracing one another, releasing them from the debt they owe you. It is hard because it feels like letting them off.

As God in Christ forgave you. The measure and the motive. A friend borrows your car and dents it. Someone has to pay for the repair. If you forgive him, the dent does not vanish: you pay for it yourself. Forgiveness always works like that. The one who was wronged bears the cost and does not make the other pay. At the cross God did exactly this. He did not pretend our debt did not exist; in Christ he paid it himself. Christian forgiveness follows the same pattern. Having been forgiven so much, we cannot refuse to forgive others so little (Matthew 18:21–35). We are only passing on what we have already received (Romans 2:4; Psalm 103:13).

How it hides. Sarah fell out with Mark six months ago. He was dismissive, spoke sharply in front of others, and never apologised. She serves beside him on Sundays but keeps her distance, has told two friends what happened, and tells herself she has forgiven him because she no longer thinks about it every day. She has let go of the sharp pain but kept the verdict: it hurts less, but in her mind he is still guilty and still owes her. The way forward is a decision made in prayer at the cross: “Lord, I release this; I received forgiveness I did not deserve; I give the same.” Then behaviour follows: a genuine word to him, an end to the quiet commentary. It may need to be made again tomorrow.

Where Christians differ: must the offender repent first? Jesus said, if he repents, forgive him (Luke 17:3), so some Christians hold that forgiveness, like God’s, is complete only when the offender repents. This commentary’s view: both are true when forgiveness is seen in its two parts. In the heart, before God, the wronged person lets go of bitterness and the wish for revenge, whether or not the other repents (v. 31; Mark 11:25). The restored relationship, the forgiveness spoken and received, waits for repentance, as God’s reconciliation with us does. So a believer must not nurse a grudge, but neither must he pretend that nothing happened.

What it does not mean. This verse is one step from a cruelty if it is misused, and it has been said, in a kind voice, to people it then badly hurt. Forgiveness does not mean the wrong was small, or calling evil good. It does not mean you must feel warmly. It does not always mean restoring trust at once: trust is rebuilt over time, and wisdom may require boundaries, especially where there has been abuse. It never means returning to a place where you are still being harmed, or dropping a safeguard. It does not remove just consequences: a forgiven thief may still need to repay, and crimes should be reported to the authorities God has appointed (Romans 13:1–4). And it is not the same as reconciliation, which needs both sides. What forgiveness does mean is releasing the debt, refusing revenge, refusing to keep bringing the wrong up, and wishing the other person good. Where the wound is deep, it is often done again on Tuesday, having been done on Monday, without that meaning it was insincere the first time.

If I have forgiven, why do I still remember it and feel it? Because forgiving is not forgetting, and feelings heal more slowly than decisions are made. When God says he will remember our sins no more (Jeremiah 31:34), he has not lost the memory; he means he will never hold them against us. That is what you are promising too: not that the memory will vanish, but that you will not use it as a weapon, in your words, in how you treat the person, or in private rehearsals. When the memory returns, and the old heat with it, that is not proof that you never forgave. It is the moment to forgive again: “Lord, I released this, and I release it again.” Over time the memory usually loses its sting, until it reminds you more of God’s grace than of the wound.

In the flow. The chapter ends here; the thought does not: “be imitators of God, as beloved children” (5:1–2).

In everyday life. Who do you need to forgive today? Begin by remembering what God has forgiven you. And if you cannot get there yet, pray as someone who wants to want it: “Lord, I am not able to release this; make me willing.” That prayer is the beginning of obeying.

4.theology:
Ephesians 4 shows that justification and sanctification belong together. The grace that declares the sinner righteous also begins to make him righteous: not all at once, but surely. The commands of this chapter are not conditions for being accepted; they are the life of people already accepted. What God has done always comes first and grounds what we are told to do.

The chapter also teaches what it means to be a church: not a set of private spiritual journeys that happen in the same building, but members joined to one another, helped by their gifts and harmed by their sins.

At the centre stands the renewal of the mind. Change comes not by willpower or behaviour management but by the Spirit’s work, received through the ordinary means of grace: the word, prayer, honest fellowship and obedience to what we already know. Believers do not renew themselves, but they can put themselves daily in the way of the one who does (Romans 12:1–2; 2 Corinthians 3:18; Philippians 2:12–13).
4.examples:
Then: The Ephesian believers had come out of a culture full of the patterns Paul describes in verses 17–19: idol worship, sexual licence, and a morality where the main thing to avoid was public shame. To put that off was not a small adjustment but a new identity. Truth-telling, honest work and free forgiveness made the church a visible sign that a different humanity was possible.

Now: The pressures are the same: the conscience growing quieter, the appetite demanding more, the temptation to manage people instead of telling them the truth. The command still stands, not because we must earn our standing, which is secured in Christ, but because we have been made new. Renewal is what happens when a Christian opens the Bible instead of the phone, prays instead of brooding, and speaks the honest word instead of the comfortable one, and then does it again tomorrow.
4.overview:
With chapter 4 Ephesians turns from what God has done (chapters 1–3) to how his people are to live (chapters 4–6). The first call is to walk worthy of their calling, in humility, gentleness and patient love, keeping the unity the Spirit has created. Within that unity the ascended Christ has given grace to each believer, and leaders to equip all his people for ministry, until the body grows to maturity in Christ the head.

Then Paul describes the new life. Believers must no longer live like the Gentiles, darkened in understanding and hardened in heart. They have put off the old self and put on the new. The chapter ends with examples: truthfulness, anger that does not sin, honest work that makes giving possible, speech that builds up, not grieving the Holy Spirit, and kindness and forgiveness that pass on God’s forgiveness in Christ.

5.title: Walking in Love and the Mystery of Marriage
5.text: <sup>1</sup>Therefore be imitators of God, as beloved children. <sup>2</sup>And walk in love, as Christ loved us and gave himself up for us, a fragrant offering and sacrifice to God. <sup>3</sup>But sexual immorality and all impurity or covetousness must not even be named among you, as is proper among saints. <sup>4</sup>Let there be no filthiness nor foolish talk nor crude joking, which are out of place, but instead let there be thanksgiving. <sup>5</sup>For you may be sure of this, that everyone who is sexually immoral or impure, or who is covetous (that is, an idolater), has no inheritance in the kingdom of Christ and God. <sup>6</sup>Let no one deceive you with empty words, for because of these things the wrath of God comes upon the sons of disobedience. <sup>7</sup>Therefore do not become partners with them; <sup>8</sup>for at one time you were darkness, but now you are light in the Lord. Walk as children of light <sup>9</sup>(for the fruit of light is found in all that is good and right and true), <sup>10</sup>and try to discern what is pleasing to the Lord. <sup>11</sup>Take no part in the unfruitful works of darkness, but instead expose them. <sup>12</sup>For it is shameful even to speak of the things that they do in secret. <sup>13</sup>But when anything is exposed by the light, it becomes visible, <sup>14</sup>for anything that becomes visible is light. Therefore it says, “Awake, O sleeper, and arise from the dead, and Christ will shine on you.” <sup>15</sup>Look carefully then how you walk, not as unwise but as wise, <sup>16</sup>making the best use of the time, because the days are evil. <sup>17</sup>Therefore do not be foolish, but understand what the will of the Lord is. <sup>18</sup>And do not get drunk with wine, for that is debauchery, but be filled with the Spirit, <sup>19</sup>addressing one another in psalms and hymns and spiritual songs, singing and making melody to the Lord with your heart, <sup>20</sup>giving thanks always and for everything to God the Father in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, <sup>21</sup>submitting to one another out of reverence for Christ. <sup>22</sup>Wives, submit to your own husbands, as to the Lord. <sup>23</sup>For the husband is the head of the wife even as Christ is the head of the church, his body, and is himself its Savior. <sup>24</sup>Now as the church submits to Christ, so also wives should submit in everything to their husbands. <sup>25</sup>Husbands, love your wives, as Christ loved the church and gave himself up for her, <sup>26</sup>that he might sanctify her, having cleansed her by the washing of water with the word, <sup>27</sup>so that he might present the church to himself in splendor, without spot or wrinkle or any such thing, that she might be holy and without blemish. <sup>28</sup>In the same way husbands should love their wives as their own bodies. He who loves his wife loves himself. <sup>29</sup>For no one ever hated his own flesh, but nourishes and cherishes it, just as Christ does the church, <sup>30</sup>because we are members of his body. <sup>31</sup>“Therefore a man shall leave his father and mother and hold fast to his wife, and the two shall become one flesh.” <sup>32</sup>This mystery is profound, and I am saying that it refers to Christ and the church. <sup>33</sup>However, let each one of you love his wife as himself, and let the wife see that she respects her husband.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul sets the whole Christian life under one pattern: Christ’s self-giving love. Sexual sin, impurity, greed and crude talk are the reverse of that love, and they have no place among people God has made holy.
verseByVerse.theology:
Love as an offering to God

Paul describes Christ’s death in the language of Israel’s sacrifices: an offering God receives with delight. It was the perfect offering all those sacrifices pointed to.

That gives ordinary love a surprising dignity. Costly service, forgiveness given at personal cost, another’s need put before one’s own comfort: Paul uses the same altar language for such things (Philippians 4:18). They too are offered to God, and he receives them for Christ’s sake.

Paul calls greed idolatry (v. 5) because it looks to things rather than to God for security and joy. Lust shares that root: both treat what God has not given as owed to us, and both treat people as things to be consumed. The gospel answers both at the root, with “the love of Christ that surpasses knowledge” (3:19).
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Greek philosophers spoke of likeness to God as the goal of the soul, but their way to it led upward and away from people. Paul points the other way: the God we imitate came down and gave himself up for his enemies.

Now: Sexual freedom is often presented today as self-expression, and greed as healthy ambition. Paul does not answer with a longer list of rules but with who we are: children loved by a God who gave his Son for us. The call to walk in love is not a burden laid on us from outside. It comes from a Father who wants his children to share his likeness and his joy.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore be imitators of God, as beloved children.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Meaning first. Ephesians 5 continues Paul’s call to walk as God’s new people: imitating God as his loved children and walking in love, as Christ gave himself for us (vv. 1–2); rejecting sexual sin, greed and crude talk (vv. 3–7); walking as children of light (vv. 8–14); walking wisely, filled with the Spirit (vv. 15–21); and in marriage, picturing Christ and his church (vv. 22–33).

Therefore. The verse continues 4:32: “forgiving one another, as God in Christ forgave you”. The chapter division hides the link. What God has done becomes the pattern for what we do.

Imitators of God. Greek mimētai, from which we get mimic: the only place in the New Testament that calls believers imitators of God (compare Matthew 5:48; 1 Peter 1:15–16). Not in his power or knowledge, but in his character as he has shown it. Paul’s first readers knew “likeness to God” as the philosophers’ goal for the soul, but their route was always upward: withdrawal, discipline, secret knowledge. The higher you climbed, the fewer people you were any use to. Paul reverses the direction. The God we imitate came down, gave himself up for his enemies and died in public between two criminals, which is why Paul at once defines the likeness as walking in love (v. 2). So imitating God does not lift us above ordinary people. It sends us down among them, to love and to serve.

As beloved children. No father explains to a three-year-old how to be like him. The boy simply appears one Saturday with a plastic hammer, or stands with his hands in his pockets the way his father stands. It is what nearness does. The fastest way to become like the Father is not to try harder at it, but to be with him more (Acts 4:13).

Beloved in the Beloved. Paul has already given the Father’s Son that name: God has “blessed us in the Beloved” (1:6). We are dearly loved children because we have been placed in the one the Father calls his beloved Son (Matthew 3:17), and the love that rests on him now rests on us (John 17:23). To be in Christ means that God has joined us to his Son by faith, so that the Father’s welcome of him becomes his welcome of us: not strangers on probation, but children he is glad to see (Galatians 4:4–7). That also tells us where to look for the likeness. No one has ever seen God; the only Son has made him known (John 1:18), and whoever has seen him has seen the Father (John 14:9). To imitate God is to watch Jesus: the hands laid on lepers, the patience with slow disciples, the prayer for the men driving in the nails. The family likeness was first worn perfectly by the eldest Son, and we are being conformed to his image, so that he might be “the firstborn among many brothers” (Romans 8:29).

For worship. The Father had one beloved Son from all eternity, and he was not content to have only one. So the Son took our likeness, that we might come to wear his. Every small family resemblance in a Christian, a grudge let go, a kindness to an enemy, is the Father seeing his Son again in another face, and delighting in what he sees.

verseByVerse.quote: And walk in love, as Christ loved us and gave himself up for us, a fragrant offering and sacrifice to God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Walk in love. Not soar in love, or feel love, but walk: one foot after the other, so many times you stop counting. Love here is not a temperature to be checked but a direction to be kept. If you wait until you feel it you will not move. A man walking north is walking north whether or not he is enjoying the weather.

As Christ loved us. The word is agapē: love that chooses the other’s good at cost to itself. And Christ was loving not admirers but enemies (Romans 5:8). This love was never a response to loveliness in its object, which is exactly why it can be commanded of you towards people who have not earned it.

Gave himself up for us. Not only things or time, but himself, to death, in our place (Galatians 2:20), freely (John 10:18). Freely given and enormously costly: that is the shape of Christian love.

A fragrant offering and sacrifice. In plain words: a gift that God accepts with delight. In the Old Testament an animal was burned on an altar and the smoke rose up to God. After the flood Noah stepped off the ark into a world where everything had died. He built an altar, and the LORD smelled the pleasing aroma and said in his heart that he would never again curse the ground (Genesis 8:21). Every sacrifice in Israel pointed to this one: “by a single offering he has perfected for all time those who are being sanctified” (Hebrews 10:14). That does not mean the Father enjoyed his Son’s pain. It means the offering fully satisfied his holy justice: the punishment our sin deserved was truly borne, so that God can welcome sinners without ceasing to be just. Paul’s word for such a sacrifice is propitiation: an offering that turns away God’s just anger (Romans 3:25–26).

Your love, the same fragrance. Paul uses that exact phrase, “a fragrant offering”, once more, and not about the cross. The Philippians had sent a parcel to a man in prison, and Paul calls their gift “a fragrant offering, a sacrifice acceptable and pleasing to God” (Philippians 4:18). Someone packed a bag for a friend in trouble, and the apostle reaches for the language of the altar. The meal cooked for the family whose week has collapsed, the bill quietly paid: Paul says these go up. And that answers an ache many carry without naming it: the weariness of loving someone who does not notice. The daughter who drives every Saturday to sit with a mother who no longer knows her name. The person who has held a marriage together alone for eleven years and never once been thanked. Read the last two words: “to God”. The direction of the smoke is up, not across. Whether the person noticed, deserved it, returned it or remembers it is a different question from whether it arrived. It arrived. Nothing you have ever spent in love has gone nowhere.

Before it is a pattern, it is a gift. If “as Christ loved us” were only a standard to reach, none of us would pass. But before the cross is a pattern to copy, it is a gift to receive: he “loved us and gave himself up for us”. And we are “the aroma of Christ to God” (2 Corinthians 2:15). The smoke from Calvary has never stopped rising, and the Father has never stopped being pleased with it. What pleases God in you is not the quality of your loving this week, but the fragrance of an offering someone else made, which you are covered in. No bad week can sour it.

What it does not mean. Not that love has no limits or must tolerate sin. Christ’s love aims at our holiness (v. 27). Nor does “gave himself up” mean absorbing whatever harm is done to you and calling it love: Christ’s self-giving was chosen and aimed at rescue (see on 5:22). The command to walk in love has never contained a command to stand still and be destroyed.
verseByVerse.note: A “fragrant offering” recalls the Old Testament sacrifices that pleased God.

verseByVerse.quote: But sexual immorality and all impurity or covetousness must not even be named among you, as is proper among saints.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Love’s counterfeits. The word “but” sets these sins against the verse before. There Christ gave himself up for us; here are three ways of taking others for ourselves, the cross turned inside out. Sexual immorality uses another’s body for my pleasure, where Christ gave his body for another’s life. Greed reaches for more than its share, where he who was rich became poor for our sakes (2 Corinthians 8:9). Impurity feeds on what it should protect, where he gave himself to make his bride clean (v. 26).

The setting. In Ephesus sexual licence was woven into ordinary life and its religion: festivals, temple banquets and drunken revels where licence was expected. Prostitution was legal and taxed, and a husband’s use of slaves or prostitutes was not counted as adultery. (The popular claim that the temple of Artemis kept sacred prostitutes is not well supported; she was a virgin goddess.) Sexual sin and idolatry were often the same act, which is why Paul ties them together (v. 5).

Sexual immorality. Greek porneia: every sexual act outside marriage between a man and a woman, including adultery, sex before marriage, prostitution, homosexual acts and pornography (the words share a root). Not because the body is evil; it belongs to God (1 Corinthians 6:19–20). Sex is meant to say with the body what a husband and wife have promised with their words: “I am wholly yours, for life.” Outside marriage the body makes that promise while the person withholds it (1 Corinthians 6:16).

All impurity. Greek akatharsia, uncleanness. A wider word: the moral filth of which sexual sin is one part. It covers impure thoughts, words, images and desires as well as acts (Matthew 5:28). “All” closes the loopholes: what never reaches the bed still defiles the heart.

Covetousness. Greek pleonexia, wanting more: the craving to have more than God has given. In Ephesus the temple of Artemis was also the great bank of the province, and Demetrius raised a riot with profit and piety in one speech (Acts 19:25–27). Greed and lust are one appetite: the conviction that what God has given is not enough (1 Thessalonians 4:6). And greed is the sin respectable people commit and rarely confess.

Must not even be named among you. Paul has just named all three, so he does not mean silence: not the sermon that warns, the confession that admits, or the parent who explains to a teenager what pornography does to a soul (vv. 11–13). He forbids the naming that makes a thing ordinary: the affair discussed as entertainment over coffee. Things become acceptable by being mentioned often enough in a relaxed tone.

As is proper among saints. A saint is not a spiritual hero. It is anyone God has set apart as his own, and every believer already is one (1:1). Paul is saying: “you are saints, so live in the way that fits.”

What it does not mean. Not that owning, earning or saving is wrong. Providing for your family and managing money well are good stewardship (1 Timothy 5:8), and he “richly provides us with everything to enjoy” (1 Timothy 6:17). Paul was ambitious and said so (Romans 15:20). Greed measures itself against a neighbour and wants a larger share; godly ambition measures itself against the task and wants it done well, for others and for God. Is it held open-handed as a trust, or clutched as security? Likewise, desire for marriage, and sex within it, is good (1 Corinthians 7:2–5).

What it does not mean: temptation is not the same as sin. Paul condemns sexual sin, not the experience of being tempted. The difference matters greatly, both to keep us from excusing sin and to keep tender consciences from despair.

Jesus was tempted. He “in every respect has been tempted as we are, yet without sin” (Hebrews 4:15). Being tempted, even strongly and repeatedly, cannot in itself be sin, or Christ would have sinned. He never once grasped at more than his Father gave, and he now helps the tempted with the sympathy of one who has stood where they stand (Hebrews 2:18).

How temptation becomes sin. “Each person is tempted when he is lured and enticed by his own desire. Then desire when it has conceived gives birth to sin” (James 1:14–15). A thought or image arrives, an attraction is felt: that is temptation. Sin is conceived when the heart says yes: when we welcome it, dwell on it, replay it, or act on it (Matthew 5:28). Luther, borrowing an old saying, put it plainly: “You cannot stop the birds flying over your head, but you can stop them building a nest in your hair.” The unwanted thought that flashes in and is hated is a call to fight, not a verdict of guilt.

Where Christians differ: is our fallen nature itself sinful? This is a different question from whether temptation is sin. Roman Catholic teaching holds that the inclination to sin left in the baptised (concupiscence) is not itself sin until we consent. Reformed theology holds that the corruption of nature that remains in believers is truly sin, though in Christ it is pardoned and is being put to death (Westminster Confession 6.5; the 1689 London Baptist Confession 6.5; Romans 7:17–23). The Confession is describing the bent of our fallen nature, the sin that dwells in us, not the experience of being tempted. Jesus had no fallen nature, yet he was tempted in every respect as we are, without sin (Hebrews 4:15), so being tempted cannot in itself be sin. This commentary’s view: the Reformed view is more faithful to Romans 7, and it fits everything said above. Three things must be kept distinct. First, temptation, the thought, image or pull that presents itself to us, is not sin: Christ faced it, and the believer who meets it and turns away has not sinned but resisted. Second, the fallen nature that makes us open to temptation is the remnant of sin we fight and grieve over; for those in Christ there is no condemnation (Romans 8:1), and it is a reason for humility and dependence, not for guilt over every passing thought. Third, consenting to temptation, entertaining it, feeding it or acting on it is sin committed, which needs repentance.

What this means in practice. A believer who feels sexual attraction to someone not his spouse, or who struggles with unwanted desires of any kind, including same-sex attraction, is not by that fact one of the “impure” Paul describes in v. 5. He is a soldier in a fight. Turn away at once (2 Timothy 2:22), turn the mind to something good (Philippians 4:8), pray, tell a trusted believer, and remove what feeds the desire (Romans 13:14). God will provide the way of escape (1 Corinthians 10:13). And if you fall, do not hide: confess quickly and receive his forgiveness (1 John 1:9). Persistent, tormenting thoughts lose much of their power in the light (v. 13).

Is this not just an old-fashioned, repressive view of sex? It was never old-fashioned; in Ephesus it was the new thing. The world the church entered treated slaves, prostitutes and even wives as bodies to be used, and the Christian ethic was radical because it protected them: one standard for men and women alike, and no one’s body a thing for another’s pleasure. Every society draws sexual lines somewhere, and ours draws them too, at consent. The question is not whether there will be limits but who sets them, and Scripture’s answer is the God who made the body and, in his Son, gave his own body for us. His limits are a fence around a gift, not a cage around a prisoner. And for anyone who has already crossed them, the God who sets the limits is the God who washes: “such were some of you,” Paul told another church, “but you were washed” (1 Corinthians 6:11).

verseByVerse.quote: Let there be no filthiness nor foolish talk nor crude joking, which are out of place, but instead let there be thanksgiving.
verseByVerse.commentary:
From deeds to words. Speech shows the heart (Luke 6:45) and also shapes it: what we joke about, we begin to take lightly.

Filthiness and foolish talk. Filthiness is shameful, obscene talk. Foolish talk (mōrologia, from mōros, foolish: fool-talk) is empty, senseless speech, especially the kind that drifts into the indecent.

Crude joking. Greek eutrapelia: the ready wit. Aristotle listed it as a virtue; Paul names it a vice, because of what that cleverness is usually used for: making degrading things funny, through innuendo, and turning people into material. It is out of place, like muddy boots at a wedding.

But instead let there be thanksgiving. The surprising cure. Not restraint but thanksgiving, which replaces the habit instead of merely suppressing it (4:28). Crude joking treats people and God’s gifts, especially sex, as material for a laugh. Thanksgiving treats them as gifts and names the Giver. A man who begins genuinely thanking God for his wife will find the jokes about her drying up without ever having made a rule.

The mouth that gave thanks. The word is eucharistia. On the night he was betrayed, the Lord Jesus “took bread, and when he had given thanks, he broke it” (1 Corinthians 11:23–24). The darkest night in history, and his mouth spoke thanks. Crude joking makes people smaller to get a laugh; the words of Christ made the small great: the woman of the city, the tax collector up a tree, the thief beside him (Luke 4:22). Those who eat at his table cannot comfortably go on using their mouths to degrade what he gave his body to redeem.

What it does not mean. Not that Christians must be humourless; that produces not holiness but strain. There is wit on the lips of Jesus: a camel through the eye of a needle (Mark 10:25), the log in your own eye (Matthew 7:3–5). The target is humour that degrades.

What about the comedy and drama I watch? The same test applies to the screen as to the office, because laughing along on the sofa is still laughing along. Christians are free to enjoy good comedy, and to watch serious drama that shows sin honestly; Scripture itself tells of David’s adultery without making it funny or enticing. The question is what the programme is doing with the sin it shows: grieving it, exposing it, or selling it as entertainment. A show whose humour runs on innuendo and contempt is training your sense of what is normal every evening you give it, whether or not you notice. So ask plainly: does this leave me more thankful or more jaded? Do I switch it off when the children come in because I know what it is? If you already know the answer, the remote is in your hand.

verseByVerse.quote: For you may be sure of this, that everyone who is sexually immoral or impure, or who is covetous (that is, an idolater), has no inheritance in the kingdom of Christ and God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
You may be sure of this. Paul states it as settled truth. The same three sins as v. 3, but now as nouns that describe a person by his way of life: the sexually immoral person (pornos), the impure person, the covetous person (pleonektēs): people whose lives are ruled by these things, not people who have ever fallen into them.

(That is, an idolater). Not that greed is like idolatry. It is it. Most of us can see how a man worships a carved image, and cannot see how a man worships a bank balance. So ask what an idol does for its worshipper. It tells him who he is and that he is safe; it receives his best hours; it sets the terms of his joy; and it decides what he will sacrifice: time, integrity, his marriage, his children’s memory of him. Run those through a man who cannot stop wanting more, and every one fits (Matthew 6:24; Colossians 3:5). And it is the hardest idol to see, because greed wears the clothes of diligence and prudence.

Has no inheritance in the kingdom of Christ and God. God’s children inherit his kingdom (1:14, 18); those who live as slaves to these things show that they are not his children. “The kingdom of Christ and God”: one kingdom, shared by the Son and the Father, a quiet witness that Christ is God. And we inherit only as fellow heirs with Christ (Romans 8:17; Hebrews 1:2). So the question this verse finally puts is not whether you have kept a list, but whether you belong to him. The greedy man is looking for treasure in the wrong place; in Christ are hidden all the treasures (Colossians 2:3).

A question that troubles many believers. A Christian who struggles with lust, pornography or greed may read this verse and fear that he is lost. Three things help. First, Paul is describing a settled pattern of life that a person accepts and does not fight, not the believer who falls, hates it, confesses it and keeps fighting (Romans 7:18–25; 1 John 1:8–9). The difference is not whether you sin, but whether you are at peace with it or at war with it. The one who cries, “Wretched man that I am! Who will deliver me from this body of death?” (Romans 7:24) is not the voice of the excluded, but of one who belongs to Christ and knows he is not yet what he will be. The mark of the believer is not that he never falls, but that he cannot stay down. Second, Paul includes the covetous, which should humble every reader: no one can read this list and think it is only about other people. Third, Paul writes this to people already saved by grace (2:8–9) and sealed by the Spirit, that is, marked as God’s own and kept safe by him (1:13–14). In 1 Corinthians 6:9–11 he gives a similar list and then says, “And such were some of you. But you were washed.” So if this verse troubles you, that trouble is itself a sign of life. The person Paul warns is not troubled at all. The cure for a troubled conscience is not to soften the warning, but to run to Christ.

Where Christians differ: can a true believer lose the inheritance? Many sincere Christians in the Arminian tradition (which holds that God’s saving grace can finally be resisted) believe that true Christians can fall away for good, and read this verse as a warning that a believer who returns to these sins will lose the kingdom. This commentary’s view: the warning is real and must be taken seriously, but it does not describe a true believer losing what God has sealed (1:13–14; 4:30). Those who are truly God’s children will not settle into a life ruled by these sins; if someone does so and never repents, it shows he never truly belonged to Christ, whatever he professed (1 John 2:19; 3:9). God uses warnings like this to keep his people persevering.

In everyday life. An idol only holds power while it goes by another name. What loss would feel like the end of you? What did you last spend a sleepless night over? Whatever answers those is functioning as your god. Name it, and you can stop asking it for what it was never able to give.

verseByVerse.quote: Let no one deceive you with empty words, for because of these things the wrath of God comes upon the sons of disobedience.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Let no one deceive you. Paul’s other letters show what such voices said: that the body did not matter, or that grace made sin harmless (1 Corinthians 6:12–13; Romans 6:1).

Empty words. Such words are always half true, and that is why they work. Here are three, each with its answer. God is gracious; this does not really matter. But grace is not God’s indifference to sin; it is what it cost him to deal with it. To say grace makes sin unimportant is to say Calvary was an overreaction. Everyone struggles with this. A reason to be gentle with others, not to stop fighting; and the word “struggle” is often used by someone who has stopped struggling and would like to keep the word. A loving God would never judge. A father who watched his child being destroyed and felt nothing would not be loving. Wrath is not the opposite of love; indifference is.

Where empty words come from. Rarely from the enemies of the faith. From a friend who wants us comfortable, from a teacher who has learned that the pleasant half of the message fills a room, and most often from ourselves, at eleven at night, building a case in our own favour.

The wrath of God. Not a tantrum, but the fixed resolve of a holy God against everything that destroys those made in his image. It is shown now (Romans 1:18) and will come in full at the judgment (Colossians 3:6). “Sons of disobedience” means people whose character is disobedience, as all of us were before Christ (2:2–3). And here is the wonder: the wrath that comes on the sons of disobedience fell first and fully on the obedient Son, so that all who trust him are saved from it.

What it does not mean. Not that believers should fear God’s wrath as their sentence. Christ has borne it for those who trust him (Romans 5:9; 8:1). The warning is aimed at the conscience that wants permission, not at the believer who fights, grieves and returns. His holiness took our sin seriously enough to judge it, and his love took it seriously enough to bear it himself.

In everyday life. When a line of reasoning arrives that happens to permit exactly what you already wanted, treat its convenience as evidence against it.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore do not become partners with them;
verseByVerse.commentary:
Setting and background. Converts in Ephesus lived among family and trade guild members who still practised these things in temple feasts, guild gatherings and private homes.

Do not become partners with them. “Partners” (symmetochoi, co-sharers) appears in only one other place in the New Testament, earlier in this letter, where it is translated “partakers”: Gentiles are now “fellow heirs, members of the same body, and partakers of the promise in Christ Jesus” (3:6). So he is asking which partnership you are really in. A believer already has a partner, and it is Christ himself: his promise, his body and his inheritance, shared with outsiders at the cost of his blood. Holiness here is not first a fence around the world but faithfulness to someone. You cannot be a co-sharer in Christ and a co-sharer in the works of darkness at once. A person cannot give his whole loyalty to two sides. And “become” is present tense: do not drift into becoming partners. Compromise is rarely a decision. It is usually a silence: the laugh you gave so as not to seem difficult, the objection you did not raise. Behind most of those silences is the fear of not being liked, and the cure for it is not grim courage but knowing whose approval you already have: “am I now seeking the approval of man, or of God?” (Galatians 1:10).

What it does not mean. It does not mean withdrawal from unbelievers (1 Corinthians 5:9–11). Jesus was called “a friend of tax collectors and sinners” (Matthew 11:19). He sat at their tables yet never once shared in their sin; he came among us without becoming like us in our darkness, so that we might share in his light. The line runs not between people but between practices: not whether you go to the party, but whether you take part in what happens there. You can be among people, and love them, without joining in what they do.

In everyday life. In a situation you would rather not have to describe, ask not “Am I doing anything wrong?” but “If the people I love and the Lord I serve were both watching, what would my being here be saying?”

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The picture moves from love to light. Believers were once darkness and are now light in the Lord, so they bear light’s fruit, refuse the works of darkness and bring them into the open, where Christ shines on those he wakes.
verseByVerse.theology:
Light, darkness and the witness of holiness

Paul does not say his readers were in darkness but that they were darkness, and are now light. That is the language of new birth: not moral improvement but a change of nature, God’s own work.

The call to take no part in darkness but to expose it (v. 11) asks for something harder than either withdrawing from the world or blending into it: being there, among people, without joining in what is wrong. A church that is visibly holy serves the world as well as its own members, because by contrast it shows what the world cannot see about itself.

The short hymn of v. 14 carries the urgency of the passage. The church is the company of people Christ has woken. And it wakes others less by shouting at the darkness than by shining in it.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Ephesus had a flourishing trade in magic and mystery rites, practices that drew their power from secrecy. Christians who lived openly before God, with nothing to hide, were themselves a witness against that culture.

Now: Our world is often less hostile than drowsy, numbed by comfort and distraction and taking its way of life as simply normal. A church that is awake, seeing life in the light of God’s word and living accordingly, is itself an invitation to come and see what happens when Christ shines on someone.

verseByVerse.quote: for at one time you were darkness, but now you are light in the Lord. Walk as children of light
verseByVerse.commentary:
At one time you were darkness. Paul is not being vague about that past; he has written its biography earlier in this letter. Dead in trespasses, following the course of this world, children of wrath (2:1–3); “having no hope and without God in the world” (2:12); darkened in understanding, callous (4:18–19). Darkness here is not a mood; it is a life with a history. And notice: not “in the dark” but darkness itself. Before Christ it was not only around us; it was our nature. That means more than doing dark things from time to time. It means the source itself was dark: our desires, our thinking and our will were turned away from God, so that even our good deeds were done without love for him (Romans 8:7–8). We did not stumble into the dark by accident; left to ourselves we preferred it, as Jesus said, loving darkness rather than light (John 3:19). And we could no more change that by trying harder than a dark room can light itself.

But now you are light. Not “you are in the light” or “you have some light”. You are light: a change of nature, not only of location. It means the centre has changed. The Spirit of Christ now lives in you, so you begin to love God and what he loves, you want the truth about yourself to be seen rather than hidden, and you shine on the people around you as a lamp lights a room (Matthew 5:14–16). It is not light you generate; you are “light in the Lord”, bright the way the moon is bright, with all of it received from him who is the light of the world (John 8:12). Nor does it mean you no longer sin. It means that when you do, you no longer love it: you hate it, confess it and fight it, because your nature has changed sides. And notice what Paul does not say happened. God did not find a spark in you and fan it; darkness has no raw material in it. What happened was creation: “God, who said, ‘Let light shine out of darkness,’ has shone in our hearts” (2 Corinthians 4:6). That is Genesis 1:3 spoken over a human being, into a dark that contributed nothing. Hold on to that if you have ever suspected that God got less than he bargained for with you. Nobody was a promising case.

In the Lord. Think of the moon. It is truly light; sailors have crossed oceans by it. Every particle of that light is borrowed, and turned away from the sun it is a cold rock. Neither fact cancels the other. So the honest reader who thinks about what went through his mind on the drive home and concludes that “light” cannot describe him is searching himself for a glow of his own, and the verse never said he had one. Do not search inside yourself for a glow of your own. Turn round and face Christ, as the moon faces the sun.

Walk as children of light. In Hebrew idiom a son of something is marked by it (Luke 16:8; John 12:36). The same word as in 5:1: both times the family you belong to is the reason for the behaviour, never the price of admission. Most of us are trying to walk well enough to earn the identity. Paul hands you the identity and then asks for the walk.

In the flow. The “for” at the start of verse 8 gives the reason for verse 7: you are no longer what they are.

In everyday life. Think of the last time you sinned badly enough to be ashamed. Sin in a child of light sits wrong, will not settle, wants confessing. A stain shows on white cloth and disappears on black, and the fact that yours showed is telling you what colour the cloth is.

verseByVerse.quote: (for the fruit of light is found in all that is good and right and true), and try to discern what is pleasing to the Lord.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The fruit of light. Fruit grows; it is not manufactured. Not rules to perform, but fruit to bear, and Jesus said where it comes from: “I am the vine; you are the branches. Whoever abides in me and I in him, he it is that bears much fruit, for apart from me you can do nothing” (John 15:5). Goodness, righteousness and truth are not three virtues we assemble by effort. They are the family likeness of the Son, the good shepherd, the righteous one and the truth (John 10:11; 1 John 2:1; John 14:6), ripening in people joined to him. So the remedy for a barren season is not first a grimmer effort at goodness but nearness to Christ, as a branch is near the vine, turned towards the light he sheds.

Textual note. Later manuscripts read “fruit of the Spirit” (as in the King James Version), from Galatians 5:22. This commentary’s view: “fruit of light” is original.

Try to discern. Greek dokimazō: to test and approve, as a metalworker tests gold. The Christian life cannot be reduced to a rule-book; life keeps producing cases no rule-book addressed (Romans 12:2; Philippians 1:9–10).

What is pleasing to the Lord. And notice the object. Not, discern what is permitted, but what is pleasing. Most of us instinctively ask a boundary question: is this allowed? Where exactly is the line? That question can always be answered, and it is asked by someone who wants to know how close he may go. Paul’s question cannot be answered that way. Take a promotion offering more money and sixty hours a week, with two children at home. The boundary question returns nothing useful: no commandment is broken. Ask Paul’s question, and the relevant things arrive from every side: the years with those children you cannot get back; whether this is stewardship or, in respectable clothes, the greed Paul has just called idolatry (v. 5); what your real motive is; what your wife would say if she thought you truly wanted the answer. None of that can be looked up. It is what a person sees who knows the Lord well enough to know what pleases him.

What it does not mean. Not that each of us invents our own morality. Discernment is trained by Scripture and by constant practice (Hebrews 5:14). A Christian of thirty years has asked the question ten thousand times. Like a cook who has tasted for a lifetime, he can tell more quickly what is good.

verseByVerse.quote: Take no part in the unfruitful works of darkness, but instead expose them. For it is shameful even to speak of the things that they do in secret.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Unfruitful works of darkness. Darkness produces only barren works (Galatians 6:8). “Take no part” has the same root as “partners” in v. 7.

Expose them. Greek elenchō: to bring into the open, convict, show something for what it is. What does that mean on a Thursday? Not hunting for what people hide; not exposing persons, for Paul says expose the works; and not loudly denouncing a world behaving exactly as one would expect, since judging outsiders is not our business (1 Corinthians 5:12–13). It has three ordinary forms. First, living so that the contrast shows: a man who simply does not join in has made something visible without a word (Matthew 5:16). Second, refusing to let a thing pass as normal: not a sermon, but the quiet sentence that declines to laugh, or says, “I don’t think that’s right,” and lets the silence sit. Third, and hardest, going privately to a brother about something you can see and he cannot (Matthew 18:15; Galatians 6:1).

The light that came into the world. Jesus described his own coming in these very terms: “the light has come into the world, and people loved the darkness rather than the light because their works were evil”; “everyone who does wicked things hates the light … lest his works should be exposed” (John 3:19–20), with the same verb Paul uses here. Christ was the light that exposed, and the world answered by trying to put him out. Yet he exposed in order to save, for “God did not send his Son into the world to condemn the world” (John 3:17). The woman at the well had her history laid bare in a few sentences, and she ran into the town saying, he “told me all that I ever did” (John 4:29), not crushed but set free. That is the pattern for all Christian exposing: the truth told, and the person not abandoned. And he was himself stripped and exposed to public shame on the cross, so that our hidden shame might be covered and healed.

The Ephesians had already seen this done. Ephesus was famous across the ancient world for magic. Its written spells were famous enough to have a name, the Ephesian Letters, and its mystery cults sold secrecy itself: rites at night, knowledge only for initiates. These were works of darkness in the plainest sense, things that drew their power from being hidden. When the gospel took hold there, many who had believed came confessing and disclosing their practices, and those who had practised magic brought their books and burned them in the sight of all, worth fifty thousand pieces of silver (Acts 19:18–19), at ruinous cost, when they could have sold them on. That is exactly what exposing the works of darkness looks like: what was secret brought into the open by the very people who had done it, and its power broken in the light. Some of those who first heard this letter had probably stood in that crowd. Paul is not asking for something new; he is asking them to go on living what they did that day.

Shameful even to speak of. Verse 12 governs the manner of exposing. You can bring a thing into the open without describing it in detail. An account so vivid that hearers are entertained instead of sobered has stopped exposing darkness and started selling it.

Between two ditches. One ditch is withdrawal: a church keeps so far from the world that its light falls on no one but itself. The other is blending in: a church grows so like the world that there is no difference left to see. Paul asks for the road between: be there, among people, without joining in what is wrong. Only that leaves anyone with something to see.

What if the thing I know about is a crime, or someone is being harmed? Then exposing it means telling those who can stop it, and quickly. The private approach of Matthew 18:15 is for a brother’s sin against you; it was never meant for the abuse of a child, violence in a home or serious fraud, where going quietly to the offender can warn him and leave the victim in danger. God has given the civil authorities the sword to punish wrongdoing (Romans 13:4), and reporting a crime to them is obedience, not betrayal. Tell the police or the proper safeguarding body, and tell your church’s elders, but do not let anyone, a church leader included, persuade you to keep it inside the church instead. Speaking up for those who cannot speak for themselves honours Christ far more than protecting the reputation of his people (Proverbs 31:8–9).

In everyday life. Before you speak about someone’s sin, ask what you are hoping for. If part of you hopes to be proved right, or seen as the one who noticed, that is not light; it is the pleasure of holding a torch.

verseByVerse.quote: But when anything is exposed by the light, it becomes visible, for anything that becomes visible is light. Therefore it says, 'Awake, O sleeper, and arise from the dead, and Christ will shine on you.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Anything that becomes visible is light. When sin is brought into God’s light, it is seen for what it is. Then comes a difficult phrase, and its likely meaning is this: what is exposed and confessed does not stay darkness; it is changed into light. When a person’s sin is brought into the light and he repents, he himself becomes light (1 John 1:7–9). Think of a believer who has carried a hidden sin for years. The moment it is confessed to God and to a trusted friend, its grip weakens, not because confession is magic, but because secrecy is the one condition sin truly needs. Shame’s whole power is one sentence: “If they knew what you are, they would be finished with you.” Confession tests it. You say the thing aloud, and your friend does not recoil; he prays with you, and next week he asks how you are getting on. The lie is disproved in front of you by someone who now knows the worst and is still sitting there. That is why James says, “confess your sins to one another … that you may be healed” (James 5:16). The healing comes through the “one another”.

Therefore it says. Probably an early Christian hymn, perhaps sung at baptism, echoing Isaiah 26:19 and 60:1.

Awake, O sleeper. Sleep pictures a life unaware of God and of danger. It is first a call to the unconverted. But Paul is writing to saints, and the words are wide enough to reach the man who woke years ago and has since dozed off in a comfortable pew. Scripture keeps addressing him: “the hour has come for you to wake from sleep” (Romans 13:11); “Wake up, and strengthen what remains” (Revelation 3:2). The sleeping Christian has renounced nothing and would answer every doctrinal question correctly. But no sin has been fought in years, prayer has become words without an address, and he cannot remember when he last expected God to do anything. Everything looks normal and nothing is happening. And the sleeper does not know he is asleep, which is why the summons has to come from outside: a hymn, a sermon, a friend, a verse that will not leave him alone.

Arise from the dead. This is more than sleep. Without Christ a person is spiritually dead: cut off from God and unable to respond to him (2:1). A dead man cannot obey a command to get up. So the call must itself give the life it asks for, and it does: “an hour is coming, and is now here, when the dead will hear the voice of the Son of God, and those who hear will live” (John 5:25).

Christ will shine on you. The command is not the point of the sentence; the promise is. The light is already shining, and the only thing between the sleeper and the sunrise is a pair of closed eyes. And Isaiah promised that the glory of the LORD would rise upon his people (Isaiah 60:1); the church’s song says, “Christ will shine”. The first Christians put Jesus where Isaiah put the LORD. They sang to him as God.

For worship. Dawn does not wait for the sleeper to deserve it. The Son of God rose on the first morning of the week, and he has been rising on sleepers ever since. He once called a dead man by name, and Lazarus came out (John 11:43–44). Every believer is a morning he made: a darkness that never asked for light, and was shone on anyway.
verseByVerse.note: These lines are not found in the Old Testament; they may come from an early Christian hymn, echoing Isaiah.

parallels.desc: awake and sing, you who dwell in the dust
arise, shine, for your light has come

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul’s third picture of the walk is wisdom: using the time well in evil days, understanding the Lord’s will, and being filled with the Spirit, a filling that shows in song, thanks and humble submission to one another.
verseByVerse.theology:
The fullness of the Spirit and the worshipping church

“Be filled with the Spirit” (v. 18) is a present, passive command: go on being filled. We do not fill ourselves; God fills us, as we use the means he gives (his word, prayer, the church’s worship, obedience) and as we ask (Luke 11:13).

“Submitting to one another” (v. 21) is the hinge into the household instructions that follow. Its root is the humility of Christ, who “did not count equality with God a thing to be grasped, but emptied himself” (Philippians 2:6–7).
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The cult of Dionysus, god of wine, sought nearness to the divine through drunkenness and abandon. Against that, Paul sets a church filled not with wine but with God’s Spirit.

Now: Our age has endless ways to fill an inner emptiness: entertainment, substances, the constant pull of the screen. The hunger returns each time. A church that sings with gratitude, gives thanks and puts others first offers the watching world a glimpse of what it was made for.

verseByVerse.quote: Look carefully then how you walk, not as unwise but as wise, making the best use of the time, because the days are evil.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Look carefully then how you walk. Literally see accurately how you walk, like someone picking his way along a narrow path. A surgeon does not walk into an operating theatre the way she walks into a supermarket: not anxious, but focused. Paul asks for that wakefulness in the whole of life.

In the flow. For the third time in the chapter Paul says “walk” (vv. 2, 8, 15), taking up 4:1. The one Christ has woken (v. 14) must now watch his steps.

Unwise and wise. In Scripture wisdom is skill in living God’s way, rooted in the fear of the Lord (Proverbs 9:10). Nobody makes a dramatic decision to waste his life. The unwise simply never decide not to.

Making the best use of the time. Literally buying up the time (exagorazomenoi), a merchant’s word, from the same root as redemption. Time cannot be saved, only spent. The man who says he has no time for prayer has not run out of time; he has bought something else with it. And the word for time is kairos: opportunity. Opportunities have expiry dates: a conversation with an ageing parent while he can still follow it; a friend in crisis, asking questions now, who in eighteen months will have rebuilt his defences; a child at the age when he still wants your company. None of these announces its closing time (Colossians 4:5; Psalm 90:12).

Because the days are evil. The current runs against you (2:2; 6:12). A boat on a river does not stay still by doing nothing; it drifts downstream.

The age that has already dawned. The evil days are not the whole story. The Bible speaks of two ages: the present one, spoiled by sin, and the age to come, when God makes everything new. Christ gave himself “to deliver us from the present evil age” (Galatians 1:4), and when he rose, the new age began, like first light before full day. So we live where the two overlap. The days are still evil, yet every hour belongs to the season in which the risen Lord is gathering his people before he returns. To buy up the time is to spend it on what he is doing.

Never in a hurry. Redeeming the time is not maximising output, and it gives no ground for guilt about rest. Jesus had some three years and the weight of the world on him, and still stopped for a blind man on the road (Mark 10:46–52) and slept in a boat during a storm (Mark 4:38). He knew his hour, and when it came he went to meet it, buying with his own life the redemption of a people who had squandered theirs. A frantic life and a wasted life can be equally unredeemed. The question is not how much you got through today, but what you bought.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore do not be foolish, but understand what the will of the Lord is.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Foolish. Greek aphrōn: not low intelligence, but living without thinking about God.

Understand. Christian obedience uses the mind: not what is convenient, but “What does the Lord want here?”

The will of the Lord. Christians agonise over this phrase, mostly by confusing two senses. There is God’s hidden will: everything he has planned will happen. It governs all things, and he has not told us its details: “The secret things belong to the LORD our God” (Deuteronomy 29:29). And there is his revealed will, what he has told us plainly he wants, which fills the Bible. Almost everything people mean by “finding God’s will” concerns the hidden one: which house, which career, which person, and the fear of missing the single correct path. But that will was never given to you to read. Meanwhile the revealed will sits open on the desk: “this is the will of God, your sanctification” (1 Thessalonians 4:3); “give thanks in all circumstances; for this is the will of God in Christ Jesus for you” (1 Thessalonians 5:18). God’s will is not a hidden dot you must locate and are ruined for missing. It is a direction he has already described in detail, and a person he is making you into. The one pursuing holiness, giving thanks, telling the truth, loving his wife and doing good work is in the will of God, whichever of two reasonable job offers he accepts.

The will has a centre. When this letter first speaks of God’s will, it says what the will is about: he has made known to us the mystery of his will, a plan for the fullness of time, to unite all things in Christ, things in heaven and things on earth (1:9–10). In plain words: God’s great aim is to bring everything together under Christ. His will is not first a set of private instructions for each of us. It is one purpose with Christ at its heart, and our lives are caught up in it. So understanding the will of the Lord begins with knowing the Lord, and Jesus said what the Father wants most: “that everyone who looks on the Son and believes in him should have eternal life” (John 6:40). The Son came down from heaven not to do his own will but the will of the one who sent him (John 6:38), and he did it all the way to the cross. The believer who asks, “How does this decision serve his purpose to gather all things under Christ?” has found the right question, even before he has found the answer.

verseByVerse.quote: And do not get drunk with wine, for that is debauchery, but be filled with the Spirit,
verseByVerse.commentary:
The setting. At the festivals of Dionysus, god of wine, drunkenness was thought to bring people close to the divine. Wine promised a counterfeit nearness to the god; the true God gives himself. The true way to be filled with God is not wine but the Spirit.

Do not get drunk with wine, for that is debauchery. “Debauchery” (asōtia) is a life out of control, the prodigal son’s reckless living (Luke 15:13; Proverbs 23:29–35). And ask what the glass is being asked to do. Drink is often reached for to quiet the fear, numb the shame, or supply a courage and comfort we are not finding in God. That is why Paul’s cure is not only less wine but more of the Spirit.

But be filled with the Spirit. Why compare wine and the Spirit? Both can fill a person and influence how he speaks and acts. Wine takes away self-control; the Spirit gives it (Galatians 5:23) and leads to praise, thanks and humble service (vv. 19–21). In plain words: let the Spirit govern you. The point is who is in control, not what it feels like. A sail filled with wind goes where the wind takes it.

Not drunk at nine in the morning. Paul’s contrast had been drawn once before, in public. On the day of Pentecost, when the disciples were filled with the Holy Spirit, mockers said, “They are filled with new wine” (Acts 2:13). Peter answered that they were not drunk, at that hour of the morning, but that Jesus, exalted to the right hand of God, had received the promised Spirit from the Father and poured him out (Acts 2:15, 33). The filling of the Spirit is the gift of the ascended Christ, and the Spirit leads back to him: “He will glorify me” (John 16:14). So a Spirit-filled life is a Christ-filled life, in which the word of Christ dwells richly (Colossians 3:16) and the songs are about him.

A command that is passive. Keep on being filled. How can someone be commanded to have something done to him? A sail cannot make wind, but it can be raised or left furled. Everything that opens a life to the Spirit is canvas going up; grieving or quenching him is furling the sail, after which a man may sincerely complain that he feels becalmed. Every believer already has the Spirit (1:13); being filled is a continuing life, less like a tank topped up once than like breathing.

How is a believer filled? The best guide is Colossians 3:16–17, Paul’s parallel passage. Set them side by side. Here: be filled with the Spirit, addressing one another in psalms and hymns and spiritual songs, singing, giving thanks always, submitting to one another (5:18–21). There: let the word of Christ dwell in you richly, teaching one another in psalms and hymns and spiritual songs, singing, giving thanks, and then wives, husbands and children (Colossians 3:16–18). The results are the same, in the same order, almost in the same words. Only the cause is put differently. So these are not two separate attainments, one ordinary and one rare. They are two descriptions of one reality, because the Spirit wrote the word and works through it. In practice: take in God’s word, ask (“how much more will the heavenly Father give the Holy Spirit to those who ask him!” Luke 11:13), obey what you already know, confess sin quickly instead of letting it pile up, so as not to grieve him (4:30; 1 John 1:9), do not quench his promptings (1 Thessalonians 5:19), stop numbing your inner life with substitutes, and join God’s people in worship.

How would I know? Paul does not send you inward to check your feelings. He gives the test himself (vv. 19–21), and it is all outward: Is there song in you? Is there thanksgiving, always and for everything? Are you submitting to others, which is the least likely product of any counterfeit filling in the world? That is why the comparison with drunkenness fits. Nobody has to be told when a man is drunk: it shows in how he speaks and how he treats people. The other influence should be just as visible. The Spirit does not fill people to make them more impressive or dominant, but more like servants. If you want to know which is filling you, ask the people who live with you.

Should I expect to feel something when I am filled with the Spirit? Sometimes, but feelings are not the test. At times God gives a strong sense of his nearness: joy in worship, a sudden settled assurance, sweetness in prayer or in reading Scripture, a peace in a crisis that you know you did not produce (Romans 5:5; 1 Peter 1:8). Receive those with thanks. But the filled life is just as real on the grey days, when you obey without any glow and keep loving a difficult person out of plain faithfulness. When the believers in Acts 4:31 were filled, what followed was not a sensation but boldness to speak the word. So do not chase experiences, and do not doubt the Spirit’s work because you feel flat. Feelings follow sleep, health and temperament; the fruit Paul names follows the Spirit.

Where Christians differ: is the filling a second blessing? Some Pentecostal and charismatic teaching links being filled with a second experience after conversion, often called the baptism in the Spirit and marked by speaking in tongues. This commentary’s view: every believer is indwelt and sealed by the Spirit from conversion (1:13; Romans 8:9; 1 Corinthians 12:13). Being filled is the ongoing life of a Spirit-governed believer, nourished by the word and shown in the fruits that follow (vv. 19–21). Believers may be filled afresh many times, as the apostles were (Acts 2:4; 4:31), and God may grant times of special strength; but no Christian is a second-class believer without the Spirit. Many charismatic and Pentecostal believers love Christ deeply, and their hunger for more of the Spirit is right; the question is only whether Scripture promises a distinct second stage, and Paul here describes a filling every believer is to seek again and again.

What it does not mean. Not a ban on wine, God’s gift “to gladden the heart of man” (Psalm 104:15; John 2:1–11). The sin is being controlled by it. A Christian should not drink in a way that causes a brother to stumble (Romans 14:21), and some wisely choose not to drink at all. Nor does it mean that a Spirit-filled person is loud or ecstatic; the marks Paul gives are worship, gratitude and humility.

Where is the line between drinking and being drunk? It is crossed well before you are falling over. Drunkenness begins when drink starts to take the controls: when your judgment, your speech or your restraint is no longer fully your own. An honest test is whether you would say, do and drive exactly as you would sober. If you drink in order to feel the loosening, to unwind by switching yourself partly off, you are already asking wine to do what Paul says the Spirit does. Watch, too, for dependence: needing a drink to get through an evening, hiding how much you have had, being irritable without it. Those are signs to stop altogether and to tell someone. And the same principle reaches beyond alcohol to anything taken to alter the mind for pleasure, recreational drugs included: your mind is meant to be governed by the Spirit, not handed over to a substance.

verseByVerse.quote: addressing one another in psalms and hymns and spiritual songs, singing and making melody to the Lord with your heart, giving thanks always and for everything to God the Father in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ,
verseByVerse.commentary:
The first sign of the Spirit’s filling. Not spectacular experiences, but singing, thanksgiving and submission (vv. 19–21). In Greek all three hang on the command “be filled”: they are what the filling looks like.

Addressing one another. Singing is not only to God but to each other (Colossians 3:16). Think of the man in the third row who buried someone on Tuesday, and the words will not come out of him. They are being sung over him by people who can manage it this week, and he is carried on a sound he had no strength to make. And at three in the morning in your worst week, what comes is rarely a paragraph from a sermon; it is a line you have sung a hundred times. What you sing is what you will believe when you cannot think. And the church does not sing alone. The Lord Jesus sang a hymn with his friends on the night he was betrayed (Mark 14:26), and he now leads the praise of his brothers in the midst of the congregation (Hebrews 2:12).

Psalms, hymns and spiritual songs. Probably the psalms of the Old Testament, hymns of praise, and other songs prompted by the Spirit. Paul does not legislate the repertoire; what interests him is the direction the singing travels.

Where Christians differ: psalms only, and instruments? Some Reformed churches sing only the biblical Psalms (exclusive psalmody), reading all three words as kinds of psalm, and it is a serious position: all three words appear in the Greek Old Testament’s own psalm headings. Some also sing without instruments, holding that the New Testament gives no warrant for them in worship. This commentary’s view: the Psalms deserve a far larger place in our worship, but Scripture-filled hymns are also fitting: the New Testament itself contains Christian songs about Christ (5:14; Philippians 2:6–11; Revelation 5:9–10). And instruments are a help to singing, not a substitute for it; the Psalms call God’s people to praise him with lute and harp (Psalm 150:3), and nothing in the New Testament withdraws that.

Singing and making melody to the Lord with your heart. Psallō first meant to pluck a string, and the instrument Paul names is you. If you were once told you cannot sing and have believed it ever since, the Lord is listening to the instrument, and yours is in tune. But “with your heart” is not permission to stand in silence; the other half of the verse needs someone to hear you.

Always and for everything. Not only in all circumstances (1 Thessalonians 5:18), but for all things, and anyone who has buried a child may ask whether it can mean what it says. It does not mean calling evil good. Scripture never asks you to call a tumour a blessing or a betrayal a gift. Nor is grief a failure of faith: about a third of the Psalms are complaints, and God put “How long, O LORD?” into the church’s hymnbook permanently.

To God the Father in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ. Here is what makes it possible. Thanks is given to a Father, not to fate or a process, and this letter has told you what kind: one who chose you before the world began (1:4) and adopted you at the cost of his Son (1:5). You are not asked to believe that everything that happens is good, but that nothing reaches you except through that Father’s hands, and that he can make what was meant to destroy you serve you. “We know that for those who love God all things work together for good” (Romans 8:28): not feel it, but know it, which you can still say with a wet face. And “in the name of” Jesus is not a password. We give thanks through Christ as our mediator, the one who stands between the holy Father and us and brings us in, as children admitted at his invitation (John 16:24; Hebrews 13:15). By the Spirit, through the Son, to the Father.

What it does not mean. Job, having lost his property and ten children in one day, fell on the ground and worshipped: “The LORD gave, and the LORD has taken away; blessed be the name of the LORD” (Job 1:21). He does not bless the loss. He blesses the Name: gratitude, in the wreckage, to a Father who has not moved. And this verse describes what a Spirit-filled life overflows into; it was never meant to be handed to a grieving person as an instruction across a hospital bed. If you cannot do it today, you have not failed the verse.

verseByVerse.quote: submitting to one another out of reverence for Christ.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The hinge. Verse 21 completes the description of being filled with the Spirit and introduces the household sections (5:22–6:9). And in Greek v. 22 has no verb of its own; it borrows “submit” from v. 21. So the marriage passage cannot be lifted out and applied on its own. Detached from the filling of the Spirit it is being misused.

Submitting. “Submitting” (hypotassomenoi) was originally a military word: to arrange under, to take one’s ordered place, to put another’s good and rightful leadership before one’s own way. Two things must be said about it, and neither may be dropped. First, it says nothing about worth. The Son is equal with the Father in being, power and glory; yet in the work of salvation he willingly came as the one the Father sent and obeyed him, even to death (John 5:30; Philippians 2:6–8), and at the end he will hand over the kingdom to the Father (1 Corinthians 15:24, 28). That submission belongs to his mission, not to any inferiority of nature: order and equality are not rivals. Second, it is voluntary. The Greek form of the verb (the middle voice) describes something a person does himself: chosen, not forced. Submission is something a person gives; nobody can submit someone else. No one in this passage is told to make others submit. A man who sets out to make another submit has already made it impossible, and shown that what he wants is not submission but control.

Leadership in every sphere. The order this verse assumes is not something Paul invented. It is God’s gift in creation, and a common grace that blesses believer and unbeliever alike. Every group, from a family to a team, a company or a nation, flourishes only when someone leads and others are willing to follow; without that, it dissolves into the days when “everyone did what was right in his own eyes” (Judges 21:25). The household instructions that follow apply this to the home and to work, and Scripture applies it to the state and the church as well (Romans 13:1; 1 Peter 2:13; Hebrews 13:17). But all human authority is delegated. It comes from God, it answers to him, and it is limited by him: where it commands what he forbids, “We must obey God rather than men” (Acts 5:29). And Christ has redefined it as service: whoever would be great must be the servant of all (Mark 10:42–45). The study Leadership explores this further.

Where Christians differ: mutual submission? Egalitarians (for example Gordon Fee) read “submitting to one another” (allēlois) as fully mutual: every believer submits to every other in the same way, so that husbands submit to wives as wives submit to husbands, and there are no distinct roles of leading and following in marriage. Complementarians (who hold that men and women are equal in worth but given different, complementary roles in marriage and the church; for example John Stott in his own nuanced way, and Wayne Grudem more strongly) point out that the verses that follow specify who submits to whom: wives to husbands, children to parents, slaves to masters, never the reverse, and husbands are told not to submit but to love. They note that the verb, when the New Testament uses it of relationships between people, regularly describes submitting to someone in a position of authority (Luke 2:51; Romans 13:1; 1 Peter 2:13), and that “one another” can mean some to others, as when Revelation 6:4 says people slay one another (not everyone killing everyone). This commentary’s view: the complementarian reading, with its truth fully honoured. Verse 21 sets the spirit in which all Christians relate: humble, other-centred, putting others first (Philippians 2:3–4). Husbands, parents and masters are not exempt from that spirit. But within that humility, the following verses show that God has given a particular order in marriage and family, where some lead and others follow, and both serve. Mutual humility does not erase distinct roles, any more than Christ’s humility erased his headship.
