Many egalitarian Christians reach their view out of love for Scripture and a right concern that women never be belittled or harmed; they are brothers and sisters, and this commentary shares that concern even where it reads the text differently.

What every first reader would have felt. The ancient household codes addressed the head of the house about managing his wife, children and slaves. Paul speaks to the wife, the child and the slave first, as responsible people who answer to Christ themselves. And he asks more of the one holding the power: the husband gets three times as many lines, and is commanded to love “as Christ loved the church and gave himself up for her”. The heavier cost is laid on the stronger.

Out of reverence for Christ. Literally in the fear of Christ: not dread, but awe before the Lord who has loved him to the death. It is both the reason for submitting and the limit of it. The reason: you do not yield because the other person has earned it, but for the sake of the Lord who gave up everything for you. The limit: because the reverence is for Christ, it can never require what Christ forbids. A submission that would demand you sin has lost the only reason it ever had. (The King James Version reads “in the fear of God”, following later manuscripts; the earliest read Christ.)

What it does not mean. Not that anyone must submit to sin, cruelty or abuse; submission to people is always limited by obedience to God (Acts 5:29). Nor that leaders are above others in worth. Every believer is equally a child of God and equally loved.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The humble submission of v. 21 now reaches marriage. Paul speaks to wives and then, at greater length, to husbands, and shows that the union of husband and wife was designed to picture Christ and the church.
verseByVerse.theology:
Marriage, headship and the gospel mystery

The central claim of this passage is that marriage pictures the relationship between Christ and the church. That is why its shape is not arbitrary: the husband’s headship and the wife’s willing trust reflect Christ’s self-giving rule of his church and her glad response to him.

The husband’s headship is defined by the cross (v. 25). The head of the church died for her, washes her, and nourishes and cherishes her (v. 29); the husband follows the one who “came not to be served but to serve” (Matthew 20:28).

The wife’s submission is the free response of a woman secure in Christ, not compliance under pressure, and it never extends to sin or abuse. Neither calling can be lived from one’s own resources. Both depend on the Spirit who fills the church (v. 18), and both rest on Christ, whose love for his bride never fails.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: In the Roman world a husband’s authority over his household was very great and was assumed to exist for his benefit. Paul turned that around: the Roman husband used his authority to be served; the Christian husband was to use his to serve.

Now: Christian marriage faces two opposite pressures: a culture that treats marriage as a partnership to be ended when it stops meeting individual needs, and a shallow version of headship, in which a husband demands to be followed but will not give himself up for his wife as Christ did. Ephesians 5 answers both with a love that keeps its promises, gives itself as Christ did on the cross, and is kept going by the Spirit.

verseByVerse.quote: Wives, submit to your own husbands, as to the Lord.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The setting. Now Paul shows what the submission of v. 21 looks like in each relationship of the home, and he begins with the wife, addressing her directly, as a responsible person who chooses freely before God. On leadership and submission in every sphere of life, see on Ephesians 5:21.

Wives, submit. The verb is not in the earliest Greek manuscripts here (later ones supply it, as the King James Version does); it is carried over from v. 21: wives are called to the same posture Paul has just urged on every believer, now applied to their own husbands. To submit is to arrange yourself under, to support and follow his leadership. It is the wife’s own choice, offered to Christ. It is not the husband’s right to demand; Paul never tells husbands to make their wives submit. It speaks of role, never of worth. Before God, a man and a woman in Christ stand on exactly the same ground (Galatians 3:28). And the Son himself shows that to submit is not to be less. In the work of salvation he submits to the Father (1 Corinthians 11:3; 15:28), yet he is no less God than the Father, equal with him in nature.

To your own husbands. Not women to men in general, at work or in the church foyer, but a wife to the one man she made promises to. The verse has often been stretched far past that boundary.

As to the Lord: “do it for my sake”. Your best friend goes abroad for a year and asks you, “Please look after my elderly father while I am gone. Do it for me.” So you visit the father, drive him to his appointments and listen to his stories. The father is the one you are helping, but you are doing it for your friend. That is what “as to the Lord” means: Christ says, do it for my sake. Three things follow. First, the father is real, and you really serve him. No one pretends that a husband is Jesus: “as to the Lord” does not mean “as if he were the Lord”, and his word is not Christ’s word. Second, it does not depend on the father being pleasant, because you were never doing it for his thanks. So her submission does not rise and fall with how impressive her husband is on a given day. It rests on Christ, who is always worthy of trust, and who never asks his people to go where he has not gone first. He submitted to his Father in the garden (“not my will, but yours, be done”, Luke 22:42), he bore an unjust trial without hitting back (1 Peter 2:23), and he went to the grave for us. Third, you would never do something your friend would hate. If her husband asks her to do what Christ forbids (to lie, to join in sin, to hide abuse, to give up her faith or her conscience), her loyalty to Christ comes first, and she must obey God rather than men (Acts 5:29). Colossians says the same in other words: “as is fitting in the Lord” (Colossians 3:18). See also As to the Lord in the Theological Dictionary.

What submission looks like. Mostly the texture of ordinary life: not undermining his leadership in front of the children, speaking well of him, and choosing to trust after her voice has been fully heard. She brings her full wisdom, gifts and voice, and a good husband depends on it (Proverbs 31:10–31). A husband is offered a post in another city; the wife is deeply reluctant, because her friendships, work and ageing parents are here. They talk it through honestly, and he still believes they should go. Submission is trusting his judgment after her concerns have been truly weighed, and not letting the decision harden into a grievance, while he carries its weight and owes her every sacrifice to make it work.

And if he is not leading? The relocation example assumes a husband who listens and carries the cost. Many women are not in that marriage. They are married to a man who is not abusive, but spiritually passive or self-absorbed: who will not pray with her, leaves every hard decision to drift, and is present in the house but absent from the marriage. Scripture does not pretend she does not exist. Peter writes to exactly this woman: “even if some do not obey the word, they may be won without a word by the conduct of their wives” (1 Peter 3:1–2). He does not tell her that her position is hopeless or that her only options are nagging and despair. He tells her that her steady life has power in it, and that God can use it to reach a man sermons have not reached. That is not a consolation prize; it is a real calling, and a harder one than that given to the wives of good men. And the church should come alongside her and call the husband to his responsibilities.

Common questions. What if her husband is not a believer? Peter tells such wives to submit, so that their husbands may be won by their conduct (1 Peter 3:1–2), but never by joining in sin. What if there is abuse or danger? Then the limit of “as to the Lord” applies: no one is required to submit to violence. A husband who abuses his wife is not exercising headship but violating it catastrophically. A wife in danger should seek safety at once, report crimes to the authorities, and receive the church’s protection. Using this verse to keep a woman in danger is a terrible misuse of Scripture.

Does abuse mean only physical violence? No. Abuse is a pattern of control through fear, and it can be carried on without a blow: threats and intimidation, constant belittling, cutting a wife off from friends and family, controlling all the money so that she cannot act, sexual coercion, checking her every move. These are not the hard edges of headship but its opposite, because Christ never rules his bride by fear. A wife who recognises this pattern should tell someone outside the home: a trusted friend, a pastor, and where there is danger, the police or a domestic abuse helpline. Separating for safety is right, and no one should tell her that leaving to protect herself or her children breaks her vows; he has broken them. Whether such a marriage may finally be ended is a question for the elders to weigh with her, carefully, in the light of Scripture’s teaching on desertion (the Westminster Confession 24.6).

Where Christians differ: is this cultural? Egalitarians see the instruction as a first-century cultural arrangement, like slavery, which the gospel eventually set aside. This commentary’s view: the complementarian view: husband and wife are equal in worth, with different roles that fit together. Paul does not ground the wife’s submission in culture but in two things that do not change: creation (v. 31, Genesis 2:24; compare 1 Corinthians 11:8–9; 1 Timothy 2:13) and Christ’s relationship with the church (vv. 23–24). Slavery is regulated in Scripture but never grounded in creation or in Christ; Paul tells slaves to take their freedom if they can (1 Corinthians 7:21) and lists slave-traders among the lawless (1 Timothy 1:10). So the pattern holds today; it is to be lived with gladness and humility, and never used as a weapon. Many faithful Christians read it otherwise, often out of grief at how these verses have been misused; the answer to misuse is the passage’s own limits, not its removal.

What it does not mean. Not inferiority: husband and wife are equal heirs of the grace of life (Genesis 1:27; 1 Peter 3:7). Not silence, or giving up her judgment or conscience. Not submission of all women to all men. And not a burden uniquely hers: it follows the call to all believers to submit (v. 21), and is followed by the far heavier charge to the husband (v. 25). If the wife is called to submit, the husband is called to die.

verseByVerse.quote: For the husband is the head of the wife even as Christ is the head of the church, his body, and is himself its Savior. Now as the church submits to Christ, so also wives should submit in everything to their husbands.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Where Christians differ: does head mean authority or source? Some egalitarian scholars (for example Catherine Kroeger and Gordon Fee) argue that in Greek kephalē often meant source, like the head of a river, so that the husband is the source of the wife (as Eve came from Adam), not her authority. Others (for example Joseph Fitzmyer and Wayne Grudem) studied the ancient uses and found that when kephalē is used of a person in relation to others, it regularly means one in authority or prominence. This commentary’s view: authority, exercised as Christ exercises it. In this very letter Paul uses head of Christ in a way that clearly means authority: God put all things under his feet and gave him as head over all things (1:22). And here the wife’s response to the head is to submit (v. 24), which fits authority, not source. Yet Paul also uses head for the one who nourishes and gives growth to the body (4:15–16; v. 29). Christ’s headship includes both: he rules his church and he gives it life. The husband’s headship is meant to mirror both. And Paul does not leave the word to be defined from a dictionary. He defines it himself, with a cross (vv. 25–27).

Even as Christ is the head of the church, his body. The comparison gives the husband real authority, and then changes what that authority looks like. To be head as Christ is head means taking final responsibility: when things go wrong he does not look for someone to blame but asks what he failed to do. Adam was with his wife when she was tempted and said nothing (Genesis 3:6), and God called to the man first (Genesis 3:9). It means starting love instead of waiting for it, and leading the spiritual life of the home instead of handing it to his wife as her department. Not “I lead, therefore I decide”, but “I lead, therefore I bear the cost of this for her sake.”

And is himself its Saviour. Here Paul marks the limit of his own picture. The husband is head as Christ is head. He is not Saviour. And that diagnoses two mirror-image ways marriages go wrong. There is the wife who has made her husband her saviour, needing him to make her finally secure, and so finds him failing at a job he was never given. And there is the husband who has taken that role on, thinking he must fix her and be her sufficiency, and ends up exhausted or controlling. He is to love her as Christ loved the church. He is not to be Christ to her, and she must not ask it of him.

Now as the church submits to Christ, so also wives should submit. The church submits to one who has already given himself for her entirely. First he showed his love; then she trusts and follows. That is a word to husbands first: a husband who wants to be followed but will not give himself has turned the picture upside down. A man who has to remind his wife that he is the head is like a man who has to remind people that he is funny. Christ washed feet (John 13:5) and went to a cross. Headship like that does not need to be asserted, because it is visible. But it is not a condition for the wife. Paul does not say, “Submit if your husband loves you as Christ loved the church.” Her submission is “as to the Lord” (v. 22): it is offered to Christ, who has given himself for her entirely, so it does not wait until her husband earns it, any more than his love waits until she deserves it (v. 25). Each owes Christ their part, whatever the other does. What sets the limit is not how well he loves her but what Christ forbids: never sin, and never abuse (see v. 22).

In everything. In every area of married life, still limited by “as to the Lord” (v. 22): no husband has authority to command what Christ forbids.

What it does not mean. Not that the husband rules his wife as a master rules a servant. Godly headship listens, consults, serves and takes responsibility. She may be the more mature and the more discerning. A husband who hears her honest disagreement as a threat is protecting his ego; Christ is not threatened by the church’s questions. And if he is resting while she is exhausted, he is not leading; he is being served. A husband who uses this verse to dominate has forgotten how Christ loved the church: he “gave himself up for her” (v. 25). That is how a husband shows his headship: not by being served, but by a love that is self-sacrificing and costly.

What should I do if my wife will not follow my lead? Not try to make her. Nothing in this passage tells a husband to secure his wife’s submission; that is her obedience to Christ, not your project. Your command is to love her as Christ loved the church, and it has no condition attached (v. 25). So begin with yourself. Ask her honestly, and listen without defending yourself: “Has my leading been safe to follow? Have I listened, carried the cost, kept my word, prayed with you?” A wife’s resistance has often been taught by years of decisions made carelessly or selfishly. Where you have failed, own it specifically. Then keep leading gently in ordinary things: in prayer, in kindness, in taking responsibility. If the deadlock continues, ask your pastor or a wise older couple to help you both. Leadership that is truly Christlike is rarely refused for long. And if it still is, your call to love her does not lapse; Christ’s love for his church has never depended on how well she follows.

verseByVerse.quote: Husbands, love your wives, as Christ loved the church and gave himself up for her,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Husbands, love. Familiarity has flattened how strange this was. Marriage in that world was for property, heirs and an orderly household. Some moralists urged kindness, but none had measured a husband’s love by a Saviour dying for his bride. And Paul does not say, “lead your wives”. He says, “love your wives”: agapaō, a love that gives itself and keeps its promises, not a feeling that comes and goes.

As Christ loved the church. The standard is not other husbands, or what she deserves, but Christ. And ask what the church was like when he gave himself up for her. Paul has already said, and not gently: dead in trespasses and sins, following the prince of the power of the air, by nature children of wrath (2:1–3). In plain words: spiritually dead, following the devil, and deserving God’s anger. That is the bride. He did not find her radiant and decide she was worth it; he gave himself up for her in that condition, and the radiance came afterwards, which is exactly what Paul goes on to say he is doing (vv. 26–27). So the love does not respond to loveliness; it produces it, and that closes the escape hatch every husband reaches for: when she is easier to live with, when she deserves it. Christ did not wait for a bride worth dying for. He died, and so gained one.

Gave himself up for her. The measure is the cross. Headship means going first in sacrifice: his comfort, preferences, time and if necessary his life for her good. And this standard is meant for an ordinary week. It looks like a husband who notices what she carries and relieves it without being asked: after her hard week with the children, he takes over the evening without comment. It looks like giving up his preferences cheerfully, without the pointed silence. It looks like praying for her and asking how she is doing with God, and choosing her above career and comfort when they truly conflict. And it looks like asking forgiveness specifically and promptly: “I was unkind this morning, and I am sorry; will you forgive me?” with no “but you also”. Repeated over years, that small act builds a marriage in which she knows she is safe with him.

For whom did Christ die? Paul says he gave himself for the church, his bride: which points to a love that had particular people in view and actually saves them (Acts 20:28; John 10:11). That is, Christ did not die only to make salvation possible for anyone who might take it up; he died to save his bride, a particular people the Father gave him, and he will lose none of them (John 6:37–39). This is what Reformed churches call definite (or particular) atonement. Many faithful Christians hold that Christ died in the same way for every person, and they love the cross no less; the difference is over what the cross actually achieved, and verses like this one, where Christ gives himself for his bride, are why this commentary holds that it secured salvation for a people he knew by name. That does not narrow the invitation. Everyone who comes to him is welcomed (Matthew 11:28).

Where the power comes from. A husband who has read this far honestly is in a hard place. If you have been measuring yourself against Calvary, the reasonable conclusion is despair, and it is half right: you cannot love like this, and the standard is not lowered. Only one Husband ever has, and his perfect obedience is counted as yours (Romans 5:19), so your failures do not undo your standing. And this command does not stand on its own feet. All Paul’s teaching about the home (5:22–6:9) grows out of one command seven verses earlier: “be filled with the Spirit” (v. 18). This is the same Spirit-filled life reaching the home. This love is fruit the Spirit grows in a Christian, not a test to pass before Christ accepts you. So the question for a husband who keeps failing is not chiefly, “How do I try harder?” He has tried, in bursts, for years. The question is whether the man who comes through the door at six is being filled, because a marriage is lived largely on the overflow. A husband whose Bible has been shut for months will find that the tenderness he truly intends is simply not available on a Thursday evening when he is tired and she says the wrong thing. And there is comfort here. This love is not temperament, giving naturally warm men an advantage; it is fruit, and fruit grows on a branch because the branch is attached (John 15:4–5). The husband who grew up in a house where nobody said anything kind, and has no model for this, is not disqualified. He is asked to stay attached, which he can do.

What if I no longer feel any love for my wife? Then you are in exactly the place this command was written for. Paul does not tell you to feel love; he tells you to love, and the verb is about what you do: give yourself up for her good. Feelings very often follow actions rather than lead them. So begin doing what love does: the kindness you stopped bothering with, the attention, the apology, the evening given to her. Pray for her daily by name, and ask God to restore what has cooled. Look honestly at what may be draining your affection: resentment never dealt with, exhaustion, or attention given elsewhere, a screen included. Many couples who once felt nothing have found warmth return after a season of patient, deliberate love. And if you cannot find a way forward, ask for help early, from your pastor or a wise counsellor, not after the walls have gone up.

verseByVerse.quote: that he might sanctify her, having cleansed her by the washing of water with the word, so that he might present the church to himself in splendor, without spot or wrinkle or any such thing, that she might be holy and without blemish.
verseByVerse.commentary:
That he might sanctify her. “Sanctify” (hagiasē): make holy, set apart for him. Christ’s love does not leave us as we are; it aims at our holiness, now in part and perfectly at the end. Having cleansed her: washed from sin’s guilt and stain. Guilt is what sin deserves before God’s judgment; the stain is what sin does to us, the dirt and the grip it leaves. Christ removes the guilt once for all when he justifies us, declaring us righteous for his sake, and he removes the stain over a lifetime as he makes us actually holy, which is sanctification (2 Corinthians 3:18; 1 Thessalonians 5:23).

By the washing of water with the word. “Washing” is a bath. A bride was bathed before her wedding, and in Ezekiel 16:8–14 God washes his bride Israel and adorns her. Early Christians also thought of baptism. “With the word”: probably the gospel promise preached and believed.

Where Christians differ: does baptism itself cleanse? Roman Catholic, Orthodox and Lutheran traditions understand verses like this to teach that baptism itself, as God’s act, washes away sin and gives new birth (baptismal regeneration). This commentary’s view: Christ is the one who cleanses, and he does it by his word, the gospel received by faith. Already you are clean because of the word that I have spoken to you (John 15:3); God cleansed the Gentiles’ hearts by faith (Acts 15:9); we have been born again through the living and abiding word of God (1 Peter 1:23). That is why Simon Magus could be baptised and still be in the gall of bitterness (Acts 8:13, 23), while the thief on the cross, who as far as we know was never baptised, went that day to paradise (Luke 23:43). Baptism is the visible sign of the cleansing (the 1689 London Baptist Confession 29.1), not its cause (1 Peter 3:21: not the removal of dirt, but the appeal of a good conscience). To collapse the two is to trust the picture instead of the gospel it pictures. Many believers in those traditions trust Christ alone and treasure baptism as his gift; the disagreement is over what the water does, not over whether Christ saves.

So that he might present the church to himself in splendour. In an ancient wedding, the bride was prepared by others and presented to the groom. Here the groom does both, and receives her to himself. He is not repairing a damaged asset out of duty. He is getting her ready because he wants her. It was for the joy that was set before him that he endured the cross (Hebrews 12:2). And this is that joy: his bride, ready at last and his for ever. If you belong to him, you are part of what he was looking forward to.

Without spot or wrinkle or any such thing. Not the same defect twice. A spot is a stain: something that landed on her from outside, the mark of what has soiled her. A wrinkle is not contamination at all; it is what comes with time, the mark of wear and years. He removes both. The promise is larger than cleaning. Everything that has stained her, and everything that has merely aged and tired her, is dealt with together: the guilt and the exhaustion (Revelation 19:7–8; 21:2, 5). That is worth hearing if what you feel about yourself is less like dirtiness and more like fatigue. He is not only washing his bride; he is making her new. And the goal, “holy and without blemish”, is the one God named before the foundation of the world (1:4): what the Father chose us for, the Son brings to completion.

For husbands. A husband cannot sanctify his wife; but his love aims the same way. Think of a wife who grew up under a critical father and struggles to believe she is truly loved by God. When she waves off a gift, he names specifically what he sees; when she doubts God’s love after a hard season, he opens Scripture with her, not to win an argument but to wash her with the word; he prays against the particular lies she has told him she believes. He is not her therapist or her pastor. He is her husband.

What it does not mean. Not that the husband is his wife’s spiritual improver, who notices her faults and holds up the standard until she rises to it. Christ does not cleanse his bride by listing her blemishes, but at his own expense. And a husband is not responsible for his wife’s sins; but he is responsible for loving her towards holiness.
verseByVerse.note: Before a wedding the bride was washed and adorned.

parallels.desc: I bathed you with water

verseByVerse.quote: In the same way husbands should love their wives as their own bodies. He who loves his wife loves himself.
verseByVerse.commentary:
As their own bodies. “In the same way” means in the way Christ loves the church, his body. Not as possessions, but as part of himself: husband and wife are one flesh (v. 31). A man does not ignore a pain in his shoulder because he is busy, or tell his own body it is being too sensitive when it signals distress. He attends to it, because it is his. Do the same for your wife. James, absorbed in a demanding season at work, has not noticed Sarah pulling back for three weeks, quieter at dinner and carrying something he has not asked about. He tells himself he will check in when the pressure eases. He would never apply that reasoning to a pain in his own chest. Her withdrawal is his signal; her heaviness is his concern.

He who loves his wife loves himself. Paul nowhere commands a man to love himself; he assumes it. You already know how to do this. A hundred times a day you notice that you are hungry, tired or sore, and you do something about it. Now give her that same attention.

Two measures, one instruction. In verse 25 the standard is Christ’s love for the church; here a man’s care for his own body. But the church is Christ’s body (1:23; 5:30). So when Christ loves the church, he is caring for his own body. The highest standard and the most everyday one turn out to be one and the same command.

verseByVerse.quote: For no one ever hated his own flesh, but nourishes and cherishes it, just as Christ does the church, because we are members of his body.
verseByVerse.commentary:
No one ever hated his own flesh. Paul is not writing to men trying to destroy their wives. He is writing to men who are simply not feeding them, and that is how most marriages actually fail: not in an atrocity, but in a slow drop in temperature. He has never raised his hand or his voice; the bills are paid. And she has been cold for four years. Nothing was done to her; something was never done for her.

Nourishes and cherishes. Neither verb is heroic. To nourish is to feed something up to full growth (6:4): twenty years of meals, no single one of which looks like love. To cherish is literally to keep warm, used of a mother bird on her nest (Deuteronomy 22:6; 1 Thessalonians 2:7). Feed her, and keep her warm.

What keeping her warm looks like. A wife is kept warm when she never has to wonder whether she is loved. She knows it, because he shows it every day in small ways. He greets her as someone he is glad to see. He asks about her day and listens to the answer. He touches her with affection when he wants nothing in return. He thanks her, and tells her what he admires in her. He keeps harsh words away from her, his own first of all. When she is tired, ill or afraid he comes nearer instead of withdrawing. None of this costs much on any one day. It is keeping it up, year after year, that makes a home warm, and it is the lack of it that leaves a wife cold beside a husband who has done nothing wrong.

Just as Christ does the church. And check the tense. Not that Christ nourished and cherished the church, but does: present and continuous. The giving up of himself is finished and will never be repeated (v. 25); the feeding and warming have not stopped for a single day since. While you read this sentence, he is doing it, through his word and at the Lord’s Supper. And that answers an ache. Paul has promised a church presented in splendour, without spot or wrinkle (v. 27), and you look at your church and yourself and see spots and creases everywhere. Has he changed his mind? No. The presentation is future; the feeding is what he is doing in the meantime, and it is present. He is not standing at the far end of the aisle with his arms folded, waiting for you to make yourself presentable. He is at the near end, feeding you.

Members of his body. The word (melē) is the ordinary word for limbs and organs: not subjects of Christ, or admirers, or only servants, but parts of him. Saul of Tarsus, as far as we know, never met Jesus of Nazareth in the flesh, and was knocked flat on the road by a voice asking, “why are you persecuting me?” (Acts 9:4). He had been arresting Christians, and the Christ of heaven called it an attack on himself. That is not sentiment; it is anatomy. Touch the hand, and the head says, me. And look at it from your own side: it is the safest thing in the letter. A body does not amputate a part for being weak; a broken arm gets more of the body’s attention than a sound one (1 Corinthians 12:22–26). For Christ to neglect you, he would have to neglect himself, and this verse has just told you no one has ever done that.

Textual note. Later manuscripts add “of his flesh and of his bones” (as in the King James Version), from Genesis 2:23. This commentary’s view: probably not original.

In everyday life. One test cannot be cheated: what happens to her face in the two seconds after you come through the door? Warmth is measured at the door. And to the wife reading this as a list of what she does not have: the wanting of warmth is not weakness; say so plainly to someone, and if there is more than coldness in your home, tell someone who can act. But you have not gone unfed. Christ has been feeding you all along.

For worship. The Lord who nourishes his church fed five thousand on a hillside, and cooked breakfast on a beach for disciples who had just failed him (John 21:9–13). He is feeding us still, and the food is himself, until the Lamb in the midst of the throne is their shepherd, and God wipes away every tear (Revelation 7:16–17).

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore a man shall leave his father and mother and hold fast to his wife, and the two shall become one flesh.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Therefore. Paul has just said we are members of Christ’s body (v. 30), and to prove it he quotes a verse about a wedding. The logic only works if Genesis 2:24 was about Christ and the church all along (v. 32). Marriage was built, in the week the world was made, as a working model of something that had not yet happened.

Genesis 2:24. The foundational text on marriage, spoken before the fall, and quoted by Jesus (Matthew 19:4–6).

Leave his father and mother. A new primary loyalty. It is not mainly about distance. A man can live four hundred miles from his mother and still be run by her: a decision made together on Tuesday quietly reopened on the phone on Wednesday; a man who defends his wife to nobody and explains her to everybody. And parents can refuse to release as firmly as sons refuse to leave.

Hold fast. Literally to be glued (proskollaō). Glue two boards properly and leave them overnight, then try to separate them. They do not come apart at the join; the join is now the strongest part. The wood tears, and each board comes away carrying fibre from the other. That explains what a contractual view of marriage never can: why the ending of a marriage does not feel like the ending of an agreement. To anyone who has been through divorce or been left, this is not another sentence passed on you. It explains the shape of the wound. You were not weak when it went on hurting long after everyone assumed you should have recovered. Something God joins had been pulled apart, and it tore. Where the fault was yours, there is complete forgiveness in Christ; where it was done to you, God himself calls such tearing apart violence (Malachi 2:16). Neither his love for you nor his use of you is reduced by one degree.

The two shall become one flesh. A union of the whole life: two bodies, two lives shared, a promise made, and no one else let in. Even union with a prostitute makes one flesh (1 Corinthians 6:16), and it does damage because the body says, “I am wholly yours”, when nothing else in the life says so. Marriage is a bond witnessed by God (Malachi 2:14), not dissolved by fading feeling. Yet the two do not cease to be two; a marriage in which one swallows the other distorts the union.

Fulfilled before it was obeyed. Once Paul has told us who it is about, every clause has a second face. “A man shall leave his father”: and the Son of God did, not ceasing to be one with the Father, but leaving the glory he had before the world existed: “I came from the Father and have come into the world” (John 16:28; 17:5). “And hold fast to his wife”: he has held fast to a bride who has let go of him a thousand times, and never once loosened his grip. “And the two shall become one flesh”: he took flesh to do it. That is why Christian marriage is not finally an achievement to be measured. It is a picture, and the original is holding even in the weeks when the copy is not.

May a marriage ever be ended? God designed it for life: what therefore God has joined together, let not man separate (Matthew 19:6). But Jesus himself allows divorce for sexual immorality (Matthew 19:9), and Paul allows it when an unbelieving spouse deserts (1 Corinthians 7:15). This commentary’s view: in cases of adultery or desertion the innocent party is free to divorce and remarry (Westminster Confession 24.5–6), though reconciliation is better wherever it is possible. Persistent, serious abuse can amount to such desertion, and the elders help judge each case; but anyone in danger should seek safety at once, and abuse is never to be tolerated or covered.

I divorced and remarried on grounds that were not biblical. Should I now leave my present marriage? No. The sin lay in how the earlier marriage was ended, and that sin is to be confessed, and is fully forgiven in Christ (1 John 1:9). But your present marriage is a real marriage, made with vows before God, and breaking it would add a second wrong to the first, not undo it. The law of Moses even forbade a divorced woman who had married again from returning to her first husband (Deuteronomy 24:1–4). So repent honestly of what was wrong, seek to make peace where you can, perhaps with a former spouse or with children who were hurt, and then give yourself wholeheartedly to the marriage you are in. Take any particular questions to your elders. God’s grace was never only for people whose histories are tidy; it was sent for the rest of us.

Where Christians differ: the definition of marriage. Some churches now affirm same-sex marriage. This commentary’s view: the historic Christian view, held with compassion: Scripture defines marriage as the union of one man and one woman, and that pattern is part of its meaning, since it pictures Christ and his church. Jesus grounded marriage in God’s making them male and female (Matthew 19:4–5), and the picture needs two who are different joined as one, as the Bridegroom and his bride are distinct. Those who differ often do so out of love for gay friends and family, and Christians who hold the historic view must hold it with that same love, honouring every person as made in God’s image.

For worship. In Eden the LORD God himself brought the woman to the man (Genesis 2:22). The Father has been doing the same for his Son ever since: “All that the Father gives me will come to me” (John 6:37). For the divorced, the deserted and the never-married, here is a Husband who will never tear himself away.

parallels.desc: a man shall leave his father and mother and hold fast to his wife

verseByVerse.quote: This mystery is profound, and I am saying that it refers to Christ and the church.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Mystery. Not a puzzle, but something hidden and now made known (3:3–5). In a city where secret religions sold their secrets to the few who joined, Paul’s mystery is read aloud to a room of ordinary people, and its point is that outsiders have been let in.

It refers to Christ and the church. Paul is saying something remarkable. God did not first invent marriage and then find it a useful illustration. He designed marriage from creation to point to the greater marriage. And that reframes the whole Bible. He wedded himself to Israel: “your Maker is your husband” (Isaiah 54:5). When she was unfaithful he grieved as a wounded husband, and he showed how he would win her back by telling the prophet Hosea to take back his own unfaithful wife (Hosea 2:19–20; 3:1). Scripture opens with a wedding in a garden (Genesis 2:24) and closes with a wedding at the end of history, the marriage supper of the Lamb (Revelation 19:7–9). Everything between is, in one sense, the long story of a Bridegroom coming for his bride. God made man and woman for one flesh so that the world would never be without a living picture of the love that would one day bring the Son of God down from heaven to win us.

Where Christians differ: a sacrament? The Latin Vulgate translated “mystery” as sacramentum, one ground on which the Roman Catholic Church counts marriage among seven sacraments. The instinct is not contemptible: it wants to say marriage is holy, and it is. The Reformers held that marriage is a holy creation ordinance for all people, not a sacrament of grace for the church. This commentary’s view: marriage is honourable and holy, a living picture of the gospel, but not a sacrament, that is, not one of the signs Christ gave his church, as baptism and the Lord’s Supper are. It points to the gospel; it does not hand out its grace.

For the single. After twelve verses on marriage, what of the reader who has no marriage? The man of forty who assumed he would be married by now; the widow; the woman whose husband left. The Lord Jesus never married, and Paul, writing this sentence, was unmarried (1 Corinthians 7:7–8). The two people in the New Testament who understood the mystery of marriage most deeply had, as far as we know, no experience of it, and neither thought himself impoverished. The most complete human life ever lived was a single one. And if marriage is the sign, the union of Christ and his church is the reality, and the single Christian already has the reality in full: the same Bridegroom, the same love, on exactly the same terms. “In the resurrection they neither marry nor are given in marriage” (Matthew 22:30), not because something good is taken away, but because no one needs the signpost once they have reached the place. Every marriage on earth ends, by its own vows, at a graveside; the marriage it pointed to never does. And God said it first to the very people the ancient world pitied most. To the eunuch, who could never marry or have children, he says: “I will give in my house and within my walls a monument and a name better than sons and daughters” (Isaiah 56:3–5). “Better than sons and daughters”: a promise of more, made to the one with least.

What it does not mean. If every faithful marriage pictures the gospel, what does a bad marriage say about the gospel? Nothing at all. A sign knocked flat in a ditch does not move the city it pointed to.
verseByVerse.note: A “mystery” is something once hidden and now revealed by God.

parallels.desc: your Maker is your husband

verseByVerse.quote: However, let each one of you love his wife as himself, and let the wife see that she respects her husband.
verseByVerse.commentary:
However. After the great mystery, Paul comes back down, in one word, to a husband and a wife who have to get through Tuesday.

Each one of you. Personal responsibility. Paul does not address the couple; he addresses two individuals, separately, and gives each one command, and neither command has a condition attached. He does not write, “love your wife once she respects you”, or “respect your husband once he loves you like Christ”. Yet that is the deadlock most struggling marriages sit in. She is waiting for him to love her, and is not wrong to want it; he is waiting for her to respect him, and is not wrong either. Both are willing to move, once the other has. They can hold that position for years. Paul cuts through it by speaking to each one. Your half of this verse cannot wait for the other half, and no one can keep it with you or for you. You can only go first.

He moved first. That is exactly what Christ did. He did not wait for his bride to honour him before he loved her; while she was still turned away, he came and gave himself, and her love for him began there. “We love because he first loved us” (1 John 4:19). So the spouse who goes first is not being naive, or rewarding bad behaviour; he or she is copying the Bridegroom. And it can be done without being sure of the response, because the one who moved first for us has already given us the love that matters most, and no one at the dinner table can take it away.

Love his wife as himself. For a man of few emotional words it means learning to ask and stay: not “are you okay?” but “tell me how you are really doing”, and then sitting with the answer instead of fixing it.

And let the wife see that she respects her husband. Literally “fears”: reverent honour, in how she speaks about him as well as to him. In practice: keeping the correction for a private moment; letting him make a decision she thinks slightly wrong, when the stakes are low, and not reopening it; saying something genuinely admiring of him where he can hear it.

What it does not mean. Not terror or blind agreement, and not absorbing harm; the limits of v. 22 stand. What it governs is chiefly manner. The hardest sentence in a marriage can be said with honour or with contempt, in nearly the same words. A wife married to a man who has given her little to admire is not asked to manufacture admiration. She is asked to refuse contempt, which is very often the last thing standing between a marriage and its end. And wives need respect and husbands need love too. Ask your spouse which they are short of, and believe the answer.

In everyday life. A husband who can quote “let the wife see that she respects her husband” and could not say, without looking, what he was told in the same breath is not studying Scripture; he is arming himself. His half is the one addressed to him, and it is the only one he was given to keep.

5.overview:
Paul goes on describing the new life of God’s people, and his word for it is “walk”. Loved children walk in love, as Christ loved them and gave himself up for them. They live as light in the Lord, refusing the works of darkness and bringing them into the open. They walk wisely, and instead of being ruled by wine they are filled with the Spirit, which shows in singing, thanksgiving and a humble readiness to put others first out of reverence for Christ.

That humility then takes shape in the home (5:22–6:9). In marriage, the wife’s glad trust in her husband and the husband’s self-giving love for his wife are both modelled on Christ and the church, and Paul shows that marriage was designed from the beginning to picture that greater union.

6.title: Household Duties and the Armour of God
6.text: <sup>1</sup>Children, obey your parents in the Lord, for this is right. <sup>2</sup>“Honor your father and mother” (this is the first commandment with a promise), <sup>3</sup>“that it may go well with you and that you may live long in the land.” <sup>4</sup>Fathers, do not provoke your children to anger, but bring them up in the discipline and instruction of the Lord. <sup>5</sup>Bondservants, obey your earthly masters with fear and trembling, with a sincere heart, as you would Christ, <sup>6</sup>not by the way of eye-service, as people-pleasers, but as bondservants of Christ, doing the will of God from the heart, <sup>7</sup>rendering service with a good will as to the Lord and not to man, <sup>8</sup>knowing that whatever good anyone does, this he will receive back from the Lord, whether he is a bondservant or is free. <sup>9</sup>Masters, do the same to them, and stop your threatening, knowing that he who is both their Master and yours is in heaven, and that there is no partiality with him. <sup>10</sup>Finally, be strong in the Lord and in the strength of his might. <sup>11</sup>Put on the whole armor of God, that you may be able to stand against the schemes of the devil. <sup>12</sup>For we do not wrestle against flesh and blood, but against the rulers, against the authorities, against the cosmic powers over this present darkness, against the spiritual forces of evil in the heavenly places. <sup>13</sup>Therefore take up the whole armor of God, that you may be able to withstand in the evil day, and having done all, to stand firm. <sup>14</sup>Stand therefore, having fastened on the belt of truth, and having put on the breastplate of righteousness, <sup>15</sup>and, as shoes for your feet, having put on the readiness given by the gospel of peace. <sup>16</sup>In all circumstances take up the shield of faith, with which you can extinguish all the flaming darts of the evil one; <sup>17</sup>and take the helmet of salvation, and the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God, <sup>18</sup>praying at all times in the Spirit, with all prayer and supplication. To that end, keep alert with all perseverance, making supplication for all the saints, <sup>19</sup>and also for me, that words may be given to me in opening my mouth boldly to proclaim the mystery of the gospel, <sup>20</sup>for which I am an ambassador in chains, that I may declare it boldly, as I ought to speak. <sup>21</sup>So that you also may know how I am and what I am doing, Tychicus the beloved brother and faithful minister in the Lord will tell you everything. <sup>22</sup>I have sent him to you for this very purpose, that you may know how we are, and that he may encourage your hearts. <sup>23</sup>Peace be to the brothers, and love with faith, from God the Father and the Lord Jesus Christ. <sup>24</sup>Grace be with all who love our Lord Jesus Christ with love incorruptible.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul addresses children and parents, then slaves and masters, speaking first to the weaker party in each pair and placing everyone in the home under the same Lord.
verseByVerse.theology:
Authority, service and the lordship of Christ

These household instructions are sometimes read as Paul simply accepting the social order of Rome. That misses what he does with it. Each relationship is changed from within: both parties have obligations, and both answer to a Lord who stands above every human order.

Paul does not tell slaves that their situation is just. He tells them that no situation, however unjust, is beyond the reach of Christ, and that faithful work done for him will be rewarded by him, whatever the human master gave or withheld (v. 8).

The word to masters (v. 9) is just as searching: the master has a Master, and before the impartial God distinctions of rank count for nothing. Believed and applied, that truth made slavery a contradiction among Christians, though it took far too long for many to see it.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Under Roman law the father of the household held great legal power over his wife, children and slaves. Paul addresses children and slaves directly, as people who can answer to God for themselves, and he lays duties on fathers and masters towards the weak that Roman law did not require.

Now: A Christian home where authority is used in love, where children are both corrected and encouraged, and where Christ is spoken of and his word read, quietly shows the world around it a different way to live.

verseByVerse.quote: Children, obey your parents in the Lord, for this is right.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Meaning first. Ephesians 6 completes the household instructions and then lifts our eyes to the spiritual battle behind all of life. Children and parents, slaves and masters, all stand under one Lord (vv. 1–9). Believers stand against the devil, not people, in the Lord’s strength and the whole armour of God, all worn in watchful prayer (vv. 10–20). The letter closes with news through Tychicus and a blessing of grace (vv. 21–24).

Children. Picture the letter read aloud in a crowded room in Ephesus, the children at the edge of it, half listening. Then the reader says: “Children.” Heads come up. In a world where the moral writers spoke about children rather than to them, an apostle speaks to them directly. He does not say, “Fathers, make your children obey.” He speaks to the child, gives the child a reason, and expects the child to answer for himself, as a member of the church who can hear Christ and respond. The word covers children still living under their parents’ authority, not adults.

Obey. Hypakouō: literally to listen under, to listen and do what is said. This is a different word from the one used for wives, who were told to arrange themselves under (hypotassō). A wife is not a child, and a husband must not take this verse, written to children, and apply it to his wife. A child is told to obey because he does not yet know enough to run his own life. That will change as he grows up, and so will the command. And it is parents, both father and mother: in the Roman world the father held legal power, but Paul gives the mother equal standing as one to be obeyed. For how this fits the wider pattern of leading and following in every sphere, see on Ephesians 5:21.

In the Lord. Two things, put simply. First, the reason: a Christian child obeys his parents as part of following Jesus, so that obeying his mother and father is a way of obeying Christ (Colossians 3:20 says this pleases the Lord). Second, the limit: he obeys as a Christian, so he can never be required to obey a parent against Christ. Picture a ten-year-old told to tidy her room, be home by six, or stop hitting her brother: she obeys, and in doing it she is obeying the Lord. If a parent told her to lie to a teacher or to steal, “in the Lord” says no. Everyday life is almost always the first kind; the second is rare, but real.

For this is right. Paul gives three reasons in three verses, each of a different kind. It is right (dikaion): it fits the way God made the world, so that even someone who had never seen the commandment would sense it (v. 1). It is commanded, written into the law at Sinai (v. 2). And it is blessed: it carries a promise (v. 3). So the child’s own conscience says it, God’s word says it, and the good that follows confirms it. Paul never says: “Obey because your parents can shout louder.”

The child who obeyed. There has been exactly one child in history who had every right to disregard his parents. He had made them. At twelve he astonished the teachers in the temple, and Luke ends that story: “he went down with them and came to Nazareth and was submissive to them” (Luke 2:51). Then eighteen years of silence. The Son of God spent most of two decades doing what he was told in a small town by a carpenter and his wife. Long before the hard obedience of the cross (Hebrews 5:8), he gave the ordinary obedience of a boy in a carpenter’s house. A child who obeys is not doing something beneath the dignity of heaven. He is doing what the Lord of heaven did first, for longer, with far less reason to.

What it does not mean. Not obedience in sin. “In the Lord” rules out obeying a parent who commands what God forbids; then “we must obey God rather than men” (Acts 5:29). Nor does it require that children submit to abuse. A parent’s authority is borrowed, never absolute; no parent has the right to injure a child. If you are a young person reading this in a house where you are being hurt, frightened, or asked to keep a secret about what an adult does to you, this verse is not telling you to submit to it. Tell someone, a teacher, a pastor, another adult you trust, and keep telling until somebody acts. That is not disobedience; it is obedience to the Lord in whose name the command was given. And any adult who quotes this verse to keep a child quiet has turned Christ’s words against the very person Christ stopped a letter to address. Nor does it mean that grown children who have left home must obey their parents for life: marriage creates a new household (Genesis 2:24; 5:31). But honour never ends (v. 2).

What if my parents are not Christians and will not let me go to church? Obey them in everything you lawfully can, and honour them even when you disagree; God does not ask you to deceive them or sneak out. Being kept from church is hard, but it is not the same as being commanded to sin. No parent can stop you praying, reading your Bible or trusting Christ, and that is where your faith lives. Ask respectfully whether you may go, or meet a Christian friend, or have the pastor call; a parent who sees a child growing kinder, more honest and more helpful often softens over time. Pray for them by name. Remember that this lasts only while you live under their roof. And if they ever command you to deny Christ or to do what God forbids, then you must obey God rather than men (Acts 5:29), respectfully and without contempt.

For worship. The Lord in whose name this command is given delighted to do his Father’s will. He did it as a boy in a carpenter’s house. He did it in Gethsemane on the night before he died, when he prayed, not my will but yours. His obedience was never grudging. And God now counts that perfect obedience as belonging to everyone who trusts him: to every child who has sulked and slammed a door, and to every parent who has failed a child. The same Lord once took children in his arms and blessed them (Mark 10:16), and he has not changed.

verseByVerse.quote: Honor your father and mother (this is the first commandment with a promise), that it may go well with you and that you may live long in the land.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Honour. More than obedience. To honour (timaō) is to treat as weighty, to respect and value. Obedience applies to children at home; honour applies for life. For adults it means speaking of parents with respect, not retelling their failures as entertainment even when every word is true; courtesy as they grow slower and more repetitive; listening to their wisdom (Proverbs 23:22); and practical care when they grow old (1 Timothy 5:4, 8). Jesus condemned religious leaders who used a loophole called Corban, declaring their money dedicated to God, to avoid supporting their parents: “making void the word of God by your tradition” (Mark 7:9–13). That is what he thought the commandment required: money, provision, the unglamorous cost of caring for people who can no longer care for themselves.

This is the first commandment with a promise. Paul is quoting the fifth commandment (Exodus 20:12; Deuteronomy 5:16), and he quotes it to children who were not Jews. In Christ the law no longer stands as a wall dividing Jew from Gentile (2:14–15), but God’s moral commands still show every Christian how to live. A Christian is not saved by keeping commandments, but a command like this one still shows him what love for his neighbour looks like (Romans 13:8–10). Why “first”? The second commandment already speaks of God’s steadfast love to thousands (Exodus 20:6), but that describes what God is like, added to a warning. This is the first command that says: do this, and here is what I promise you. God has singled it out and hung a promise on it.

That it may go well with you and that you may live long in the land. In Exodus the promise ran: “in the land that the LORD your God is giving you”, a promise about Canaan. Paul quotes it and quietly drops the last clause. A promise about one territory becomes a promise about life anywhere, offered to Greek children in Asia Minor with no stake in Canaan at all. He has done this all through the letter: the good things God promised to Israel are now held out to people of every nation.

What it does not mean. Not a guarantee that every obedient child will live long, or that early death proves disobedience. Godly children die young. If you have buried a child who loved and honoured you, this verse is no verdict on that child, and no word against your grief. Like the Proverbs, it states how God normally works, not a mechanical rule: a person who learns to honour rightful authority and receive correction generally lives a longer, less damaged life, and a society where the generations honour one another holds together. The promise finds its final fulfilment in eternal life. Nor does honouring parents mean pretending their faults do not exist, or placing them above a spouse.

And if my parents did not deserve it? Paul attaches no clause about sufficiently good parents, and many readers have a father who was frightening, a mother who was cruel, or a parent who simply left. They read this verse with dread, hearing it demand that they pretend the childhood was something it was not. It demands nothing of the kind. Honour is not approval, and it is not pretending. You can honour a person and tell the truth about them; the Bible records the failures of its own heroes without ceasing to treat them with dignity. Honour is compatible with a boundary: the adult child who limits contact with a destructive parent, calmly and without contempt, for the sake of his own household, has not broken this commandment. It is compatible with grief, and with the long, unfinished work of forgiving. What it rules out is contempt: the sneer, the public mockery, the settled determination to make them pay. At its core the duty is small, and survives almost any history: to refuse to treat the people who gave you life as though they were nothing.

The Son at the cross. Watch Jesus keep this commandment. He is on the cross, bearing the sin of the world, and he sees his mother standing there. With what breath he has, he arranges her care: “Woman, behold, your son!” “Behold, your mother!” And “from that hour the disciple took her to his own home” (John 19:26–27). He was in the act of redeeming the world, and he stopped to make sure his mother would have somewhere to live. And the Father he obeyed is the one “from whom every family in heaven and on earth is named” (3:15); to those whose earthly parents failed them, he is the parent who never leaves (Psalm 27:10).

In everyday life. Notice how you speak about your parents when they are not there: to your spouse, a friend, your children. Our real assessment lives in the stories we choose to repeat, and we are training the next generation in exactly how they will one day speak about us.

verseByVerse.quote: Fathers, do not provoke your children to anger, but bring them up in the discipline and instruction of the Lord.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Fathers. Paul has just spoken to children; the natural counterpart would be “parents”. He says “fathers”, the one who held the power. In Roman law the father (paterfamilias) could decide whether a newborn lived or was abandoned to die, sell his children into slavery, or punish them severely even when grown. Into that world Paul says: limit your power by love. The principle applies to mothers too, but fathers bear particular responsibility for the spiritual leadership of the home. And the prohibition comes first: in a relationship that unequal, the damage a man can do without meaning to is the first problem to deal with.

Do not provoke your children to anger. The tense describes a settled pattern, not a bad afternoon. Every father loses his temper; Paul forbids the atmosphere. Colossians names the outcome: “lest they become discouraged” (Colossians 3:21), lose heart, have the wind go out of them. That is the injury: not an angry child, but a child who has quietly stopped trying, because he has worked out that nothing he does will be enough. And almost none of the provocations is a sin a man would confess. Criticism that only notices what is missing. Expectations that keep moving. Comparison with a sibling. Promises casually broken, because a child’s disappointment is easy to absorb. Sarcasm, which a child cannot answer and does not forget. Inconsistency, punishing one day what was ignored the next. Rules without reasons. Hypocrisy, demanding what he does not do. Absence: the father in the house and behind a screen. And the commonest of all: a man warm when things go well and cold when they do not, so that a child grows up managing his father’s mood and learns, without being told, that love is earned by performance.

Why it matters so much. A child’s first picture of authority is a human one, at a kitchen table; his first working model of a father is the man sitting there. Nobody easily thinks his way out of that model. The father who is arbitrary teaches his children that God is arbitrary; the father who is never satisfied teaches them that God is never satisfied, and they may spend thirty years trying to unlearn it. And a father should ask what he is really after: a child who knows the Lord, or a child who makes him look good. A child made into his father’s trophy, or his second chance at success, feels the weight of it long before he can name it.

But bring them up. The word (ektrephō) means to nourish, to feed up to full growth, the verb used of a husband nourishing his own body (5:29): warmth and tender care, as a gardener tends a plant.

In the discipline. Paideia: training, including correction, the word used of God disciplining his children in love (Hebrews 12:5–11): setting boundaries, correcting wrong, giving consequences, and praising what is right. The father who never corrects anything fails this verse as surely as the one who crushes. The two errors look opposite and share a root: both are easier than the patient, costly work of shaping a person who will one day not be under your authority at all. Beside discipline stands instruction (nouthesia): literally putting in mind, teaching by word. Children need not only rules but reasons.

Of the Lord. This is the goal: not only well-behaved children, but children who know the Lord. The father is not forming the child in his own image, or into the career he wishes he had had. The child belongs to God, and the father is bringing him up for God. With young children, it looks like presence, affection, calm and consistent boundaries, and God woven into ordinary talk (Deuteronomy 6:6–7). With older children, genuine interest in their world (the father who does not know his child’s best friend has not yet earned the right to be heard), and correction that is private and aimed at character. With teenagers, fewer orders and more honest conversation, and above all letting them see a real father’s walk with God: praying, confessing sin, coming back to Christ after failure. Children pick up more from what they see than from what they are told.

The Lord who trained twelve. “The discipline and instruction of the Lord” has a living pattern, because the Lord himself spent some three years bringing up a band of slow, quarrelsome men. He corrected plainly: “Get behind me, Satan” (Matthew 16:23). He explained again what they had failed to grasp (Mark 8:17–21). He never withdrew his warmth when they failed: “having loved his own … he loved them to the end” (John 13:1). And when they argued about who was greatest, he set a child in the middle of them and taught them (Mark 9:36). If you want to see what firm correction without lost patience looks like, look at him.

What if there is no Christian father in the home? Then God has not left your children without a Father, nor you without help. Timothy was raised in the faith by his mother Eunice and his grandmother Lois, while his father seems to have been an unbelieving Greek (Acts 16:1; 2 Timothy 1:5; 3:15), and he became one of Paul’s most trusted men. A single mother, or a believing mother whose husband is indifferent, can do everything this verse describes: nurture, correct, teach and pray. God calls himself the father of the fatherless and the protector of widows (Psalm 68:5). And the church has its part: godly men in the congregation can befriend, include and show faithfulness to children who have no believing father at home. If you are carrying this alone, ask for that help. It is not a failure; it is the family of God doing its work.

Where Christians differ: physical discipline? Proverbs says, whoever spares the rod hates his son (Proverbs 13:24), and many Christians understand that to allow measured physical correction of young children, given calmly, never in anger, never to injure, and always with love and explanation. Others take the rod as a figure for discipline in general, and some believe physical discipline is unwise in every case. This commentary’s view: whatever a parent decides, this verse rules out anything that provokes, humiliates or harms a child. Discipline that crushes a child’s spirit (Colossians 3:21) is not the Lord’s discipline, and abuse must never hide behind Scripture.

What it does not mean. “Of the Lord” does not mean that fathers can make their children Christians: only God gives new life (2:1–5). Fathers sow and water; God gives growth. And the verse does not mean children’s faith or failures are entirely the parents’ fault: children are responsible persons too (Ezekiel 18:20).

Our children have turned away from the faith. Did we fail them? Perhaps in some ways, as every parent does, but their unbelief does not prove it. God himself, the only perfect Father, grieved over children he had reared who rebelled against him (Isaiah 1:2). Faith cannot be handed down; new birth is God’s work, not the parents’ (John 1:13). If you see real failures, confess them to God, and where it would help, apologise to your adult child plainly. Then keep the door open: love them without nagging, keep a place for them at the table, take an interest in their lives, and do not turn every visit into a sermon. Let them see a parent who still walks with Christ and is kind. Above all, keep praying, for years if need be. Many prodigals have come home in their thirties and forties, and the father in the parable was watching the road (Luke 15:20).

In everyday life. Do not ask yourself whether you provoke your children. Ask one of them: “Is there something I do that makes you feel you can never quite get it right?” Then say nothing until they have finished, and do not explain. And to the father whose children are grown, who recognised himself in that list: it is not too late to say so. An apology to an adult child, specific, without excuses, without a single “but you also”, is one of the most powerful things in the world. And God has been a Father to your children in ways you never managed, and he is able to repair what you broke.

For worship. At the Jordan, before Jesus had preached a sermon or healed anyone, a voice came from heaven: “This is my beloved Son, with whom I am well pleased” (Matthew 3:17). The approval came first, before there was any record to earn it. That is the Father who has adopted us in the Beloved, his dear Son (1:5–6). He is pleased with his children because of what his Son has done, not because of what they have done. He disciplines us for our good (Hebrews 12:10), never in a temper, and he does not tire of his children.

verseByVerse.quote: Bondservants, obey your earthly masters with fear and trembling, with a sincere heart, as you would Christ,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Bondservants. Douloi: slaves. Perhaps a third of the people of a city like Ephesus were slaves, and many of the first Christians were slaves (1 Corinthians 7:21), while some were masters. Roman slavery was not based on race: people became slaves through war, debt, crime or birth. Some were teachers, doctors or managers; others laboured in mines and fields in terrible conditions. But a slave was legally property, and it was still bondage and an assault on human dignity.

Speaking to the property. The codes of the period spoke to the owner about managing his property. Paul speaks to the property, as a person with a conscience, a Lord, and choices to make about his work. A man with no legal standing is told that his ordinary labour is offered to Jesus Christ and will be assessed by him.

Obey your earthly masters. Literally masters according to the flesh: their human masters. The phrase hints at a contrast: they have another Master in heaven (v. 9). The earthly master’s authority is real but limited. On authority and submission at work and in every sphere, see on Ephesians 5:21.

With fear and trembling. Not cringing terror of the master. Paul uses the same phrase of the Christian life itself: “work out your own salvation with fear and trembling, for it is God who works in you” (Philippians 2:12–13). It is the seriousness of someone who knows God is watching. The trembling has been redirected upward, over the master’s head.

With a sincere heart. “Sincere” (haplotēs) means single, undivided: without hidden motives, without one face for the master and another behind his back. For a slave, whose whole existence invited a double life, that was a startling thing to ask and a great gift: you may be owned, but you need not be divided.

As you would Christ: “do it for my sake”. A friend going abroad asks you to look after his elderly father: “Do it for me.” You really do help the father, but you do it for your friend (see on 5:22). So here. The slave is not told that his master deserves this, and no one pretends the master is Jesus. He is told to look past the master to Christ, who stands behind every task and receives it as done for him. That changes the motive: not fear of the whip or hope of the master’s favour, but love for the Lord who sees everything. And it sets the limit. What is done for Christ’s sake can never include what Christ forbids: lying or stealing for the master, joining in his sins, or submitting to his abuse. In practice it meant doing the work well, honestly and without sulking, whether anyone checked or not. See also As to the Lord in the Theological Dictionary.

A Lord who took the slave’s name. The word for slave here is doulos, and it is the word Paul uses for what the Son of God did: though he was in the form of God, he emptied himself, taking the form of a servant (doulos), and became obedient to the point of death, even death on a cross (Philippians 2:6–8). So when a slave in Ephesus heard this read aloud and was told to serve as to Christ, he was hearing from a Lord who had once taken the slave’s own place and name. That Lord has since been raised and seated in heaven. And chapter 2 says that everyone who belongs to him, this slave included, has been raised and seated there with him (2:6): the slave already shares his Lord’s honour.

Where Christians differ: does the Bible endorse slavery? In the nineteenth century, slave-owners in the American South quoted texts like this to defend slavery. Paul does not endorse the institution. He regulates it while undermining it from within. He lists slave-traders, “enslavers”, among the lawless (1 Timothy 1:10), which alone condemns the Atlantic slave trade at its root; he urges slaves to gain their freedom if they can (1 Corinthians 7:21); he tells masters that they and their slaves have the same Master who shows no favouritism (v. 9); and he asks Philemon to receive his runaway slave Onesimus no longer as a slave but as a beloved brother (Philemon 16). In the church, slave and free were equals at the Lord’s Table (Galatians 3:28). It is honest to admit the difficulty: Paul nowhere commands Christian masters to free their slaves, and for centuries some Christians found that silence convenient. Why not call for revolt? A slave revolt in the first century would have been drowned in blood, as the thousands crucified after Spartacus showed, and would have branded the young church as sedition. This commentary’s view: the gospel undermined slavery from within, and Christians such as William Wilberforce rightly led its abolition. Modern slavery and human trafficking are evils Christians must oppose.

Today. An employee is not owned, and the New Testament is emphatic about the wickedness of withholding wages. But the principle reaches everyone who works under conditions they did not choose and cannot change: the manager who will never be fair, the job taken because the mortgage exists. Paul’s answer is neither resignation nor resentment. It is a change of employer at the level that matters: you still do the job your manager gives you, but you are working first for Christ, who sees what the manager misses and will repay what the manager never will (Colossians 3:23–24).
verseByVerse.note: Slavery was part of everyday life in the Roman world; many early believers were slaves or owned slaves.

verseByVerse.quote: not by the way of eye-service, as people-pleasers, but as bondservants of Christ, doing the will of God from the heart, rendering service with a good will as to the Lord and not to man,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Not by the way of eye-service. Ophthalmodoulia, a word found in no surviving Greek writing before Paul: eye-slavery, work that exists only while it is being looked at. It is not the same as laziness; eye-service can be very energetic. It is a matter of where the effort is aimed: the report polished because the right person will read it, the visible task done first. It produces a person who is always adjusting to an audience, which is exhausting in a way hard work never is. Its companion is the people-pleaser (anthrōpareskos): he works to look good, not to be good.

But as bondservants of Christ. The deepest identity of a Christian slave was not “slave of a master” but “slave of Christ” (Paul uses the same title of himself, Romans 1:1). Every Christian, slave or free, belongs to Christ.

Doing the will of God from the heart. Look at who this is said to and what he does all day: cleaning, carrying, cooking, minding someone else’s children. Nothing religious about any of it. And Paul says that when he does it well, he is doing the will of God. That removes a division many of us carry without examining: sacred activities, and then everything else, which is at best neutral. We are created for good works (2:10), and here is what a good work looks like on a Tuesday: a floor properly swept by a man nobody is watching. Luther taught that the farmer in his field and the woman at her household tasks please God as truly as the priest at the altar. The nurse on the night shift, the mother whose day’s work will be undone by bedtime, the man who drives a van: none is doing something less spiritual than the one leading the service on Sunday. So think of the part of your work no one senior will ever inspect, and do today’s dullest task as if he had asked you to do it, because he has.

I delight to do your will. Only one person has ever done the will of God from the heart without a divided moment. Hebrews hears Christ speaking Psalm 40 as he comes into the world: “Behold, I have come to do your will, O God” (Hebrews 10:7). His food was to do the will of him who sent him (John 4:34), at the carpenter’s bench as much as at the cross. And “by that will we have been sanctified”, that is, made clean and set apart for God, “through the offering of the body of Jesus Christ once for all” (Hebrews 10:10). The slave sweeping an unwatched floor from the heart walks in the footsteps of the Servant whose obedience saved him.

Rendering service with a good will. Not grudgingly, but wanting the person you serve to do well: a great thing to ask of a slave about the man who owns him, or of an employee about a manager who took credit for her work. Goodwill towards an undeserving employer is not manufactured by trying to like him. It becomes possible when you are really working for Christ, so that the manager is no longer the one who has to repay you.

What it does not mean. Not that Christians must accept unjust treatment without protest, stay in an exploitative job, or never speak up for fair conditions. Paul told slaves to take freedom if they could (1 Corinthians 7:21); James condemns employers who withhold wages (James 5:4); and Paul himself used his Roman rights (Acts 16:37; 22:25). Working heartily for the Lord and standing up for yourself are not in competition. What is forbidden is the divided heart: turning up for the hours while holding back honest effort.

Does this mean I should not care what my boss thinks of me? No. It is right to want your employer to be pleased with your work, and good to be glad when it is noticed; Joseph and Daniel both won the trust of those over them (Genesis 39:4; Daniel 6:3). The fault Paul names is letting human approval become your master: working well only when it will be seen, bending your conscience to the mood of the office, or being flattened for a week by one cool remark. The cure is not to stop caring but to change whose opinion weighs most. When the work is done for Christ, a manager’s praise becomes a pleasant extra instead of oxygen, and criticism becomes useful information instead of a verdict on your worth. You can receive both calmly, because you already know whose “well done” matters most (Matthew 25:21).

verseByVerse.quote: knowing that whatever good anyone does, this he will receive back from the Lord, whether he is a bondservant or is free.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Knowing. Not hoping that somehow it will come right. The sentence rests on something known, as certain on the worst Thursday of your working life as on the best. Feelings are not asked to carry this.

Whatever good anyone does.
