No threshold, no category excluded: the meal cooked for a family who did not think to say thank you, the shift quietly covered, the expense claim filled in honestly, patience held with the same difficult relative for the ninth year running. Jesus set the bar at exactly this height: a cup of cold water given to a disciple, and the giver will by no means lose his reward (Matthew 10:42). And Hebrews makes it a matter of God’s character: “God is not unjust so as to overlook your work” (Hebrews 6:10).

This he will receive back from the Lord. The verb (komizō) means to receive back what is yours, to collect what was deposited, the word Paul uses of the judgment seat (2 Corinthians 5:10). A slave’s work did not bear his name: whatever he built or mended was credited to the man who owned him. Paul tells him that a complete and accurate record exists, kept by the only one who was actually watching, and that it will be read back to him in person. It is this world’s record, the one everyone can see, that has the names wrong.

Whether he is a bondservant or is free. A slave’s faithful work will be rewarded as fully as a free person’s, each good thing entered under the name of the one who actually did it.

What it does not mean. Not that we earn salvation by good works: salvation is by grace through faith (2:8–9). What is promised is not wages earned but reward given: the Father’s pleasure in what his own Spirit produced in you (2:10). Augustine said that when God crowns our merits, he crowns his own gifts. Salvation is not what is handed back on that day; salvation is why you are standing there at all. Nor are the rewards necessarily material, or in this life. Most of it will not be settled here. But nothing is pending for ever. The wait is real; the loss is not.

The Servant who seemed to labour in vain. This promise holds because it has already been kept once, for Christ. In Isaiah, the Lord’s Servant, who is Christ, says: I have laboured in vain; I have spent my strength for nothing; yet surely my right is with the LORD, and my recompense with my God (Isaiah 49:4). From outside, his life looked like that: a short ministry, his friends scattered, his body in another man’s tomb. Then God highly exalted him (Philippians 2:9). The Lord who will hand back your hidden work had his own handed back to him on the third day.

Is it not selfish to serve God for a reward? Not when the reward is the kind that belongs to the deed. A man who marries a woman for her money is mercenary; a man who marries her for love and is rewarded with her company is not, because the reward is the very thing he loved. What Christ promises is of that second kind: his “well done”, his joy and more of himself (Matthew 25:21). Nor does the reward turn grace into wages. Even the servant who has done everything he was told can only say that he has done his duty (Luke 17:10); whatever he is given is more than he is owed. So the religious man who hopes to put God in his debt and the sceptic who thinks rewards make faith grubby are answered by the same truth: the Lord repays, but he repays as a Father delighting in his children, not as an employer settling an account.

For worship. The woman who has cared for a parent with dementia for six years; the believer who served one small church for thirty years and whose name is in no history: none of it was thrown away. He who has numbered the hairs of your head (Matthew 10:30) keeps a fuller record of your love than you do, and on that day he will read it back to you with joy.

verseByVerse.quote: Masters, do the same to them, and stop your threatening, knowing that he who is both their Master and yours is in heaven, and that there is no partiality with him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Masters, do the same to them. Paul has spent four verses telling slaves how to work. He turns to the owners and says: the same. Not a softer set of rules made for masters. In plain words: treat your slaves as people you serve for Christ’s sake, sincerely and with good will, whether or not anyone is watching, because Christ will repay you too.

And stop your threatening. The master’s usual instrument was not so much the whip as the constant possibility of it: beatings, being sold away from family, harder work. A household can be run for years on fear without a blow landing. The modern equivalent is rarely a threat spoken aloud: the review used as leverage, the public dressing-down aimed at everyone else in the room, the displeasure never stated and always available. It reliably produces compliance. Paul forbids it, not because it does not work, but because it does to a person what God does not do to you.

Knowing that he who is both their Master and yours is in heaven. The Greek word for “master” and for “Lord” is the same, kyrios. The slave has a master; the master has one too, and it is the same Lord over both. Before that throne the slave and the slaveholder stand side by side, and the master will answer to Christ for how he treated his slaves (Colossians 4:1). On leadership as accountable service in every sphere, see on Ephesians 5:21.

The Master who did not threaten. Peter, writing to slaves with harsh masters, points to the one Master who had every right to threaten and never did: “when he suffered, he did not threaten, but continued entrusting himself to him who judges justly” (1 Peter 2:23). Legions of angels were a word away (Matthew 26:53), and he used none of them to frighten anyone into compliance. He ruled by laying his life down. That is the Master in heaven to whom every earthly master answers, and a man who rules by fear rules in the way his own Lord refused to rule.

And that there is no partiality with him. The word (prosōpolēmpsia) comes from the Hebrew picture of lifting the face: a judge raising a man’s face to see who he is before deciding his case. God does not lift the face (Deuteronomy 10:17; Acts 10:34; James 2:1–9): he does not check who is important before he decides. A master was used to his rank settling things in his favour. In God’s court, whose verdict is the final one, rank counts for nothing, and a man who has used his rank to frighten the weak has reason to tremble. That is why this short verse had consequences out of all proportion to its length. Once two men believe they have one Lord and one impartial Judge, and sit at one table and call each other brother, slavery has lost its foundation. It took far too long, and Christians defended the indefensible for generations, but many of the arguments that brought it down were built from verses like this.

In everyday life. Almost everyone has power over someone: a parent over a child, an elder over a church, a customer over the person serving him, a healthy adult over an ageing relative. So ask: how do you speak to someone who cannot answer back, and has no way of making it cost you anything? That is the one situation in which nothing but character is at work.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The letter turns to the battle behind all of life. Believers stand against the devil in the Lord’s strength, wearing God’s own armour piece by piece, and the whole of it is worn in watchful prayer for all the saints and for Paul.
verseByVerse.theology:
Spiritual warfare and the victory of Christ

The Christian fights from victory, not towards it. At the cross and resurrection Christ disarmed the rulers and authorities (Colossians 2:15). The powers of 6:12 are real and active, but they are defeated enemies working under the authority of the one who conquered them.

That is why Paul’s word is “stand”, not “advance”. Standing is not passive: it needs every piece of armour and every prayer. But it is confident, because those who stand know how the battle ends.

Prayer is the air the armoured Christian breathes (vv. 18–20). And Paul’s request that the church pray for his boldness shows that preaching the gospel is itself part of the battle, needing courage the Spirit gives, not only careful preparation.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The Ephesian Christians had seen the powers at work in their own city (Acts 19). When Paul told them to stand against the spiritual forces of evil, he was arming people who had already been in the fight.

Now: Christians today are tempted either to explain the powers away as a picture of human sin, or to see a demon behind every difficulty. Paul avoids both: the powers are real but defeated, and the Christian response is to stand, in truth, righteousness, the gospel, faith, salvation, the word of God and constant prayer.

verseByVerse.quote: Finally, be strong in the Lord and in the strength of his might.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Finally. The last section of the letter (vv. 10–20) gathers everything up: the church, God’s new people, called to unity and holiness, living the gospel at home and at work, is in a spiritual war. And look at what Paul has just been talking about: telling the truth, anger, honest work, words, husbands and wives, parents and children, employers and workers. Then: “Finally, be strong.” The armour is issued for that arena, not for spiritual specialists. The war is fought over whether a man speaks kindly to his wife on a Thursday evening.

Be strong in the Lord. The verb is passive: be strengthened, go on being made strong, like “be filled with the Spirit” (5:18). And nobody says “be strong” to a strong person. The command assumes weakness; if you feel you do not have what it asks for, you have understood it. In plain words: you are not told to find strength inside yourself, but to receive his. And it is “in the Lord”. This strength is not like fuel poured into you that then runs low. It comes from where you are: joined to Christ, so that what is true of him, raised and seated above every power (1:20–21), is counted true of you (2:6). That is why the chapter’s whole demand will be that you stay where you are and do not move. His strength is drawn on not by working up a feeling but by leaning on him, as a branch draws its life from the vine (John 15:5).

And in the strength of his might. Paul uses three words for power that he used in 1:19–20, of the power that raised Christ from the dead. So the strength on offer is not a general assurance that God will help you cope. It is measured, and the measure is a resurrection. The power that brought a dead man out of a sealed tomb is named here, and its direction is towards us who believe. It arrives by his Spirit, strengthening us with power in the inner being (3:16).

verseByVerse.quote: Put on the whole armor of God, that you may be able to stand against the schemes of the devil. For we do not wrestle against flesh and blood, but against the rulers, against the authorities, against the cosmic powers over this present darkness, against the spiritual forces of evil in the heavenly places.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Put on. The clothing picture again (4:22–24): putting on the new self, and now the armour. The armour is not an extra added to the Christian life; it is the Christian life itself, lived in Christ.

The whole armour of God. Panoplia: the full equipment of a heavily armed soldier, not selected pieces but the whole kit. Paul may have looked at the Roman soldier chained to him (Acts 28:16, 20) as he wrote. But the picture comes first from Isaiah, where the LORD “put on righteousness as a breastplate, and a helmet of salvation on his head” (Isaiah 59:17), and where the Messiah wears righteousness and faithfulness as his belt (Isaiah 11:5). The armour of God is God’s own armour, worn first by Christ and now given to his people.

That you may be able to stand. The aim is to stand, to hold one’s ground, not to advance and conquer new territory. Christ has already won (1:20–22; Colossians 2:15). The church holds the ground he has won.

Against the schemes of the devil. “Schemes” (methodeia) are strategies, patient cunning (4:14). The devil rarely attacks head-on. He accuses. He is “the accuser of our brothers” (Revelation 12:10), and his verdict is always the same: “God could not love someone who did what you did.” So believers go over and over sins that Christ has already paid for at the cross. He deceives with near-truths, beginning as in Eden with a question: “Did God actually say?” (Genesis 3:1). He distracts, filling a life with good and neutral things until there is no room for prayer and Scripture. And he discourages, as with Elijah under the broom tree after his greatest victory (1 Kings 19). None of it is dramatic. A new believer, ashamed of a returning sin, stops telling anyone, reads his Bible less because he feels unclean, and drifts from his group: accused into silence. A committed professional misses church in the second year of a demanding job, and by the third lives as if God were absent: no attack anyone noticed, just the sum of reasonable compromises.

For we do not wrestle against flesh and blood. “Wrestle” (palē) is hand-to-hand combat: close, personal and exhausting. And the opponent is not human beings. The persecutor, the critic, the false teacher and the hostile government are not our real enemies. They are captives of the enemy, people to be won (2 Timothy 2:25–26). Paul himself had been a persecutor.

But against the rulers, against the authorities. The same words as in 1:21 and 3:10: ranks of spiritual beings, what the Bible elsewhere calls the devil and his angels: personal, intelligent, organised in rank and command, whose hatred is aimed at God, at Christ and at his people. Not mere figures of speech for human evil or political systems, though they work through those.

Against the cosmic powers over this present darkness. Literally world-rulers of this darkness: evil spirits who influence this fallen world (2:2; John 12:31; 1 John 5:19). The Ephesians did not need persuading. They had seen the sons of Sceva, who tried to use the name of Jesus as a technique and were overpowered (Acts 19:13–16); converts burning their magic books in public; and a riot that filled the theatre for two hours (Acts 19:23–41). These readers had watched the powers behave like something with a will.

Against the spiritual forces of evil in the heavenly places. The heavenly places (see 1:3) are the unseen realm. Evil powers operate there, but Christ is seated far above them (1:20–21), and believers are seated with him (2:6). The battle is real, but it is fought from a throne already won.

What it does not mean. Not that every problem is directly caused by a demon, or that we are not responsible for our sins. Three things work together against us (2:1–3): the world around us, our own sinful desires (which the Bible calls the flesh), and the devil. There are two ways to go wrong. One is to empty the passage, treating the powers as a first-century way of talking about social pressures, so that the armour is a metaphor for trying harder. The other is to become preoccupied: treating depression, illness, marital strain or plain sin as an attack requiring deliverance instead of a doctor, repentance or a hard conversation. C. S. Lewis warned of the same two errors: disbelieving in devils, and taking an excessive and unhealthy interest in them. Paul does not tell anyone to hunt these beings, address them, name them or bind them. He says put your armour on and stand.

Is belief in a personal devil not a relic of a pre-scientific age? Science can weigh and measure; it cannot tell us whether there are minds other than human ones. And the evil of the modern world has not looked less purposeful for all our science: the organised cruelty of the last century, patient, inventive and far beyond any one man’s malice, looks less like an accident than like something with a strategy. Jesus, who understood the human heart better than anyone, spoke of the devil as real and personal (John 8:44), and he is a surer guide than the fashions of any age. That will not settle the question for someone who does not yet trust Jesus, but it is the honest ground a Christian stands on. And the Christian view is less frightening, not more. The devil is a creature, not God’s equal; he can go no further than God allows (Job 1:12), and at the cross he was disarmed (Colossians 2:15).

Where Christians differ: spiritual warfare. Some deliverance ministries focus on identifying, naming and binding territorial spirits over cities, or casting demons out of believers. Others, influenced by modern scepticism, neglect the battle altogether. This commentary’s view: the battle is real, but the weapons Paul names are not special techniques. They are the ordinary means of grace, the everyday ways God strengthens his people: truth, righteousness, the gospel, faith, salvation, the word and prayer. A Christian doing those seven things is fully equipped whether or not he ever identifies one of his attackers. Can a Christian be possessed? No. A believer is indwelt by the Holy Spirit and sealed as God’s own (1:13–14); God has delivered us from the domain of darkness (Colossians 1:13); and he who is in you is greater than he who is in the world (1 John 4:4). A Christian can be tempted, deceived and attacked, and must resist; he cannot be owned or inhabited by a demon. And territorial spirits? Daniel shows that spiritual powers are bound up with earthly kingdoms (Daniel 10:13), but Daniel did not name or bind them; he prayed and fasted, and an angel did the fighting. Scripture never commands believers to map or address such spirits. Many who practise deliverance ministry do so out of real compassion for the oppressed; the point is that the armour Paul actually gives is enough.

Should I speak to the devil, or rebuke him by name? Scripture gives little encouragement to it. Even the archangel Michael would not pronounce judgment on the devil himself, but said, “The Lord rebuke you” (Jude 1:9). Jesus did speak to Satan in the wilderness, briefly, and only with Scripture (Matthew 4:10). The New Testament’s instruction is not to address the enemy but to resist him: “Submit yourselves therefore to God. Resist the devil, and he will flee from you” (James 4:7). The order matters: submitting to God comes first. So when you sense an attack, turn and talk to your Father, not to your accuser. Confess any sin, take hold of a promise, say it aloud, and get on with the next act of obedience. The devil is not moved by the volume of our commands, but he cannot stand against Christ, in whom you stand.
verseByVerse.note: Paul may have written with a Roman soldier guarding him.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore take up the whole armor of God, that you may be able to withstand in the evil day, and having done all, to stand firm.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Therefore. Because the enemy is real and powerful (v. 12). A soldier told he faces a trained, organised, heavily armed enemy does not debate whether to put on his armour.

Take up. Paul changes the verb. In verse 11 it was “put on”, the word for getting dressed. Here it is “take up” (analabete): a soldier shouldering his equipment at the call to battle. The purpose is “that you may be able to withstand” (antistēnai), the root of “resist the devil” (James 4:7).

The whole armour of God. And it is “of God”, which answers the anxiety this chapter always raises. Every piece is a description of God himself before it is a description of you: his truth, his righteousness, his gospel, his salvation, his word. You are not asked to manufacture six spiritual qualities and hope they are strong enough. You are handed his.

In the evil day. The whole present age is evil (5:16; Galatians 1:4), but within it come particular days, and they rarely announce themselves. Sometimes it is the phone call at an odd hour, the scan, the sentence from a spouse that reorganises everything. Quite as often it is the afternoon a temptation arrives with a force it has never had, or the week God goes silent and prayer feels like talking to the ceiling. And note the order: take up the armour that you may be able to withstand in that day. No soldier wants to be buckling on armour in the middle of an assault. What holds a Christian upright in a crisis is the reading done in unremarkable weeks, the praying that became a habit before it was needed, the confession kept short, the friends who already had permission to ask hard questions.

And having done all, to stand firm. Paul has described a cosmic war and issued a full set of divine armour, and the objective, stated four times in this paragraph and never upgraded, is that you should still be on your feet at the end. Not that you should have won or seen results; that you should not have fallen over. There are years in which nothing gets better: the marriage is still hard, the depression has not lifted, the prayer is still unanswered. Paul’s word for a man in that condition, if he is still there, still believing, still coming back, is victory. Standing is not a consolation prize. It is the objective.

The hour of darkness. There was one evil day above all others. In Gethsemane Jesus said to those who came for him, “this is your hour, and the power of darkness” (Luke 22:53). Every power this passage names was given its moment and spent it on him: betrayal, desertion, false witness, mockery and the cross. He had prayed while his friends slept, he went into that day equipped, and he stood. When it was over he had not fallen; he had finished (John 19:30). Our evil days are small beside his, and they are fought on ground he has already held.

What it does not mean. Not that believers can lose their salvation if they fail to stand. God keeps his people (1:13–14; John 10:28–29), and he keeps them precisely by giving them this armour and the will to wear it. But neither may believers be careless: God’s keeping works through our watchful perseverance, not apart from it (Philippians 2:12–13).

Should I pray on the armour, piece by piece, every morning? You may, and many Christians find it a helpful pattern, so long as it never becomes a charm, as though forgetting the words left you unprotected. The armour is not put on by naming it but by doing what each piece means. So ten quiet minutes in the morning might look like this: read a passage of Scripture and carry one verse into the day (the sword); confess anything specific, and thank God that you stand in Christ’s righteousness, not your own (the breastplate); resolve to be honest in everything today (the belt); remind yourself of the gospel in a sentence (the shoes and the helmet); and ask for help with the temptation or worry you can already see coming (the shield). Then on Monday at eleven, when the email lands, you will have something in your hand. Armour is worn by being used.

verseByVerse.quote: Stand therefore, having fastened on the belt of truth,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Stand therefore. The fourth “stand” (see v. 13). In the Greek it is the main verb, and what follows, having fastened, having put on, having shod, taking up, hangs from it. So the armour is not a row of tasks to complete before you are allowed to stand; it describes what standing consists of. A man wearing these things is a man standing.

Having fastened on the belt. Literally having girded your loins. Before fighting a Roman soldier gathered up his tunic and tucked it into a strong leather belt, so it would not catch, and the belt also held the sword and the lower armour in place. Without it, everything else hung loose.

Of truth. Isaiah says the Messiah will wear faithfulness as the belt of his loins (Isaiah 11:5). Two sides: the truth of God’s word, the gospel (1:13), and personal truthfulness, an undivided life (4:25). And truth here has a face: “the truth is in Jesus” (4:21). So fastening this belt is not chiefly an intellectual achievement. It is staying close to a Person, and letting his account of things overrule yours.

Why first? Because of who the enemy is. Jesus named his native language: “he is a liar and the father of lies” (John 8:44). Deception is almost his whole armoury. Accusation is a lie about your standing; temptation a lie about what will satisfy you; discouragement a lie about what God is doing. So the first piece answers the first thing thrown at you. A man who cannot tell what is true will not know he is being attacked at all.

The relief of one story. Integrity is a demand, but it is first a relief. A man maintaining two versions of himself is remembering which account he gave to whom, steering conversations away from certain subjects, never fully present with people who love him. He is tired in a way sleep does not touch; David, keeping silent about his sin, said his bones wasted away (Psalm 32:3). A man with one story has nothing to maintain. And the belt carried the sword, the word of God (v. 17): a man cannot draw with conviction on a word he is not living in. The enemy has nothing to say to a man with nothing to hide. And in Christ, who is the truth, there is no shading and no second story; he knows us completely and has not withdrawn his love, so that we who were liars may live with nothing left to hide.

What it does not mean. Not that we must have every theological question answered before we can stand. The belt is the central truth of the gospel, held firmly, and an honest life, and truth is held in love (4:15). And you cannot put right a dishonesty you cannot see. The lies we tell ourselves are the hardest to catch, because we already believe them (Jeremiah 17:9), which is why in practice the belt usually needs another person: someone in your life with permission to tell you what they see.

In everyday life. Watch for shading over the next seven days: the figure rounded in your favour, the false impression you did not correct, the story of the meeting in which you come out slightly better than you did. Count them instead of defending them, and confess them to the one who already knows (1 John 1:9). The belt loosens a notch at a time, and every notch is deniable.
verseByVerse.note: The soldier’s belt held his tunic and sword in place.

parallels.desc: righteousness shall be the belt of his waist

verseByVerse.quote: and having put on the breastplate of righteousness,
verseByVerse.commentary:
The breastplate. Some twenty pounds of iron on the torso, with one job: keeping iron out of the heart and lungs. A soldier could fight on with most wounds; what no soldier survived was a blade through the chest. So the piece tells you where the serious blows land: on the heart, the centre from which the whole life is run (Proverbs 4:23).

Of righteousness. Again from Isaiah 59:17, where the LORD puts on righteousness as a breastplate when he comes to save. Righteousness means being right with God and doing what is right. Which does Paul mean?

First, imputed righteousness. The righteousness of Christ credited to believers by faith (Romans 3:21–26; 2 Corinthians 5:21; Philippians 3:9). God counts Christ’s perfect obedience and his death for sin as ours, and on that ground declares us righteous in his sight (Romans 4:5–6). The holy God does not pretend we are good; he credits us with the goodness of his Son. And here is why it matters. The shield (v. 16) is for darts, and darts are lies. But not every accusation against a Christian is a lie. The charge that undoes people is very rarely a fabrication. It is a fact, correctly dated, brought up at the worst moment: “You did that; you know you did.” A defence that depends on the charge being untrue fails the first time the charge is true. Watch how Paul handles the same moment: “Who shall bring any charge against God’s elect? It is God who justifies. Who is to condemn? Christ Jesus is the one who died” (Romans 8:33–34). He does not say nobody has anything on you. He points to the judge, and to the one at the judge’s side. The judge is the God who has already declared you right. Beside him is Christ, who died for the very thing you are charged with. In plain words: when the accusation is true, the answer is not “I did not do it” but “Christ died for it”. The breastplate does not argue about the charge sheet; it stands between the charge sheet and your heart, and it is made of somebody else’s obedience.

Second, practical righteousness. A life of holiness and integrity (4:24; 5:9). If the plate is Christ’s, what does my own holiness protect? Not your standing; that never rested on it. What deliberate, unconfessed sin costs you is your confidence, the thing that keeps a man on his feet. Paul has already warned about this: “give no opportunity to the devil” (4:27). A sin you keep is a place for him to stand in your life, and he will use it. The plate is Christ’s; doing up the straps, living it out day by day, is yours, and a man in excellent armour can still leave a buckle undone. And every piece Paul names is for a man facing the enemy. There is no provision anywhere for a man who turns and runs.

This commentary’s view: both. Imputed righteousness is the foundation: our standing before God rests on Christ alone. Practical righteousness flows from it and protects us in the daily fight. One answers the accuser; the other gives him no opening.

What it does not mean. Not that we must achieve a perfect life before we can resist the devil. When we fail, the remedy is not to give up but to confess and stand again in Christ’s righteousness (1 John 1:9; 2:1–2). And armour is not a feeling. Iron does not feel like anything; you find out it was there when the blow lands and you are still standing. But do not swing the other way. A man who reasons that Christ’s righteousness covers him, so how he lives does not matter, has misread Paul. Your record cannot make you right with God, but how you live still matters.

For worship. At the decisive battle, the cross, the LORD who wears this armour in Isaiah 59 went out wearing none of it: no breastplate, nothing over the chest. And when he had died, a soldier put a spear into his side (John 19:34), at exactly the height the plate would have covered. He went unarmoured at the one point Paul tells you never to leave open. That is where your breastplate came from. He had nothing over his heart, so that you would.

parallels.desc: he put on righteousness as a breastplate

verseByVerse.ref: v. 15 — The Shoes of the Gospel of Peace
verseByVerse.quote: and, as shoes for your feet, having put on the readiness given by the gospel of peace.
verseByVerse.commentary:
As shoes for your feet. Roman soldiers wore the caliga, a heavy sandal-boot with nail-studded soles for grip on rough ground. In close combat the enemy first tries not to wound you but to knock you off balance, because a man who has lost his footing can be finished at leisure. That is how the attacks of this chapter work. They rarely come as an argument you cannot answer. They come as a shove: an accusation, a disappointment, a fear.

Having put on the readiness. “Readiness” (hetoimasia) can mean preparedness to move, or a prepared base, a firm footing. Two readings: (1) the stability the gospel gives, so that we stand without slipping; or (2) readiness to go and share the gospel. This commentary’s view: the context of standing (vv. 11–14) favours firm footing first; but those who stand firm on the gospel of peace are also ready to share it. A man with no footing cannot go anywhere, and a man going nowhere did not need boots.

Given by the gospel of peace. Isaiah supplies the picture: “How beautiful upon the mountains are the feet of him who brings good news, who publishes peace” (Isaiah 52:7). A city waits on the outcome of a battle fought out of sight, and then a runner comes over the ridge, and long before he can be heard they can tell from the way he runs what he carries. Feet are not beautiful in themselves; they are beautiful because of what is arriving on them. The herald is not proposing terms; he is reporting a result, settled before he set off. That is what gospel means. And this letter has already named the first herald: Christ himself “came and preached peace to you who were far off and peace to those who were near” (2:17), on feet that would be nailed to a cross to make the peace he announced. When Christians lose their footing in evangelism, it is often because they think they are arguing a case that might be lost, instead of running with a report that is already true. We do not fight to win peace with God. Our war with him is over, and that finished peace is the ground we stand on while we fight.

Peace with God, and feeling peaceful. A believer unsure of his standing has no footing, and an anxious reader may hear: “If you do not feel peaceful, you do not have the shoes on.” That is not Paul’s meaning. Peace with God (Romans 5:1) is not a mood but a state of affairs: the ending of a war, declared from the other side, on the basis of what Christ did. The peace of God (Philippians 4:7) is a felt thing, and it comes and goes with sleep, health and circumstance. You can have the first at full strength while feeling almost none of the second. A treaty ends a war whether or not the soldiers feel calm that morning, and a Christian lying awake at three in the morning with a tight chest is standing on ground not one inch less solid. And note the verb: “we have peace with God”. Signed, and not by you.

What it does not mean. Not that Christians are aggressive towards people: the gospel we carry is a gospel of peace, and our war is against the devil, not human beings (v. 12). And “readiness” is not a rebuke telling you to hunt conversations. Peter says, always being prepared to make a defence to anyone who asks you for a reason for the hope that is in you (1 Peter 3:15). Notice the word “asks”: often the other person begins, and your part is simply to be ready when they do.

For worship. The oldest promise in the Bible is about feet: the woman’s offspring would crush the serpent’s head, though his own heel would be struck (Genesis 3:15). Christ took that wound and struck that blow, and “the God of peace will soon crush Satan under your feet” (Romans 16:20). The feet the enemy keeps trying to sweep from under us are the very feet God means to set on his head.
verseByVerse.note: Roman soldiers wore sturdy studded sandals for a firm footing.

parallels.desc: the feet of him who brings good news, who publishes peace

verseByVerse.quote: In all circumstances take up the shield of faith, with which you can extinguish all the flaming darts of the evil one.
verseByVerse.commentary:
In all circumstances. Or “in addition to all these”, “over all these”. The great shield was not strapped to the body; it was held out in front, and everything else was behind it. And the verb changes: the first three pieces are put on, worn even in camp; from now on they are taken up, seized when the alarm went.

The shield. The Roman scutum: about four feet tall, wood covered with leather, covering the whole body. Soldiers could lock their shields side by side and overhead into a wall, protecting the whole unit. Faith is not only individual: believers protect one another.

Of faith. Trust in God: in his character, his promises and his Son, not faith in faith (Psalm 18:30; 1 John 5:4).

With which you can extinguish. It is often said that before battle soldiers soaked the leather in water, so that burning arrows were put out when they struck, and the picture fits what faith is. “Faith comes from hearing, and hearing through the word of Christ” (Romans 10:17): the hide is soaked in Scripture over time, so that when the fire arrow lands there is already something in the leather that puts it out. Nobody soaks a shield while arrows are in the air, and that is the honest reason many Christians find their faith apparently useless at two in the morning. The shield was fine. It was dry.

All the flaming darts of the evil one. Arrows tipped with cloth soaked in pitch and set alight. A fire arrow does not need to hit anything vital. It only has to lodge somewhere and start something. That is how the sleepless thought works: one suggestion catches another until you lie there with a whole case built against yourself, or against God, that you would never have accepted as a single sentence. The darts are doubts about God’s goodness, accusations that you are beyond forgiveness, sudden temptations, fears, despair, blasphemous thoughts. And “all”: there is no dart faith cannot put out.

How faith extinguishes. By answering the lie with God’s truth. When the dart says, “God does not love you,” faith answers: he “loved me and gave himself for me” (Galatians 2:20). When it says, “You are too sinful,” faith answers: “There is therefore now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus” (Romans 8:1).

What it does not mean. Not that a believer who has fiery thoughts is failing. The arrival of the thought is not your sin; you did not fire it. The blasphemous, filthy or despairing thing that lands out of nowhere is not evidence of what you secretly are. It becomes yours only when you agree with it and give it a place to burn. The horror you feel at it is the sound of the shield. Nor must faith be strong to work. Faith does not save by its own strength; it is the empty hand that takes hold of Christ, who saves. Weak faith in a strong Christ is safe. That is why the most useful prayer in the Gospels came from a father whose faith was failing in public: “I believe; help my unbelief!” (Mark 9:24). Jesus did not send him away to work on his conviction. He healed the boy.

In everyday life. Many Christians are hit by the same two or three arrows for years: “You are a fraud”; “God is disappointed in you”; “Nothing will ever change.” Write down the one sentence that lands most often, in the words it uses on you. Unnamed, it feels like the truth; written down, it looks like what it is. Then find the verse that answers it and learn it before the next time. And there will be a stretch of your life when you cannot lift your shield at all: be somewhere other people are holding theirs.

For worship. On the night Satan demanded to sift the disciples like wheat, Jesus told Peter: “I have prayed for you that your faith may not fail” (Luke 22:31–32). Peter’s shield dropped that night, and still his faith did not finally fail, because it was held from the other side. The same Lord always lives to make intercession for those who draw near to God through him (Hebrews 7:25). The hand that lifts the shield is weak; the hand that holds that hand is not.
verseByVerse.note: The Roman shield was large, about four feet tall, wood covered with leather; soldiers could lock shields into a wall.

parallels.desc: he is a shield for all those who take refuge in him

verseByVerse.quote: and take the helmet of salvation,
verseByVerse.commentary:
And take. The verb (dexasthe) means receive, accept what is being handed to you. You do not forge a helmet. It is issued, and the soldier’s whole responsibility is to put out his hands and take it. Salvation is God’s gift (2:8).

The helmet. Bronze or iron, with cheek-pieces, protecting the head, the seat of thought and decision. A blow that did not kill could still stun a soldier and leave him helpless. Despair is a head wound. It rarely kills a Christian outright; it persuades him that standing is pointless, and a man who believes that will put his shield down himself.

Of salvation. Again from Isaiah 59:17: Paul takes the armour off the Divine Warrior himself and buckles it onto ordinary Christians in Ephesus. In 1 Thessalonians 5:8 he calls it “the hope of salvation”. We have been saved (2:5, 8), are being kept, and will be saved at the day of redemption (4:30), and the helmet covers the mind with all three: “he who began a good work in you will bring it to completion” (Philippians 1:6).

Why the mind? The devil attacks the mind with doubt: are you really saved? Will you really make it? Is any of this true? The helmet guards the mind with the knowledge that salvation is God’s work, not ours, and is secure. A soldier who knows the outcome of the war is already settled fights differently from one who fears defeat. My salvation does not depend on my grip on God, but on his grip on me (John 10:28–29).

Salvation has a name. In the end the helmet is not a doctrine but a Person: “you shall call his name Jesus, for he will save his people from their sins” (Matthew 1:21), and Simeon, holding the baby, said, “my eyes have seen your salvation” (Luke 2:30). A believer whose thoughts are reeling needs, before any argument, to lift his eyes to the one whose name means the LORD saves.

Where assurance comes from. God intends you to have it: John wrote so “that you may know that you have eternal life” (1 John 5:13). It comes from three places, and anxious believers usually have the order backwards. First and chiefly, the promise of God, which stands outside you and does not move: “whoever comes to me I will never cast out” (John 6:37). Second, the witness of the Spirit, who “bears witness with our spirit that we are children of God” (Romans 8:16): not usually a voice, but the settled instinct that makes a frightened person say “Father”. Third, the evidences of grace in a changed life. That third is genuine (2 Peter 1:10), but it is the only one that looks inward, and the least readable when you are lowest, and it is the one a troubled Christian spends all night on. A man who keeps digging up the seed to see whether it has sprouted ends with no plant and no assurance. Look at Christ first and yourself third.

When assurance has gone. Ask honestly which of two things has happened. Sometimes there is something specific, done, or left undone, or being quietly kept, and the conscience is doing its proper work. The answer is not more introspection but confession, and the relief is often immediate. But sometimes there is nothing specific, only fog. Then remember that the soul is attached to a body. Grief, exhaustion, illness and depression all lie, in your own voice, about God’s attitude towards you. A Christian who has not slept properly for a fortnight should be very slow to trust his own assessment of his standing before God. God sent an angel to Elijah under the broom tree with food and a second sleep before one word of correction (1 Kings 19:5–8).

In everyday life. Finish this sentence honestly: when ______ happens, I will be all right. When the scan is clear; when he calls; when the money is in place. Whatever fills the blank is the helmet you are actually wearing, the thing you trust to keep you safe, and every one of those can be taken away by a single phone call. The helmet Paul gives rests on what God has done and will finish, beyond the reach of anything that can happen to you this week.

parallels.desc: a helmet of salvation on his head

verseByVerse.ref: v. 17b — The Sword of the Spirit
verseByVerse.quote: and the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God,
verseByVerse.commentary:
The sword. Machaira: a short sword, like the Roman legionary’s, made for close combat, and the only offensive weapon in the list. Its size tells you where it is meant to be used: not chiefly as a missile fired at the culture from a safe distance, but in the fight eighteen inches from your face: the lie that has just arrived in your own head, the conversation you are actually in, the thing you are about to talk yourself into. Most of the enemy’s damage is done at close quarters, and God has issued a weapon of exactly that reach.

Of the Spirit. The sword is the Spirit’s. He breathed out the word (2 Timothy 3:16) and makes it effective in hearts (Hebrews 4:12). That is why it cannot be used against him: the man who uses Scripture to justify what grieves the Spirit finds the blade has an edge on both sides. The word without the Spirit is a sword in an untrained hand; the Spirit without the word is feeling cut loose from truth.

Which is the word of God. This is the only piece Paul stops to explain. He uses rhēma, often a particular saying: Scripture applied to a particular attack. Jesus showed how in the wilderness. Three times he was tempted, and three times he answered, “It is written” (Matthew 4:1–11), and all three answers come from Deuteronomy 6–8, Moses’ sermon about Israel’s forty years in the wilderness and how Israel failed at exactly those points. So the Son of God, forty days hungry, tempted where Israel collapsed, answers from the very passage that records the collapse, and wins on the same ground. And he won with about three chapters of one book. You do not need to have mastered sixty-six books before the sword is any use. You need to truly possess some of it.

Scripture corrected by Scripture. In the second temptation the devil quotes Scripture too, Psalm 91, torn from its setting. Jesus does not say the psalm is wrong; he says, “Again it is written” (Matthew 4:7), and gives another text. A promise lifted out of context and turned into a lever to make God serve your plans is answered by the rest of the Bible. That is why the whole of it must be read, and why a Christian who knows only his favourite verses carries a weapon that can be taken from him.

Defensive and offensive. The sword parries attacks, as Jesus did. But it also advances: through the preaching of the word, captives are set free (Acts 26:18). Every time the gospel is preached and someone believes, the sword has struck. It does not always bring instant results, but it does not return empty (Isaiah 55:11).

In everyday life. Jesus said the Spirit will “bring to your remembrance all that I have said to you” (John 14:26). He reminds you of what you have already taken in; he does not usually hand you a verse you have never read. So take the verse that answers the accusation that lands on you most often, and carry it until it is yours. And say it aloud when the attack comes, as Jesus did. A lie answered silently is just two thoughts meeting in one tired head. A word of God spoken aloud is something entering the room from outside you.

For worship. Of the six pieces, five are silent: they simply hold. The last thing God puts in your hand is the only one that speaks, and it is his own voice. The Word who became flesh answered the liar with it in the wilderness, and he will at last slay the lawless one with the breath of his mouth (2 Thessalonians 2:8).
verseByVerse.note: The Roman sword was a short blade for close combat.

parallels.desc: he made my mouth like a sharp sword

verseByVerse.quote: praying at all times in the Spirit, with all prayer and supplication. To that end, keep alert with all perseverance, making supplication for all the saints,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Praying at all times. The grammar ties prayer to the whole armour: the soldier stands, armed, praying. Prayer is not a seventh piece; it is the air the armoured soldier breathes, how he draws on reinforcements he cannot produce in the field. Paul says “all” four times: all times, all prayer, all perseverance, all the saints (1 Thessalonians 5:17). Prayer kept for emergencies leaves the ordinary days, where most of the battle is fought, without reinforcements.

In the Spirit. Some take this to mean praying in tongues (compare Jude 20; 1 Corinthians 14:15). But this letter has already shown what Paul means: “through him we both have access in one Spirit to the Father” (2:18). Prayer is to the Father, through the Son, in the Spirit: the whole Trinity involved in one person saying one sentence in his kitchen. As a child may walk into his father’s study while visitors wait outside, a believer may speak to God at any moment, because the Spirit has made him a son (Romans 8:15), and the Spirit helps him while he prays: “we do not know what to pray for as we ought, but the Spirit himself intercedes for us” (Romans 8:26–27). Halting prayer is therefore not second-rate prayer; it is prayer in which the weakness has already been allowed for.

With all prayer and supplication. Every kind of prayer: praise, thanks, confession. And “supplication” (deēsis) is the particular request arising from a particular need. That is the warrant for praying specifically. Name the person, the job, the scan, the son, the sum of money. God is not honoured by vagueness, and prayer that risks nothing specific can never be seen to be answered, which may be part of its appeal.

To that end, keep alert. Stay awake, like a sentry at night (agrypnountes). And a praying sentry watches the ground he has been given: which friend has gone quiet in the last two months, which marriage in your church has changed its tone, which man has stopped coming and has not been asked why. Most of this never becomes a conversation; it becomes prayer, and your prayer may be the shield he does not know he is standing behind.

The one who stayed awake. In Gethsemane Jesus asked three friends to stay awake with him, and three times he found them sleeping (Mark 14:37–41). He prayed alone: “Remove this cup from me. Yet not what I will, but what you will” (Mark 14:36). And earlier that night he had prayed for them, and for all who would believe in him through their word (John 17:20). The church keeps watch in prayer because it was saved by the one who stayed awake.

With all perseverance. Jesus told a parable to the effect that “they ought always to pray and not lose heart” (Luke 18:1–8): a widow with no standing, against a judge who neither feared God nor respected man, and her one asset was that she would not go away. Jesus is not saying God must be worn down. His point is this: if even a bad judge gave in at last, how much more will a good Father hear. The widow kept asking in spite of an unwilling judge; you keep asking because your Father is willing. And the danger Jesus names is not that God will fail to answer, but that we will lose heart, that the praying will quietly stop in the third or fourth year, even for the name that has been on your list for years.

Making supplication for all the saints. The battle is fought together. Each believer prays for others and is prayed for; a soldier who fights alone is easily picked off. Paul has modelled this in his own prayers (1:15–23; 3:14–21).

What it does not mean. Not that “praying in the Spirit” means only praying in tongues; every believer is called to pray in the Spirit. Nor does “at all times” mean continuous words. It means a heart turned towards God through the day, and regular, persevering times of prayer. And it is not a vending machine: Scripture deals honestly with the prayer that receives a no (2 Corinthians 12:8–9).

What does praying at all times look like for a busy parent? Mostly short, honest prayers woven through the day, held together by a little time set apart. With small children you may never get an unbroken half-hour, and God knows it. So pray as you go: a sentence during the nappy change, thanks over the washing-up, a cry for patience on the stairs, a blessing over a sleeping child. Nehemiah prayed in the moment between a king’s question and his own answer (Nehemiah 2:4–5). Tie prayer to things that happen anyway: the school run, the kettle, bath time. Then guard one small regular time, even five minutes before the house wakes or after it sleeps, with a Bible open. Pray aloud with your children too; they learn more from hearing you pray than from being told to. A tired parent’s scattered prayers are not second-class prayer; they are exactly what Paul means.

In everyday life. Name three Christians you find difficult, the one who wearies you, the one who was unfair to you, the one whose views you find hard to sit near, and pray for their good by name this week. You will find it very hard to go on resenting someone you are asking God to bless.

For worship. The armour never made anyone self-sufficient, and God never meant it to. Somebody prayed for you today, by name, and you will not know who in this life. The Father heard every one of those prayers, and some of what you call your own standing has been his answer to them all along.

verseByVerse.quote: and also for me, that words may be given to me in opening my mouth boldly to proclaim the mystery of the gospel, for which I am an ambassador in chains, that I may declare it boldly, as I ought to speak.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And also for me. The great apostle asks ordinary believers to pray for him. He did not see himself as above needing their prayers, and every gospel worker needs the prayers of the church.

That words may be given to me. Even Paul needed help to speak. This is the man who was stoned at Lystra and left for dead (Acts 14:19), flogged and shipwrecked (2 Corinthians 11:24–25), and he asks a church to pray that he will not lose his nerve. Courage was not a feature of his temperament; it was supplied in answer to prayer. “I was with you in weakness and in fear and much trembling,” he told Corinth (1 Corinthians 2:3), and one night the Lord said to him there, “Do not be afraid, but go on speaking” (Acts 18:9), which no one says to a man who is not afraid. So if your mouth goes dry when the conversation turns, nerves are not the absence of the Spirit.

In opening my mouth boldly. “Boldly” (en parrēsia, see 3:12): with freedom, frankness, courage. Paul was most likely writing from Rome, awaiting trial before Caesar (Acts 28:16–31), and might have been tempted to soften the message to protect himself.

To proclaim the mystery of the gospel. A mystery, in Paul, is a secret God has now made known. In this letter it is one thing in particular: that the Gentiles, the non-Jews, are fellow heirs, members of the same body (3:6). And that sentence is the reason he is in chains. The crowd in Jerusalem listened in silence until he reached the word “Gentiles”, and then demanded his death (Acts 22:21–22). He asks the church to pray that he will keep saying, boldly, the exact sentence that cost him his liberty. Not that the chain would come off; that the mouth would stay open. The gospel is worth that much, and Christ, whose ambassador he was, is worth more.

Openly, like his Lord. When Jesus stood before the high priest, he said, “I have spoken openly to the world … I have said nothing in secret” (John 18:20), with Paul’s word for “boldly”. The Lord whom Paul represents faced his own trial without softening a sentence (1 Timothy 6:13). An ambassador says what his King says, in the way his King said it.

For which I am an ambassador in chains. A deliberately shocking phrase. An ambassador could not be touched: to lay hands on another nation’s envoy was an act of war. So “ambassador in chains” ought to be impossible, and Paul says it aloud: the empire has manacled the representative of the King of kings (2 Corinthians 5:20). The chain (halysis) fastened him by the wrist to a soldier of the guard, in shifts, round the clock, and Paul says the result was that it became known throughout the whole imperial guard that his imprisonment was for Christ (Philippians 1:13). The chain meant to take him out of circulation delivered him a rotating audience of elite soldiers. It was not an interruption of the mission; it was a posting.

That I may declare it boldly, as I ought to speak. He repeats the request: it is what he most needs. “As I ought” is the language of obligation: “necessity is laid upon me. Woe to me if I do not preach the gospel!” (1 Corinthians 9:16). The boldness he wants is not bravado, but faithfulness to a commission he did not give himself and cannot resign.

What it does not mean. Not that Paul did not care about his release, or that praying for it is wrong (Philippians 1:19; Philemon 22). It is not a fault to ask for relief; but we are the poorer if relief is all we ever ask for. And God answered: Paul preached in Rome “with all boldness and without hindrance” (Acts 28:30–31).

In everyday life. Sort the prayer requests you have given people this year into two columns: things you wanted changed, and things you wanted to become or do inside what was not changing. Paul, facing a capital charge, asked for the second. And pray this for your pastor and for missionaries you know, by name: for words, for boldness, for clarity.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul closes with personal news, sent with a trusted brother, and a last blessing of peace, love, faith and grace.
verseByVerse.theology:
Grace first and last

Ephesians begins with grace (1:2) and ends with it (6:24), and that is more than a convention of letter-writing. The Christian life is grace from first to last: not God’s help added to our effort, but his own initiative towards people who could not help themselves (2:8–9), sustaining what it began (1 Corinthians 15:10).

Tychicus, the letter-carrier, shows how that grace usually travels. Churches are kept alive by faithful people whose names are rarely known, and the letter that unfolds God’s eternal purpose reached its readers in the hands of one of them.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Paul writes from prison and may never see these churches again. His closing blessing is spoken over people he cannot reach, entrusted to the God he has been describing for six chapters.

Now: The last word of the letter promises grace to all who love the Lord Jesus with an undying love. That love, planted by God, will outlast everything that perishes.

verseByVerse.quote: So that you also may know how I am and what I am doing, Tychicus the beloved brother and faithful minister in the Lord will tell you everything. I have sent him to you for this very purpose, that you may know how we are, and that he may encourage your hearts.
verseByVerse.commentary:
So that you also may know how I am. Their apostle, who had spent three years with them and wept with them at Miletus (Acts 20:31, 36–38), was in custody, and they had little way of finding out how he was: only rumour and distance and silence, and anyone who has waited for news of someone they love knows what that silence does in the small hours. So Paul, the one in chains, spends his letter-carrier on their peace of mind.

Tychicus. A believer from the province of Asia (Acts 20:4). He is named five times in the New Testament, and always he is going somewhere for somebody else. He carried this letter and Colossians (Colossians 4:7–8); later Paul sent him to Ephesus again (2 Timothy 4:12). Not one sentence he wrote survives. And he was holding on that road quite possibly the only copy in existence of the letter you have just read. Some of the richest theology in the New Testament travelled to us in the hands of a man we know almost nothing about, and it arrived because he was reliable.

The beloved brother and faithful minister in the Lord. Beloved: the language of family, not employment. And a faithful servant (diakonos): not gifted, impressive or eloquent, but faithful, the quality of a man who does what he said he would, on the day he said, whether or not anyone is watching. God’s eternal purpose is enormous, and it moves at the speed of an ordinary man keeping his word.

Will tell you everything. Some news was better carried by word of mouth than written, especially for a prisoner whose letters might be read. But Tychicus is sent not only to inform them but to “encourage your hearts”: the verb (parakaleō) means to comfort, to come alongside, from the same family as the Spirit’s title, the Helper (John 14:16). He comes to steady them.

The Faithful One behind the faithful man. Tychicus is faithful in the Lord, and the phrase points past him to Christ, “who was faithful to him who appointed him” (Hebrews 3:2). Tychicus would tell the church everything about Paul; Jesus said to his anxious friends, “all that I have heard from my Father I have made known to you” (John 15:15). The church has never been left in the dark about its Lord: he came himself as the message.
verseByVerse.note: Tychicus came from the province of Asia and carried this letter and Colossians.

verseByVerse.quote: Peace be to the brothers, and love with faith, from God the Father and the Lord Jesus Christ. Grace be with all who love our Lord Jesus Christ with love incorruptible.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Peace be to the brothers. “Brothers” includes sisters: the whole church family. And peace here is more than calm feelings. This letter has already said what it is: Christ himself is our peace (2:14–17). By his cross he ended the war between us and God, and between Jew and Gentile. It is the same peace the soldier stood on in verse 15.

And love with faith. Faith and love together, as on the first page: “your faith in the Lord Jesus and your love toward all the saints” (1:15), and in the middle: “that Christ may dwell in your hearts through faith … rooted and grounded in love” (3:17). Beginning, centre and end. Paul is not adding a new thought at the door; he asks God to keep giving them what he thanked God for at the start. Faith works through love (Galatians 5:6).

From God the Father and the Lord Jesus Christ. The same two persons named in the opening greeting (1:2), as the single source of every blessing.

Grace be with all. The last blessing of the letter, as of every one of Paul’s letters, is grace. Grace began it (1:2), was lavished upon us (1:7–8), saved us (2:5, 8) and was measured to each of us (4:7), and grace ends it. Paul is not just wishing them well; he hands back, in four words, everything six chapters have unfolded. And for six chapters he has said “you”; here he speaks about them: “Grace be with all who love our Lord”. Probably the letter was carried from church to church and read aloud in each. The last blessing is pronounced over whoever is in the room when it is read. You are in the room.

Who love our Lord Jesus Christ. Paul could have described the people grace rests on in many ways, and says only one. Not all who have understood this letter, which, after three chapters on God’s choosing of his people and the heavenly places, would be a fair worry. Not those with their doctrine straight or their household in order or their armour buckled. “All who love our Lord Jesus Christ.” It is the lowest bar in the letter and the most searching: a man can pass a doctrine exam he does not mean, and behave well for a season out of fear or habit, but nobody sustains love for a person he does not actually love (1 Corinthians 16:22; 1 Peter 1:8).

How do I know whether I love him? Scripture answers with a scene. On a beach in Galilee, a man who had three times denied knowing Jesus is asked three times whether he loves him. Peter does not appeal to his feelings, and certainly not to his record, which he has just wrecked. He appeals over his own head to the one asking: “Lord, you know everything; you know that I love you” (John 21:17). That is love for Christ on a bad day, and it is available to you. So do not ask, “Do I feel warmly towards him?” That will mostly tell you about your sleep. Ask about direction. In your worst week this year, did some part of you still want him, even while you were avoiding him? Does it still gladden you, under the numbness, to hear him spoken well of? Would you rather be near him than not? If you can say yes, however faintly, this verse describes you, and the blessing at the end of Ephesians has your name in it.

With love incorruptible. “Incorruptible” (aphtharsia) means imperishable, undying: a resurrection word, used of the body sown perishable and raised imperishable (1 Corinthians 15:42, 53–54). It may describe the love itself, a love for Jesus that does not fade, or it may describe the grace: grace that never ends (“grace in immortality”). This commentary’s view: the ESV’s reading, an undying love for Jesus, is most natural. So a Christian’s love for Christ, which today may feel thin and distracted, is made of the same material as the resurrection body: it will not be left in the grave with everything that perishes. Yet Ephesus later received a warning from the risen Christ that it had abandoned the love it had at first (Revelation 2:4). Undying love must be guarded.

My love for Christ has grown cold. How do I get it back? Do what the risen Christ told the Ephesians when their love had cooled: “Remember therefore from where you have fallen; repent, and do the works you did at first” (Revelation 2:5). Remember: go back to what first moved you, the cross, his patience with you, the forgiveness you were given, and look at it again, slowly. Repent: name whatever has crowded him out, a sin kept, a busyness, a screen, and turn from it. Do the first works: return to the simple things, reading the Gospels, praying honestly, being with his people, telling someone about him. Love is seldom restored by trying to feel it; it is rekindled by looking again at the one who loved you. “We love because he first loved us” (1 John 4:19). The fire is lit again from his, not yours.

What it does not mean. Not that grace is earned by love. The blessing describes those to whom grace has come: they love the one who gave it. The last sentence of Ephesians is not the place where the letter changes its mind and leaves you something to pay after all.

For worship. The last word Paul writes to these churches, in the Greek, is that one: imperishable. A letter that opened before the foundation of the world closes beyond the reach of decay. Nothing in it started with you, and nothing in it can rot. All of it is the grace of the Lord Jesus Christ, whose love for his church, unlike ours, has never once grown thin.

6.overview:
The household instructions continue with children and parents, then slaves and masters. In each pair Paul speaks first to the one with less power, and he puts both under one Lord: children obey and honour their parents, and fathers bring them up without crushing them; slaves work as for Christ, and masters drop their threats, because both answer to the same impartial Master in heaven. Paul does not endorse slavery; he places master and slave under one Lord, a truth that would in time help undo the institution.

Then the letter turns to the battle behind all of life (vv. 10–20). The real enemy is not people but the devil and his powers, and believers stand against him in the Lord’s strength, wearing God’s own armour (Isaiah 11:5; 59:17) and praying in the Spirit, for all the saints and for Paul, an ambassador in chains. The letter closes with news through Tychicus and a blessing of grace on all who love the Lord Jesus.
